0.title: Give Us a King: The Book of 1 Samuel
0.overview:
First Samuel is one of the most dramatic, psychologically rich, and theologically profound books in the entire Bible. It spans roughly a century of Israel's history — from the birth of Samuel under the corrupt priesthood of Eli's sons, to the tragic deterioration of Saul and the breathtaking rise of David. At its center stands a single, epoch-making demand: Give us a king like all the nations (8:5). That cry is not merely a political request; it is a theological crisis, and God's response — they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (8:7) — frames everything that follows.

The book is structured in three great movements. First, Samuel (chapters 1–7): the last judge, the transitional prophet-priest who holds a collapsing nation together by the sheer weight of his intercession and integrity. Second, Saul (chapters 8–15): the people's king, tall and impressive, chosen to satisfy human desire for outward glory, who cannot obey and cannot repent — a portrait of religion without heart. Third, David (chapters 16–31): the anointed one, the man after God's own heart, whose rise is as improbable as it is irresistible, tracked relentlessly by Saul's paranoid hatred and sustained only by covenant friendship and the Spirit of the Lord.

Christologically, 1 Samuel is a treasury. Hannah's prayer in chapter 2 is the seed of the Magnificat; her line — he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (2:10) — is the first use of mashiach in a clearly eschatological sense. Samuel embodies the triple office of prophet, priest, and judge that finds its perfect fulfillment in Jesus alone. The ark narratives (chs. 4–6) prophesy the glory departing and returning — Ichabod reversed by Emmanuel. And David: the shepherd-king, the anointed one upon whom the Spirit rushes, the champion who fights on behalf of his paralyzed people, the one who will not seize the kingdom by force — in every scene, the attentive reader sees the shape of One greater than David.

R. C. Sproul wrote that 1 Samuel shows us that God is not impressed by what impresses us. The book says it in seven words: Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (16:7). That inversion of human values — the youngest son anointed, the smooth stone over the giant's spear, the fugitive who becomes king — is the grammar of grace, and it will reach its apex when the carpenter's son from Nazareth is crowned on a cross.

1.title: The Barren Woman's Prayer
1.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Elkanah the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite.<sup>2</sup>He had two wives. The name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other, Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.<sup>3</sup>Now this man used to go up year by year from his city to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters.<sup>5</sup>But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, though the LORD had closed her womb.<sup>6</sup>And her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her, because the LORD had closed her womb.<sup>7</sup>So it went on year by year. As often as she went up to the house of the LORD, she used to provoke her. Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat.<sup>8</sup>And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, "Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?"<sup>9</sup>After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.<sup>11</sup>And she vowed a vow and said, "O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head."<sup>12</sup>As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli observed her mouth.<sup>13</sup>Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli took her to be a drunken woman.<sup>14</sup>And Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Put your wine away from you."<sup>15</sup>But Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.<sup>16</sup>Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman, for all along I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation."<sup>17</sup>Then Eli answered, "Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to him."<sup>18</sup>And she said, "Let your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.<sup>19</sup>They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD; then they went back to their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her.<sup>20</sup>And in due time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for she said, "I have asked for him from the LORD."<sup>21</sup>The man Elkanah and all his house went up to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow.<sup>22</sup>But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "As soon as the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever."<sup>23</sup>Elkanah her husband said to her, "Do what seems best to you; wait until you have weaned him; only, may the LORD establish his word." So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him.<sup>24</sup>And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. And the child was young.<sup>25</sup>Then they slaughtered the bull, and they brought the child to Eli.<sup>26</sup>And she said, "Oh, my lord! As you live, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here in your presence, praying to the LORD.<sup>27</sup>For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him.<sup>28</sup>Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there.
1.overview:
The history of Israel's kings opens with a man nobody has heard of and a woman who cannot have a child. Elkanah of Ramah goes up every year to Shiloh — which is where the house of God had stood all through the last miserable pages of Judges while nobody went near it (Judg. 18:31). The sanctuary is run by Eli's two sons, named here before we know anything about them, and by chapter 2 we will know a great deal.

Twice the narrator gives the reason for Hannah's barrenness, and it is not medical: the LORD had closed her womb. That is the foundation of everything she does. She is not appealing past her circumstances to a God who has not noticed them; she is appealing to the one who arranged them — and a womb God closed is a womb God can open.

She prays silently, and the high priest of Israel watches the most genuine worship in the building and calls it drunkenness. Her reply gives Scripture one of its best definitions of prayer: I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD. And what she asks for is a son she promises, in the same breath, to give away for life.

Then verse 18, which is the verse to take home: she went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad. She is not pregnant. She has been promised nothing. What has changed is that the weight is no longer hers. The answer comes afterwards — and she carries it up the hill and hands it over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A House Divided, and a Womb Closed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elkanah of Ramah goes up year by year to worship at Shiloh, where Eli's two sons are priests (vv. 1-3). He has two wives: Peninnah, who has children, and Hannah, whom he loves and who has none (vv. 2, 4-5). Twice in two verses the narrator gives the reason, and it is not medical: the LORD had closed her womb (vv. 5-6). Peninnah provokes her over it year after year, and always on the way up to the house of the LORD, until Hannah weeps and will not eat (vv. 6-7). Elkanah's comfort is am I not more to you than ten sons? (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 3 carries the first appearance in the Bible of the title LORD of hosts — the God of armies, of every power in heaven and earth — and it arrives in a sentence about a man's yearly walk to a country sanctuary.
verseByVerse.examples: Shiloh is where the house of God stood while the whole appendix of Judges walked past it (Judg. 18:31). The last book ended with nobody going. This one opens with a man who went every year, and with the two sons who were ruining the place named in the same breath.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Elkanah the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite. He had two wives. The name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other, Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children. Now this man used to go up year by year from his city to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'There was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Elkanah the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite.'

The book of the kings of Israel opens with a man nobody has heard of.

No throne, no army, no prophet, no crisis. A certain man, from a town with a double-barrelled name, in the hill country, with four generations of ancestors listed so that we know he is somebody's son and not a symbol. Ramathaim-zophim is simply Ramah, the height, and it will be Samuel's home town and his grave for the rest of the book.

'He had two wives. The name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other, Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.'

Nine words for the situation, and the last four are the wound.

Two wives is already a household with a fault line through it, and Scripture has never once shown that arrangement working. Sarah and Hagar, Leah and Rachel, and now Peninnah and Hannah: the same story of a fruitful wife and a loved one, and the misery that runs between them.

The narrator does not moralise about the polygamy. He states it and lets the next seven verses do the work.

'Now this man used to go up year by year from his city to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.'

Two things in this verse repay a stop, and the first is the address.

Shiloh. If you have just come through the book of Judges you have met that name once, in its last miserable pages, and in a sentence designed to indict everybody: the Danites set up their stolen idol and kept it as long as the house of God was at Shiloh (Judg. 18:31). The real sanctuary, the ark, the appointed priesthood, all standing a few miles up the road while a whole tribe walked past it to worship something they could carry.

Judges ended with nobody going to Shiloh. First Samuel opens with a man who goes every year.

The second thing is a title, and it is here for the first time in the Bible: the LORD of hosts.

Yahweh Sabaoth, the LORD of armies — of the armies of Israel, of the stars, of the angelic hosts; of every power that exists, ranked and under command. It is the great name for God's total sovereign force, and it will be used by prophets and psalmists for the next thousand years.

Its first appearance in Scripture is in a sentence about an ordinary man's annual walk to a country shrine. Not a battlefield, not a throne room, not a vision. The God of all the armies there are is introduced by that name in connection with a household that cannot have a baby.

Then the last clause, which lands like a stone: where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.

Their names are given here, in the first mention of the sanctuary, before we know anything about them. By chapter 2 we will know a great deal: that they took the meat by force, that they slept with the women serving at the entrance, and that they did not know the LORD. The place Elkanah walks to every year is being run by two men who are the reason it will shortly be destroyed.

That is the world this book starts in. The worship is real, the God is the LORD of hosts, and the men in charge are ruining it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, though the LORD had closed her womb. And her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her, because the LORD had closed her womb. So it went on year by year. As often as she went up to the house of the LORD, she used to provoke her. Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat. And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, "Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, though the LORD had closed her womb.'

The sacrifice at Shiloh was a shared meal, and the portions were handed round in front of everybody.

So picture the scene as it actually happened, once a year, for years. Peninnah receives her portion, and then a portion for each son and each daughter, one after another, and the pile in front of her grows while the family watches. Hannah receives a double portion, because her husband loves her, and it is a kindness that shines a light on exactly what she has not got.

Then the narrator gives the reason, and it is the sentence the chapter turns on: the LORD had closed her womb.

Not she was unable to conceive. Not a medical note, not bad luck, and not a silence. Somebody closed it, and the narrator names him. He will say it again in the very next verse, in case we thought it was an aside.

Sit with that before going on, because it is uncomfortable and it is the foundation of everything Hannah does. The God she is about to pray to is the God who did this. She is not appealing past her circumstances to a God who has not noticed them; she is appealing to the one who arranged them.

That is precisely why there is any point in praying at all. A closed womb that God did not close is a fact to be endured. A closed womb that God closed can be opened.

'And her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her, because the LORD had closed her womb. So it went on year by year. As often as she went up to the house of the LORD, she used to provoke her. Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat.'

Note when the provoking happened.

As often as she went up to the house of the LORD. Not at home, not in the ordinary run of the week — at the feast, on the pilgrimage, in the one place and the one season set aside for rejoicing before God. Peninnah timed her cruelty to the worship.

She aimed it at the one thing Hannah could do nothing about. There is a particular kind of malice that does not invent a wound but finds the one already there and presses it, and it is usually practised by somebody who has what the other person wants.

The result is stated without drama: Hannah wept and would not eat. Year by year. This is not a bad afternoon; it is a decade or more of dreading the same festival.

Anyone who has found the church building the hardest place to be — because that is where the families are, and the babies, and the people whose lives worked out — is reading about themselves in verse 7.

'And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, "Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?"'

He means it kindly, and he is trying, and the sentence is still about him.

Three questions, all of them asking her to account for her grief, and then a fourth that offers himself as the solution. Am I not more to you than ten sons? Ten is the round number for completeness; he is saying, in effect, I am worth more than a full family, so let that be enough.

It is affection, and it is not comfort. He has answered a specific sorrow by asking her to feel differently about it, which is what most of us do when somebody we love is in pain we cannot fix.

Hannah does not answer him. The next verse has her getting up and going somewhere else.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hannah rises after the meal and prays where Eli sits by the doorpost (vv. 9-10). Her vow asks God to look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, and promises the son back for life, with no razor on his head (v. 11). She prays silently, and Eli takes her for a drunk and tells her to put her wine away (vv. 12-14). Her answer is one of the great definitions of prayer: I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD (v. 15). Eli blesses her, and she goes and eats, and her face is no longer sad (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The high priest of Israel watches genuine prayer happen in front of him and calls it drunkenness. Meanwhile his own sons are stealing the offerings, and the narrator will shortly call them worthless men — sons of Belial (2:12). Hannah's plea in v. 16 is that he would not take her for a daughter of Belial. She denies to his face being what his boys are.
verseByVerse.examples: The change comes in v. 18, and it comes before anything else does. Nothing about her situation has altered; she is not pregnant and has been given no promise beyond a blessing. She eats, and her face lifts, because she has handed the thing over.

verseByVerse.quote: After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the temple of the LORD. She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly. And she vowed a vow and said, "O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose.'

Two words, and the whole chapter turns on them.

She has been weeping and refusing food, year after year, while her husband asks her why and her rival watches. Now the meal ends and she gets up. Nobody sends her, nobody suggests it, and the narrator does not tell us she had decided anything in advance.

She takes the grief that no argument had touched and carries it into the presence of God.

'Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.'

The one detail we are given about the high priest is where he was sitting.

He is on a seat, by the doorpost, at the entrance. Hold that picture, because the book will come back to it twice: Eli is sitting when the news arrives from the battle, and he falls backwards off that same seat and dies (4:18). He is a man the narrative keeps finding in a chair by a door.

'She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.'

Three verbs, and the middle one is the point. She was in bitterness of soul, and she prayed, and she wept.

The praying is not instead of the weeping. It is not a calmer, more spiritual activity that replaces the tears once she has composed herself. The distress and the bitterness and the crying are the material she is bringing.

'And she vowed a vow and said, "O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head."'

Now hear how she addresses him: O LORD of hosts.

That title appeared for the first time in Scripture three verses ago, in the narrator's description of the sanctuary. Hannah is the first person in the Bible recorded praying to God by it. A childless woman in a provincial shrine reaches past every smaller name for God and addresses the commander of every army in heaven and earth about her own body.

She has understood the doctrine of verse 5 exactly. If the LORD closed it, then the LORD of hosts is the right person to ask.

Then the four requests, and they climb. Look on the affliction — see it. Remember me — act. Not forget your servant — the same thing said again, because she cannot stop saying it. And then, at last, the thing itself: give to your servant a son.

She calls herself your servant three times in one sentence. She does not once mention Peninnah, or ask for vindication, or point out that she has been faithful for years.

Then the vow, which is the astonishing half. I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head.

Read what she is actually asking for. Not a child to hold, to raise, to have about the house and to lean on in old age. She is asking for a son in order to give him away, permanently, from infancy, and she says so at the moment of asking. The one thing she wants is the one thing she promises not to keep.

The uncut hair is the mark of a Nazirite, the vow of Numbers 6, and the previous man in Scripture to carry it from the womb was Samson — announced by an angel to parents who were told what their son would be (Judg. 13:5). Nobody tells Hannah anything. There is no angel under a tree and no fire out of a rock. She works it out herself, kneeling on the floor of a sanctuary run by corrupt priests, and offers her unconceived child to God for life.

verseByVerse.quote: As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli observed her mouth. Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli took her to be a drunken woman. And Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Put your wine away from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli observed her mouth. Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard.'

Her prayer is silent, which was unusual enough that the narrator explains it.

Prayer in that world was spoken aloud. What Eli sees is a woman at the doorpost with her lips moving and no sound coming out, going on and on, and he watches her mouth to work out what is happening.

The narrator's phrase for it is speaking in her heart, and the words repay having, because this is where the Bible shows us prayer with the volume turned off and God still hearing every syllable.

'Therefore Eli took her to be a drunken woman. And Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Put your wine away from you."'

The high priest of Israel looks at the most genuine act of worship in the building and concludes that the woman has been drinking.

Take the failure at full weight. Eli is the senior spiritual authority in the nation. He sits at the door of the house of God. His whole office is to stand between Israel and the LORD, and when a broken woman comes and pours out her soul in front of him, he cannot tell the difference between that and drunkenness.

Nor is he gentle about it. He does not ask; he accuses, and the form of the accusation — how long will you go on being drunk — assumes a habit. He has decided the kind of woman she is.

Here is the thing that makes it worse rather than merely sad. This same Eli has two sons serving at this same sanctuary, and the next chapter will tell us what they were doing: taking the sacrificial meat by force with a three-pronged fork, and sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the tent (2:13-17, 22). He does not see that either, or not clearly enough to stop it.

A man can be extremely quick to detect sin in a stranger and extremely slow about it at his own table, and Eli is the Bible's standing example.

verseByVerse.quote: But Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD. Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman, for all along I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation." Then Eli answered, "Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to him." And she said, "Let your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD."'

She corrects the high priest, and she does it without a trace of temper.

No, my lord. The denial is flat and the address is respectful, and she does not tell him what she thinks of his discernment. She simply explains what he has been looking at.

Her explanation is one of the best definitions of prayer in Scripture: I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.

The image is a vessel being emptied. Not a request being submitted, not a form of words being performed — the whole contents of a person tipped out in God's presence until there is nothing left in the jar. That is what Eli mistook for drink, and the mistake is understandable, because a soul being poured out does not look composed.

'"Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman, for all along I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation."'

The phrase she uses is sharper in Hebrew than in English, and it repays having exactly. She asks him not to take her for a daughter of Belial — a worthless woman, a good-for- nothing.

Now hold that against the first thing the next chapter says about Eli's boys. Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD (2:12) — and the Hebrew there is sons of Belial.

The same phrase. A childless woman is pleading with the high priest not to mistake her for what his own two sons demonstrably are, and neither of them knows it as she says it.

'Then Eli answered, "Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to him."'

To his credit, he takes the correction. There is no defensiveness and no attempt to save face; he hears her, believes her, and turns his accusation into a blessing.

It is not a prophecy. He does not know what she asked for — she never told him — and he promises nothing. It is a priest doing the ordinary business of a priest: saying go in peace to somebody who came in pieces, and asking God to grant a petition whose contents he has not heard.

'And she said, "Let your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.'

There is the verse to take home from this chapter.

She went her way, and she ate, and her face was no longer sad. Notice what has not happened. She is not pregnant. She has been given no sign, no promise, no answer, no assurance beyond an old man's blessing over a request he could not hear. Nothing whatever about her situation has changed.

What has changed is that it is no longer hers to carry. She brought the whole thing in and left it there, and she went and had dinner for the first time in the story.

That is what casting your care on someone actually looks like when it works: not the arrival of what you asked for, but the departure of the weight, some considerable time before anything else moves. Peter puts it in one line, and the last three words are the whole reason it is possible: casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7).

Hannah ate her supper in a sanctuary run by two men God was about to destroy, having been called a drunk by the high priest, still childless, and her face was no longer sad.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–28 — Asked For, and Given Back
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They worship and go home, and the LORD remembered her (v. 19). Samuel is born, and Hannah explains the name: I have asked for him from the LORD (v. 20). She stays behind from the yearly pilgrimage until he is weaned (vv. 21-23), then brings him to Shiloh with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour and a skin of wine (v. 24). For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition — and so she lends him to the LORD for as long as he lives (vv. 26-28).
verseByVerse.theology: One Hebrew root runs through the ending: sha'al, to ask. She asked him, the petition was granted, and the word translated lent is built from the same root. It is also the root of the name Saul — the king this child will anoint, and then be sent to reject.
verseByVerse.examples: Weaning took two or three years in that world. She had him for that long, and then walked back down the hill without him. Everything in this book — the ark, the kingdom, David, the line to Bethlehem — runs through a woman who got exactly what she asked for and gave it away.

verseByVerse.quote: They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD; then they went back to their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her. And in due time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for she said, "I have asked for him from the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD; then they went back to their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her.'

They worship first, and then they go home, and then God acts.

The clause is the LORD remembered her, and the Hebrew verb is not about memory. God does not mislay people and then recall them. Zakar is remembering that does something — attention that moves.

Scripture uses it at the hinges. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Gen. 8:1). God remembered Rachel, and opened her womb (Gen. 30:22). God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant, and the exodus began (Ex. 2:24).

Hannah had asked him to remember me and not forget your servant. The narrator uses her own word back, and reports that it happened.

'And in due time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for she said, "I have asked for him from the LORD."'

She names him, and her explanation of the name is a piece of wordplay that runs through the rest of the book.

The verb is sha'al, to ask. I asked him from the LORD. It will come back in verse 27 when she says the LORD granted her petition, and again in verse 28 in the word translated lent, which is built from the same root.

The same root gives the name Saul.

Hold that lightly for now and keep it. This child is explained by the verb to ask, and seven chapters from now Israel will ask for a king, and the man they get will be called Asked-For, and the boy named here will anoint him and then be sent to tell him God has rejected him. The book is full of asking, and of what people get when they ask for the wrong thing.

verseByVerse.quote: The man Elkanah and all his house went up to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow. But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "As soon as the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever." Elkanah her husband said to her, "Do what seems best to you; wait until you have weaned him; only, may the LORD establish his word." So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The man Elkanah and all his house went up to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow.'

The household goes up as usual, and Elkanah has a vow of his own to settle — the text does not say what it was.

'But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "As soon as the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever."'

She stays home, and she explains why in a sentence that says exactly what she intends to do.

Weaning in that world was late by ours — commonly two years, sometimes three. What she is asking for is the whole of the time she will ever have with him under her own roof, and she is asking for it in order to hand him over at the end of it. He may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever.

There is no wavering in it. She is not buying time in the hope that the vow will lapse; she names the surrender in the same breath as the delay.

'Elkanah her husband said to her, "Do what seems best to you; wait until you have weaned him; only, may the LORD establish his word." So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him.'

Her husband agrees, and the way he agrees deserves a look.

Under the law a husband could annul his wife's vow (Num. 30:6-8). Elkanah had the legal right to cancel this and keep his son, and the boy is the child of the wife he loves, born after years of waiting. He does not use it.

Do what seems best to you. And then a short prayer that the LORD would establish his word — whether Eli's blessing, or the vow itself, or the whole business. He hands the decision to his wife and the outcome to God, and goes up to Shiloh without her.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. And the child was young. Then they slaughtered the bull, and they brought the child to Eli. And she said, "Oh, my lord! As you live, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here in your presence, praying to the LORD. For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. And the child was young.'

She keeps the vow, and she does not keep it cheaply.

A three-year-old bull is a full-grown animal at the peak of its value, and the law required only a lamb for most occasions. An ephah of flour is something over twenty pounds. This is a large sacrifice for a family from a hill village, and she has brought it with her along with the child.

Then four words the narrator did not have to write: and the child was young.

He knows what he is describing. A woman walking up to a sanctuary with an animal, a sack of flour, a skin of wine and a toddler, to leave the toddler there.

'Then they slaughtered the bull, and they brought the child to Eli.'

The bull is killed and the boy is handed over in the same sentence, and the writer does not pause between them.

'And she said, "Oh, my lord! As you live, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here in your presence, praying to the LORD."'

She reintroduces herself, because he will not remember her.

There is something quietly magnificent about the way she puts it. She does not say I am the woman you accused of being drunk, though she could, and it would be fair. She says she is the woman who was standing here praying, and leaves his mistake out of it entirely.

'"For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him."'

The prayer God heard was silent, and the answer is standing beside her holding her hand.

'"Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there.'

The word is the same root again — sha'al. Asked for, and now asked-back; the whole verse is built out of the verb that gave him his name.

The astonishing word is therefore. Not nevertheless I have lent him, not although he is all I have. Therefore. Because the LORD granted the petition, the petition goes back. The gift is returned precisely on the grounds that it was given.

Consider what she is doing as she says it. This is a woman who wept through years of festivals for one thing. She got it. And she walked it up a hill and handed it to the man who had called her a drunk, in a sanctuary staffed by two priests so corrupt that God is about to wipe out the whole family, and left it there.

She had no way of knowing what would come of it. She could not know that the boy would hear God's voice in the night while Eli slept, or judge Israel for a lifetime, or anoint two kings, or that the second of them would father a line that runs to a stable in Bethlehem. She knew only that she had asked, and been answered, and said what she would do.

The last clause of the chapter has no subject in the Hebrew that everyone agrees on — it may be Elkanah, or Samuel, or Hannah herself. And he worshiped the LORD there. Somebody, in that room, having just given away a child, worshipped.

Take the whole chapter in one movement. God closed a womb (v. 5). A woman asked him to open it (v. 11). He remembered her (v. 19). And she gave the answer back (v. 28). Everything in the two books of Samuel — the fall of Shiloh, the ark, the kingdom, Saul, David, the promise of a throne that will not end — comes out of that exchange.

She thought she was asking for a baby. She was being made the door the whole story walks through.

1.theology:
The LORD had closed her womb (vv. 5-6). Said twice, in case we took it for an aside. This is not a comfortable doctrine and it is the only reason prayer makes sense here: a closed womb that God did not close is a fact to be endured; a closed womb that God closed can be opened. Hannah prays to the God who did this, and she is right to.

The LORD of hosts (vv. 3, 11). The title appears for the first time in the Bible in this chapter, in a sentence about an ordinary man's annual walk to a country shrine — and Hannah is the first person in Scripture recorded praying to God by it. A childless woman reaches past every smaller name for God and addresses the commander of every army in heaven and earth about her own body.

Daughter of Belial (v. 16). Hannah asks the high priest not to take her for a worthless woman — and the Hebrew phrase is the one the very next chapter uses of his own sons: the sons of Eli were worthless men; they did not know the LORD (2:12). She denies to his face being what his boys are, and neither of them knows it. A man can be quick to detect sin in a stranger and slow about it at his own table.

Her face was no longer sad (v. 18). Before the pregnancy, before any promise, before anything at all had changed. What lifted was not the circumstance but the weight, because she had left it in the room. That is what casting all your anxieties on him looks like when it works, and the reason it can be done is in the same sentence: because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7).

Therefore (v. 28). Not nevertheless I have lent him, not although he is all I have. Therefore. The gift is handed back precisely on the grounds that it was given. And the whole ending is built on one root, sha'al, to ask — asked for, petition granted, lent — which is also the name Saul. Seven chapters on, Israel will ask for a king, and this child will anoint Asked-For and then be sent to reject him.
1.examples:
Then: A woman dreaded one festival a year for a decade, because the pilgrimage was where her rival could reach her and where the families and the children were all in one place. She went anyway, every year, and one year she got up from the meal and took the whole thing to God.

Now: Three things. If the church building has ever been the hardest place to walk into — because that is where the babies are, and the intact families, and the people whose lives worked out — verse 7 is about you, and verse 9 is what to do about it. If you are waiting on something God has not given, notice that Hannah's face changed at verse 18 and her son arrived at verse 20, and the order is not an accident. And if you have been given the thing you asked for, verse 28 is the harder half: she got exactly what she wanted, and handed it over, and said therefore while she did it.

2.title: The Horn of His Anointed
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And Hannah prayed and said, "My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth derides my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation.<sup>2</sup>"There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God.<sup>3</sup>Talk no more so very proudly, let not arrogance come from your mouth; for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.<sup>4</sup>The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength.<sup>5</sup>Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger. The barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn.<sup>6</sup>The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.<sup>7</sup>The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts.<sup>8</sup>He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor. For the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and on them he has set the world.<sup>9</sup>"He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness, for not by might shall a man prevail.<sup>10</sup>The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed."<sup>11</sup>Then Elkanah went home to Ramah. And the boy was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest.<sup>12</sup>Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD.<sup>13</sup>The custom of the priests with the people was that when any man offered sacrifice, the priest's servant would come, while the meat was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand,<sup>14</sup>and he would thrust it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot. All that the fork brought up the priest would take for himself. This is what they did at Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.<sup>15</sup>Moreover, before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give meat for the priest to roast, for he will not accept boiled meat from you but only raw."<sup>16</sup>And if the man said to him, "Let them burn the fat first, and then take as much as you wish," he would say, "No, you must give it now, and if not, I will take it by force."<sup>17</sup>Thus the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.<sup>18</sup>Samuel was ministering before the LORD, a boy clothed with a linen ephod.<sup>19</sup>And his mother used to make for him a little robe and take it to him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.<sup>20</sup>Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, "May the LORD give you children by this woman for the petition she asked of the LORD." So then they would return to their home.<sup>21</sup>Indeed the LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew in the presence of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>Now Eli was very old, and he kept hearing all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting.<sup>23</sup>And he said to them, "Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all these people.<sup>24</sup>No, my sons; it is no good report that I hear the people of the LORD spreading abroad.<sup>25</sup>If someone sins against a man, God will mediate for him, but if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?" But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death.<sup>26</sup>Now the boy Samuel continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the LORD and also with man.<sup>27</sup>And there came a man of God to Eli and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Did I indeed reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt subject to the house of Pharaoh?<sup>28</sup>Did I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? I gave to the house of your father all my offerings by fire from the people of Israel.<sup>29</sup>Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded for my dwelling, and honor your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of my people Israel?'<sup>30</sup>Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: 'I promised that your house and the house of your father should go in and out before me forever,' but now the LORD declares: 'Far be it from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.<sup>31</sup>Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house.<sup>32</sup>Then in distress you will look with envious eye on all the prosperity that shall be bestowed on Israel, and there shall not be an old man in your house forever.<sup>33</sup>The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart, and all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men.<sup>34</sup>And this that shall come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall be the sign to you: both of them shall die on the same day.<sup>35</sup>And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall go in and out before my anointed forever.<sup>36</sup>And everyone who is left in your house shall come to implore him for a piece of silver or a loaf of bread and shall say, "Please put me in one of the priests' places, that I may eat a morsel of bread."'"
2.overview:
Hannah has just left her only child at a sanctuary run by two men God is about to destroy, and she prays — and what comes out is a psalm with no baby in it. Ten verses, not one of them about her son. The horn, the rock, the God of knowledge who weighs what people actually do, and then the reversals: bows broken and the feeble armed, the full hiring out their labour for bread, the barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn. She has taken the most private thing that ever happened to her and stated it as a law of how God runs the world.

And the song ends somewhere nobody could have predicted. He will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed — his messiah — when Israel has no king, has not asked for one, and will be told six chapters later that asking was a rejection of God. Mary will sing this song again, line for line, and she will be carrying the king it ends on.

Then the camera turns to the altar. Eli's sons are worthless men who did not know the LORD — sons of Belial, the exact phrase Hannah begged Eli not to apply to her. They send a servant to stab a three-pronged fork into the worshippers' cooking pots, and demand raw meat before the fat is burned to God, with violence if refused. Their father hears about all of it for years, asks one question, calls it no good report, and leaves them in office.

So a man of God comes with the charge, and it is aimed at Eli, not his sons: you honour your sons above me. And the answer is the sentence to carry out of the chapter: those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Song of a Woman Who Gave Her Son Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hannah prays, and what comes out is a psalm. Her horn is exalted in the LORD; there is none holy like him and no rock like him; he is a God of knowledge who weighs what people do (vv. 1-3). Then the reversals: the bows of the mighty broken and the feeble armed, the full hiring themselves out for bread and the hungry filled, the barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn (vv. 4-5). The LORD kills and brings to life, makes poor and makes rich, lifts the needy off the ash heap to seat them with princes (vv. 6-8). And the last line reaches somewhere nobody expects: he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The song does not mention the baby. Not once. A woman who wept through a decade of festivals for one child, and got him, and has just left him at Shiloh, sings ten verses about God and none about her son.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is Hannah and Peninnah, and she has turned her own case into a law: this is simply how God runs the world. Mary will sing the same song, line for line, eleven centuries later (Luke 1:46-55) — and her son will be the anointed king this one ends on.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hannah prayed and said, "My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth derides my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation. "There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Hannah prayed and said, "My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth derides my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation."'

Before anything else, notice what is not in this song.

Ten verses are coming, and there is no baby in any of them. Not a line about how long she waited, or what he looked like, or what it cost to leave him. She has just handed over the only thing she ever asked God for, and what comes out of her is a psalm about God.

The word horn is the picture of strength in the Hebrew Bible — the horn of an animal, the thing it fights with and cannot be taken from it. Hers is exalted in the LORD, lifted up, and the phrase will come back at the end of the song attached to somebody who does not exist yet.

Her enemies get one clause. My mouth derides my enemies — and Peninnah is not named, not described, and never mentioned again in the Bible. The woman who spent years provoking her gets half a line in the song and then vanishes out of Scripture.

The reason for the exulting is stated: because I rejoice in your salvation. Not in my son, not in my vindication. Your salvation.

'"There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God."'

Three statements, and the middle one is the ground of the other two.

None holy like the LORD. Holiness is the first thing she reaches for — not kindness, not power. The word means set apart, other, in a category by himself.

Then the reason: there is none besides you. He is not the best of the gods; there are no others to be better than. A woman in a country shrine in the age of the judges, when half of Israel was still hedging its bets with the Baals, says it flatly.

Then no rock like our God — the oldest image Israel had for him, from Moses' song: the Rock, his work is perfect (Deut. 32:4). Something you stand on, shelter behind, and do not have to check.

verseByVerse.quote: Talk no more so very proudly, let not arrogance come from your mouth; for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed. The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength. Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger. The barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Talk no more so very proudly, let not arrogance come from your mouth; for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed."'

She turns and addresses somebody, and the somebody is not named.

It may be Peninnah; it may be everyone like her. Either way the warning is not that God will punish arrogance but that he is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed. The picture is a balance. Every act is put on the scale by somebody who knows what it actually weighs, as opposed to what it looked like.

Consider who is saying this. A woman whose case, publicly weighed, had looked for years like a verdict against her: barren, mocked, and accused of drunkenness by the high priest. She is telling the confident to be careful, because the scales are not the ones they can see.

'"The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength. Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger."'

Now the reversals begin, and they come in pairs, and every pair runs the same direction.

The strong lose the thing that made them strong; the feeble are armed. The full are reduced to hiring out their labour for a loaf; the hungry stop being hungry. In each case the movement is not that the low are helped and the high left alone. Both ends move, and they change places.

'"The barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn."'

There is Hannah and Peninnah, in one line, with the names taken off.

The astonishing move in this song is the generalising. She has taken the most private thing that has ever happened to her, the thing she wept about at every festival for a decade, and she has stated it as a general law of how God runs the world. Not this happened to me but this is what happens.

Seven is the number of fullness rather than a headcount — verse 21 will record five more children after Samuel, which makes six. She is not doing arithmetic. She is saying that when God reverses a barrenness he does not do it by halves.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up. The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor. For the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and on them he has set the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up."'

This is the furthest any Old Testament believer goes, and it repays taking at full strength.

Not the LORD gives life and permits death. Both verbs are his, in the same sentence, in the same grammar. He kills. He brings to life. He brings down to Sheol — the grave, the place of the dead — and he raises up.

Hannah is not speculating about the resurrection; she is saying that the whole range, from the grave to life, is under one hand. And it is the same theology as chapter 1, worked out to its end. The LORD closed her womb, and the LORD opened it, and it was the same LORD. A God who only ever did the pleasant half would be no use to her, because he would not have been in charge of the years she actually lived through.

'"The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor."'

The ash heap is where the destitute sat outside a village, on the rubbish, and it is where Job sat when he had lost everything. It is the lowest address there is.

The promise is not that God will move such a man indoors. It is that he will seat him with princes, on a seat of honour — the whole distance in one movement, from the tip to the top table.

The psalms took this up almost word for word: he raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes (Ps. 113:7-8). Hannah's song went into Israel's hymn book.

'"For the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and on them he has set the world."'

Then she gives the reason he can do all this, and it goes underneath everything.

The pillars are his. The world is set on them by him. She is arguing from the foundations of creation to the reversal of one household's fortunes: the God who arranged what the earth stands on is not going to find a childless woman in Ramah beyond his reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness, for not by might shall a man prevail. The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness, for not by might shall a man prevail."'

Five words there are the argument of the whole book: not by might shall a man prevail.

Keep them. Israel is about to demand a king so that it can be like the other nations and have somebody to fight its battles, and it will be given the tallest man in the country. Then a boy with a sling will kill a giant and say the same thing in his own words — the LORD saves not with sword and spear (17:47). Hannah says it first, and she says it while nobody is listening.

'"The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed."'

Now read the last line again and remember where we are.

He will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed.

Israel has no king. There is no throne, no palace, no dynasty, no candidate. Nobody has even asked for one; that is six chapters away, and when it comes it will be treated as a rejection of God. And the word rendered anointed is mashiach — messiah.

A countrywoman from a hill village, who has just walked a weaned toddler up to a corrupt sanctuary and left him there, finishes her song by asking God to strengthen a king who does not exist, and to lift the horn of his Messiah.

Her own horn was exalted in verse 1. His will be exalted in verse 10. She has followed the thread from her own answered prayer all the way out to the end of the world — the LORD will judge the ends of the earth — and landed on an anointed king.

Now set this song beside the other one.

Eleven centuries later a young woman in another hill village, told she will bear a son by God's direct act, opens her mouth and sings almost this song again.

My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior — Hannah: my heart exults in the LORD... because I rejoice in your salvation. He has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts — Hannah: talk no more so very proudly. He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate — Hannah: he brings low and he exalts. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty — Hannah: those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger (Luke 1:46-53).

Mary knew this song. It is what a godly Israelite girl had in her head, and when the angel had gone and there was nobody to talk to, it is what came out.

Here is the difference that makes the parallel worth having. Hannah's song ends by reaching forward to an anointed king who did not yet exist. Mary was carrying him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Worthless Men at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elkanah goes home and the boy stays, ministering to the LORD before Eli (v. 11). Then the narrator turns to Eli's sons and gives his verdict in eight words: the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD (v. 12). Their practice is described in detail: a servant with a three-pronged fork thrust into the pot, and whatever it brought up the priest kept (vv. 13-14). Worse, they demanded raw meat before the fat was burned, and if a worshipper objected, I will take it by force (vv. 15-16). So their sin was very great, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Worthless men is literally sons of Belial — the exact phrase Hannah begged Eli not to apply to her one chapter ago (1:16). The high priest could not recognise a godly woman at his door and could not deal with the two sons of Belial at his altar.
verseByVerse.examples: There are two thefts here and the second is the grave one. The law gave the priest the breast and the right thigh, after the fat had been burned to God (Lev. 7:31-34). These men took what the fork found, and took it first — robbing the worshipper of his portion and God of his.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elkanah went home to Ramah. And the boy was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest. Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD. The custom of the priests with the people was that when any man offered sacrifice, the priest's servant would come, while the meat was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand, and he would thrust it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot. All that the fork brought up the priest would take for himself. This is what they did at Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Elkanah went home to Ramah. And the boy was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest.'

The family goes home and one of them does not.

The verse is written from the doorway. Elkanah went to Ramah; the boy stayed. And what the boy was doing is given in a phrase the writer keeps coming back to, here and again at v. 18 and again at 3:1: ministering to the LORD.

'Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD.'

Eight words for the two priests of Israel, and both halves are devastating.

Worthless men is, in Hebrew, sons of Belial — good-for-nothings, the word for the scum of a community. And it is the exact phrase Hannah used at this same doorway one chapter ago, when she begged Eli not to take her for a daughter of Belial (1:16).

Put the two scenes together, because the writer has. A woman comes to the sanctuary, prays in silence out of real grief, and is accused by the high priest of being worthless. Two men run the sanctuary, rob the worshippers and sleep with the women at the door, and the high priest is their father. He got it exactly the wrong way round, in both directions, in his own house.

Then the second half: they did not know the LORD.

These are priests. Their entire office is to stand between Israel and God and to teach the people who he is. And the narrator says, flatly, that they had no acquaintance with him.

The book of Judges said that of a whole generation — there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD (Judg. 2:10) — and it was the sentence the whole book turned on. Now the same charge is laid, and it is laid on the clergy.

'The custom of the priests with the people was that when any man offered sacrifice, the priest's servant would come, while the meat was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand, and he would thrust it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot. All that the fork brought up the priest would take for himself.'

The narrator describes the fraud with the patience of a man building a case.

The law was not vague about this. The priest's portion of a fellowship offering was the breast and the right thigh, specified in writing, given to him by name (Lev. 7:31-34). It was a provision, and it was enough.

What Eli's sons did instead was send a servant with a three-pronged fork to stab into the cooking pot and keep whatever came up. It is theft by lottery, and the four vessels listed — pan, kettle, cauldron, pot — are the writer's way of saying that no worshipper's dinner was safe whatever he cooked it in.

Then the sentence that shows how normal it had become: this is what they did at Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there. Not occasionally, and not to the ones who could not complain. To everybody, as the custom of the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give meat for the priest to roast, for he will not accept boiled meat from you but only raw." And if the man said to him, "Let them burn the fat first, and then take as much as you wish," he would say, "No, you must give it now, and if not, I will take it by force." Thus the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Moreover, before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give meat for the priest to roast, for he will not accept boiled meat from you but only raw."'

Here is the part that turns a racket into blasphemy, and it hangs on four words: before the fat was burned.

In every sacrifice the fat was God's. It went up on the altar first, burned to nothing, before anybody ate anything — the LORD's portion, and the law says so repeatedly: all fat is the LORD's (Lev. 3:16).

Eli's sons sent their man to intercept the meat before that happened. They are not merely taking more than their share from the worshipper; they are putting themselves at the head of the queue in front of God.

The reason given is appetite. They wanted it raw so they could roast it, because boiled meat was not to their taste. The order of precedence at the altar of Israel had been rearranged around what two men preferred for dinner.

'And if the man said to him, "Let them burn the fat first, and then take as much as you wish," he would say, "No, you must give it now, and if not, I will take it by force."'

The worshipper's answer is the most striking thing in the passage. He offers them everything — take as much as you wish — on one condition: let God have his part first.

An ordinary Israelite up from the country has better theology than the priesthood, and he is overruled by threat. I will take it by force. A priest of the LORD standing over a worshipper at the sanctuary, promising violence if he does not get the meat before God does.

'Thus the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.'

The narrator names the offence, and he does not name it as greed.

They treated the offering of the LORD with contempt. The sin was not that they were overpaid; it was what they thought of the thing they were handling. Every day, in front of people who had walked for miles to bring it, they showed that the sacrifice was food and nothing more.

That is what makes it very great in God's sight, and it is a warning aimed rather precisely at anybody who handles holy things for a living. Familiarity with the sacred is the most dangerous position in the world to occupy, because contempt does not arrive as a decision. It arrives as a habit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — A Little Robe, Year by Year
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel ministers before the LORD, a boy in a linen ephod (v. 18). And his mother made him a little robe and brought it up every year when the family came for the sacrifice (v. 19). Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah — may the LORD give you children by this woman for the petition she asked of the LORD (v. 20) — and the LORD visits Hannah, who bears three more sons and two daughters (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 is the tenderest sentence in the book. She had one afternoon a year with him, and she spent the other three hundred and sixty-four making him a coat, guessing at how much he had grown.
verseByVerse.examples: She gave one child away and was given five more. That is not the moral of the story and the narrator does not offer it as a transaction — but it is what happened, and the last clause is the point: the boy Samuel grew in the presence of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel was ministering before the LORD, a boy clothed with a linen ephod. And his mother used to make for him a little robe and take it to him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice. Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, "May the LORD give you children by this woman for the petition she asked of the LORD." So then they would return to their home. Indeed the LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew in the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Samuel was ministering before the LORD, a boy clothed with a linen ephod.'

The camera cuts from the fork in the pot to a small boy in priest's clothes.

A linen ephod is what a priest wore to serve, and Samuel is not from a priestly family — he is an Ephraimite, given by his mother. The two men who are entitled to wear it are defiling the altar, and a child who has no right to it is ministering properly.

'And his mother used to make for him a little robe and take it to him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.'

No sentence in the book is tenderer.

Sit with what it describes. She sees him once a year. For the other three hundred and sixty-four days she is at home in Ramah with a piece of cloth and a needle, making a coat for a boy she cannot measure, guessing at how much he has grown since last spring.

It is a little robe — the word is used elsewhere of a priest's garment and of Jonathan's cloak, the outer coat a man was known by. Every year she makes him a slightly bigger one, and every year she carries it up the hill and gives it to him and goes home again.

There is no complaint anywhere in the account, and no suggestion that she tried to take him back. She kept the vow, and she kept sewing.

'Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, "May the LORD give you children by this woman for the petition she asked of the LORD." So then they would return to their home.'

Eli's annual blessing is generous and it uses the chapter's key verb again: the petition she asked. He has understood exactly what happened, even if he did not understand it at the time.

'Indeed the LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew in the presence of the LORD.'

She gave one child away, and God gave her five.

Say carefully what that is and is not. It is not a transaction and the text does not offer it as one; there is no promise anywhere in Scripture that surrendering something to God results in more of it, and plenty of God's servants have given up what they never got back. What the verse records is what God did in this case, for this woman, and the writer plainly wants us to feel it.

The word is visited, which in Hebrew is the same movement as remembered in 1:19 — attention that acts.

The last clause is the one that matters most: the boy Samuel grew in the presence of the LORD. The five children at Ramah are the postscript. The one she left is the point.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–26 — Why Do You Do Such Things?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eli is very old, and he kept hearing everything his sons were doing, including that they were sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting (v. 22). He speaks to them: why do you do such things, it is no good report that I hear (vv. 23-24). And then a question with no answer in it: if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him? (v. 25). They would not listen, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death. And between the two halves of the family's ruin, one verse: Samuel kept growing in stature and in favour with the LORD and with man (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Eli's rebuke is the weakest thing in the chapter. He asks a question, reports the gossip, and calls it no good report — a public-relations problem. He never once tells them to stop, and he never removes them from the altar.
verseByVerse.examples: But his question in v. 25 is the deepest in the book, and the Old Testament never answers it. Who can intercede for a man who has sinned against God himself? There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5). Eli asked it without knowing there would be an answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Eli was very old, and he kept hearing all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting. And he said to them, "Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all these people. No, my sons; it is no good report that I hear the people of the LORD spreading abroad. If someone sins against a man, God will mediate for him, but if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?" But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death. Now the boy Samuel continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the LORD and also with man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Eli was very old, and he kept hearing all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting.'

The verb is kept hearing, and it is doing a great deal of work.

He did not fail to find out. There is no suggestion that anybody hid it, or that he was deceived, or that the reports were doubtful. It came in steadily, over years, from all over the country, and he heard all of it.

A new offence appears in this verse. The women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting were doing a recognised duty at the door of the sanctuary, and Eli's sons were sleeping with them. The Canaanite shrines up and down the country had women attached to them for exactly this purpose. Shiloh has begun to look like one.

'And he said to them, "Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all these people. No, my sons; it is no good report that I hear the people of the LORD spreading abroad."'

That is the whole of Eli's response, and it deserves measuring against what he had just been told.

He asks a question — why do you do such things? He reports his sources. And he characterises the problem as no good report: what he objects to, in the words he chooses, is what is being said about them.

He is the high priest. He has the authority to remove them from the altar this afternoon, and the law in his own keeping prescribed death for a great deal less than this. He does not remove them, does not discipline them, does not stop them, and does not go near the tent of meeting to see for himself. He speaks to them once, and the next verse tells us how that went.

Note too that he calls them my sons in the middle of it. That is exactly the problem, and God will say so in verse 29.

'"If someone sins against a man, God will mediate for him, but if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?"'

Then, in the middle of the feeblest rebuke in Scripture, the old man asks the deepest question in the book.

Follow the logic, because it is exact. When a man wrongs his neighbour, there is a court: God himself will arbitrate between them. But when the offence is against God — when he is both the party wronged and the judge — who is left to stand in the middle?

The Old Testament does not answer that question. It is asked here, and Job asks it in his own words when he says there is no arbiter between them who might lay his hand on both (Job 9:33), and it stays open for a thousand years.

For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tim. 2:5-6).

Eli asked it as a rhetorical question meaning nobody, and he was right about his own day and wrong about the answer. There is somebody. He would be born a mile from where David was born, and he would be exactly what the question required: one who could lay a hand on both, because he was both.

'But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death.'

Both halves of that sentence stand, and the writer makes no attempt to relieve the tension between them.

They would not listen — that is their act, and they are answerable for it. And it was the will of the LORD to put them to death — that is God's, stated as the reason the first half happened.

Scripture does this repeatedly and never apologises for it. God hardened Pharaoh's heart and Pharaoh hardened his own. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, in one event. Men crucified Christ by lawless hands, according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). Here two priests refuse a warning they had every capacity to heed, and behind their refusal stands a settled purpose of God, and both are true.

'Now the boy Samuel continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the LORD and also with man.'

The narrator drops this in between the sentence of death and its execution, and he does it on purpose. The house of Eli is finished; a child in a linen ephod is growing up in the same building.

There is a reason this verse sounds familiar. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man (Luke 2:52) — the summary of the only recorded detail of Jesus' boyhood, written in Hannah's son's words.

Luke, who has already given Mary Hannah's song, gives Jesus Samuel's childhood. He is telling us where to look.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–36 — Those Who Honour Me I Will Honour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An unnamed man of God arrives with a covenant lawsuit. The recital first: I revealed myself to your father's house in Egypt and chose him out of all Israel to be my priest, and gave your house all the offerings by fire (vv. 27-28). Then the charge, and it is aimed at Eli, not at his sons: you scorn my sacrifices... and honour your sons above me (v. 29). Then the sentence — the promise of a perpetual priesthood revoked, no old man left in his house, and both sons dead on the same day as the sign (vv. 30-34). And a promise: I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 30 is the chapter in one line: those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed. Eli's sin was not his sons' sin. It was that when forced to choose between them and God, he chose them — by doing nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: The faithful priest arrives twice. Zadok replaces Abiathar under Solomon, and 1 Kings 2:27 says outright that this was the fulfilment of the word spoken against the house of Eli at Shiloh. And then, at the end, a merciful and faithful high priest who does everything in God's heart and mind, and holds his office permanently (Heb. 2:17; 7:24).

verseByVerse.quote: And there came a man of God to Eli and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Did I indeed reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt subject to the house of Pharaoh? Did I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? I gave to the house of your father all my offerings by fire from the people of Israel. Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded for my dwelling, and honor your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of my people Israel?'
