Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: 'I promised that your house and the house of your father should go in and out before me forever,' but now the LORD declares: 'Far be it from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And there came a man of God to Eli and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Did I indeed reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt subject to the house of Pharaoh?'"'

An unnamed prophet arrives, and what he delivers is built like a legal case.

He is never named and never appears again, exactly like the unnamed prophet God sent to Israel before Gideon (Judg. 6:8). God has a habit of sending a man with a message and no biography.

'"Did I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? I gave to the house of your father all my offerings by fire from the people of Israel."'

The recital comes first, as it always does, and it is a list of gifts.

I revealed myself. I chose you out of all the tribes. I gave you the altar, the incense, the ephod, and the offerings to live on. Every clause is something God did for this family, and the questions are rhetorical: none of it is in dispute.

The offerings by fire are mentioned last for a reason. The very thing the sons have been stealing was already theirs by gift. They were robbing a table God had set for them.

'"Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded for my dwelling, and honor your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of my people Israel?"'

Now the charge, and it is addressed to Eli.

Read it carefully, because it would be easy to assume the prophet has come about Hophni and Phinehas. He has not. The verb is second person and the sin named is Eli's own: you honour your sons above me.

It is the indictment of a man who did nothing. He did not steal the meat. He did not sleep with the women at the door. What he did was hear about it for years, speak once, keep them in office, and go on eating — fattening yourselves, the prophet says, which puts Eli at the same table.

When it came to a choice between his sons and his God, he chose his sons, and he chose them by not choosing. That is how most such choices are made.

'"Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: 'I promised that your house and the house of your father should go in and out before me forever,' but now the LORD declares: 'Far be it from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.'"'

A promise is quoted and then withdrawn, and the withdrawal needs care.

God does not break his word, and this is not an instance of it. The priesthood given to Aaron's line was a standing arrangement with obligations attached; a promise of office is not the same kind of thing as the covenant of grace. What is being revoked is a family's tenure of a job, and the job continues — verse 35 says so.

Then the principle, and it is the sentence to carry out of the chapter: those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.

It is exact justice and it is terrifyingly simple. Eli honoured his sons above God; God will esteem Eli lightly. The measure a man uses is measured back to him, and the currency is honour.

Note what it does not say. Not those who serve me, or those who succeed for me. Eli had given his whole life to the sanctuary and was still at his post as an old man. The question is not whether God is being served but whether he is being honoured — whether, when something else in a man's life competes for the top place, God gets it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house. Then in distress you will look with envious eye on all the prosperity that shall be bestowed on Israel, and there shall not be an old man in your house forever. The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart, and all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men. And this that shall come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall be the sign to you: both of them shall die on the same day. And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall go in and out before my anointed forever. And everyone who is left in your house shall come to implore him for a piece of silver or a loaf of bread and shall say, "Please put me in one of the priests' places, that I may eat a morsel of bread."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house."'

The sentence is passed, and its cruellest feature is stated first: no old men.

Eli is himself a very old man, which is why the punishment is worded this way. He will look round his family in the years to come and find nobody who reached his age.

'"Then in distress you will look with envious eye on all the prosperity that shall be bestowed on Israel, and there shall not be an old man in your house forever."'

Israel will prosper while it happens. The nation the family was appointed to serve will flourish under Samuel and David, and the house of Eli will watch from the outside.

'"The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart, and all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men."'

One survivor is promised, and the promise is worse than the sentence. He is spared in order to watch, and the phrase for it is unbearable: to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart.

It is fulfilled with terrible precision. Abiathar alone escapes when Saul massacres the priests at Nob (22:20), and serves David for forty years, and is finally removed from the priesthood by Solomon — and the historian stops to tell us why: thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh (1 Kings 2:27).

'"And this that shall come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall be the sign to you: both of them shall die on the same day."'

A sign is given so that Eli will know the rest is coming, and it arrives two chapters later. Both sons die in a single afternoon when the Philistines take the ark, and the man who brings the news adds it almost as an afterthought (4:11, 17).

'"And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall go in and out before my anointed forever."'

Now, in the middle of a judgment oracle, a promise.

A corrupt priesthood is not answered by abolishing the priesthood. He says he will raise up a faithful priest — and the qualification is not lineage or competence but this: who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. A priest who wants what God wants.

The near fulfilment is Zadok, who replaces Abiathar under Solomon and whose line holds the office for centuries. Scripture makes the connection itself in the verse quoted above.

But look at the last clause and see that it does not stop there. He shall go in and out before my anointed forever. Anointed again — mashiach, the word Hannah used in verse 10 — and forever, which no son of Zadok managed.

The letter to the Hebrews takes up exactly this and finishes it. There is a merciful and faithful high priest who does everything in God's heart and mind (Heb. 2:17). He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb. 7:24). And he needed no sacrifice for his own sins first, which is precisely where every priest in Shiloh's line failed.

'"And everyone who is left in your house shall come to implore him for a piece of silver or a loaf of bread and shall say, 'Please put me in one of the priests' places, that I may eat a morsel of bread.'"'

The chapter ends with a picture, and it is exact retribution.

Two men who stood over worshippers demanding the best meat with a threat — I will take it by force — have descendants who will stand in front of another priest begging for a place at the bottom of the rota so they can eat a piece of bread.

They took the choicest parts. Their children will ask for a morsel.

2.theology:
A song with no baby in it. The one thing Hannah wanted, got, and gave away is not mentioned once in ten verses. And the reversal at v. 5 is her own case with the names taken off — not this happened to me but this is what happens. Seven is fullness, not a headcount; v. 21 records five more children.

The LORD kills and brings to life (v. 6). Both verbs are his, in one sentence, in the same grammar. It is chapter 1's theology worked out to the end: he closed the womb and he opened it. A God in charge of only the pleasant half would have been no use to her, because he would not have been in charge of the years she actually lived through.

Not by might shall a man prevail (v. 9). The argument of the whole book, stated before anyone needs it. Israel will demand a king to fight its battles and be given the tallest man in the country; then a boy with a sling will say the same thing in his own words (17:47).

His king, his anointed (v. 10). There is no king. Nobody has asked. The word is mashiach. Hannah's own horn was exalted in v. 1 and the Messiah's is exalted in v. 10 — she has followed the thread from one answered prayer out to the ends of the earth. Mary sings it again almost line for line (Luke 1:46-53), and the difference is everything: Hannah reached forward to an anointed king who did not exist, and Mary was carrying him.

Contempt for the offering (v. 17). The sin is not named as greed. They treated the offering of the LORD with contempt — the offence is what they thought of what they handled. Familiarity with holy things is the most dangerous position there is, because contempt never arrives as a decision, only as a habit.

Who can intercede? (v. 25) In the middle of the feeblest rebuke in Scripture, Eli asks the deepest question in it. When the offence is against God, who is both the party wronged and the judge, who stands in the middle? Job asks it too and finds no arbiter (Job 9:33). It stays open a thousand years, and then: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5). Eli meant it to mean nobody, and was right about his own day.

Both ends held (v. 25b). They would not listen, and it was the will of the LORD to put them to death. The writer makes no attempt to relieve it, as at Acts 2:23.

You honour your sons above me (v. 29). The charge is Eli's, not his sons'. He did not steal the meat; he heard for years, spoke once, kept them in office, and went on eating. When it came to a choice he chose his sons by not choosing, which is how most such choices are made. And the answer is exact: those who honour me I will honour (v. 30). Not those who serve me — Eli served all his life. Whether God gets the top place when something else competes for it.
2.examples:
Then: A woman walked home from leaving her only son with strangers and sang about the God who empties and fills, and finished by asking blessing on a king who would not exist for two generations. Meanwhile the two men she had left him with were stabbing forks into other people's dinners and threatening anyone who asked them to let God have his share first.

Now: Three things. Hannah's song is the model for what to do with an answered prayer: she generalised it. The mercy shown to her became a statement about how God treats everybody, which is the opposite of the instinct to hoard a testimony as a private possession. Second, verse 17 is for anyone who handles holy things often — preaching, leading, serving, or simply having been in church a long time. Contempt arrives as a habit and never announces itself. And third, verse 29 is the searching one. It is possible to serve God for a lifetime and still, at the point of collision, honour something else above him — and to do it not by a decision but by declining to make one.

3.title: The Word of the LORD Was Rare
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the boy Samuel was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli. And the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision.<sup>2</sup>At that time Eli, whose eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his own place.<sup>3</sup>The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.<sup>4</sup>Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, "Here I am!"<sup>5</sup>and ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call; lie down again." So he went and lay down.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD called again, "Samuel!" and Samuel arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call, my son; lie down again."<sup>7</sup>Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD called Samuel again the third time. And he arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." Then Eli perceived that the LORD was calling the boy.<sup>9</sup>Therefore Eli said to Samuel, "Go, lie down, and if he calls you, you shall say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, "Samuel! Samuel!" And Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant hears."<sup>11</sup>Then the LORD said to Samuel, "Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle.<sup>12</sup>On that day I will fulfill against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end.<sup>13</sup>And I declare to him that I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them.<sup>14</sup>Therefore I swear to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever."<sup>15</sup>Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. And Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli.<sup>16</sup>But Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." And he said, "Here I am."<sup>17</sup>And Eli said, "What was it that he told you? Do not hide it from me. May God do so to you and more also if you hide anything from me of all that he told you."<sup>18</sup>So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he said, "It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him."<sup>19</sup>And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.<sup>20</sup>And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD appeared again at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
3.overview:
The chapter opens on one of the bleakest sentences in the Old Testament: the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision. Israel still had the tabernacle, the ark, the priesthood and the sacrifices — the whole apparatus in working order. What it did not have was God saying anything. Eli's eyes have failed so that he cannot see; the lamp of God has not yet gone out, which is a clock (the menorah burned till morning) and also a picture.

God calls the boy by name three times while he sleeps, and three times Samuel runs to the wrong person. The narrator explains why, and it is the verse the chapter turns on: Samuel did not yet know the LORD. He was given to God before he was conceived, has lived in the sanctuary since he was weaned, wears the ephod, ministers daily — and has never been introduced. Eli's sons get the same words in 2:12 with no yet in them, and that one adverb is the whole distance between them.

Eli does the one good thing he does in this book: he works out who is calling, and teaches the boy how to answer, and sends him back alone to hear a word he must have known would be against himself. And it is — the charge sharper than chapter 2's: the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them.

Eli's reply sounds magnificent: it is the LORD; let him do what seems good to him. And nothing changes. The sons are still at the altar in chapter 4. The chapter closes where it could not have begun: the LORD revealing himself again at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — When the Word Was Rare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The boy is ministering to the LORD in Eli's presence, and the narrator sets the scene with one of the bleakest sentences in the Old Testament: the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision (v. 1). Eli's eyes have grown so dim that he cannot see, and he is lying down in his own place (v. 2). The lamp of God has not yet gone out, and Samuel is lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark is (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: A famine of the word is the worst thing that can happen to a people, and Amos names it as such — not a famine of bread but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11). Israel still had the sanctuary, the ark, the priesthood and the sacrifices. What it did not have was God speaking.
verseByVerse.examples: The lamp is a time-check first: the menorah burned from evening to morning (Ex. 27:20-21), so this is the last hour before dawn. It is also a picture, and the writer lets it stand without pressing it. The light has not gone out. It is very nearly out.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the boy Samuel was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli. And the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision. At that time Eli, whose eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his own place. The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the boy Samuel was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli. And the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision.'

The second half of that verse is one of the saddest sentences in the Old Testament.

The word of the LORD was rare in those days. Not absent — rare. And there was no frequent vision, which says the same thing a second way, because the writer wants us to feel it.

Take stock of what Israel still had at this moment. The tabernacle was standing at Shiloh. The ark of the covenant was inside it. There was a high priest, and a functioning rota of sacrifices, and pilgrims coming up year by year with their bulls and their flour. The whole apparatus of the covenant was in working order.

What was missing was God saying anything.

Amos gives that condition its name centuries later, and it is the worst judgment in his book: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11). A nation can keep every outward form of religion running smoothly and be starving.

'At that time Eli, whose eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his own place.'

The old man's eyes are failing, and the narrator has mentioned it for a reason.

It is a plain medical fact and the writer states it plainly. It is also, in a book this carefully written, the third time we have watched Eli fail to see something. He could not see that Hannah was praying. He could not see what his sons were doing at the altar, though he kept hearing about it. Now he cannot see at all.

'The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.'

Two things in this verse, and the first is a clock.

The lamp is the menorah, and the law required it to be tended so that it burned from evening until morning (Ex. 27:20-21). If it has not yet gone out, we are in the last hour of the night, just before dawn.

It is also a picture, and the writer sets it down without pressing it. The light in the house of God has not gone out. It is very nearly out. Israel's priesthood is corrupt, its high priest is blind, its word from God is rare — and the lamp is still burning, just, in the dark, in the hour before morning.

Then the second thing: where the boy is sleeping. In the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.

The ark is the throne of God on earth, the most dangerous object in Israel, the thing men die for touching. And a child is asleep on the floor near it, because that is where he lives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Speak, for Your Servant Hears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD calls, and Samuel answers here I am and runs to Eli — three times, and three times the old man sends him back to bed (vv. 4-8). The narrator explains why: Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him (v. 7). At the third time Eli understands what is happening and tells the boy what to say (vv. 8-9). Then: the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, "Samuel! Samuel!" and the boy answers, speak, for your servant hears (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is the sentence to stop at. He has lived in the tabernacle since he was weaned, wears the linen ephod and serves every day — and he does not know God. Not yet. The same words are used of Eli's sons in 2:12 with no yet in them, and the whole distance between the two verses is that one adverb.
verseByVerse.examples: Eli gets one thing right in this book and it is here. He cannot hear God himself, and his own house is under sentence, and he teaches the boy exactly how to answer. It is the last useful thing he does.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, "Here I am!" and ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call; lie down again." So he went and lay down. And the LORD called again, "Samuel!" and Samuel arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call, my son; lie down again." Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, "Here I am!"'

God speaks, and the first word out of the boy is the right one.

Here I am — hinneni — is the answer Abraham gave on the mountain, and Jacob at Bethel, and Moses at the bush, and Isaiah in the temple. It is not information about his location. It is a man putting himself at somebody's disposal.

Samuel says it correctly and runs to the wrong person.

'and ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call; lie down again." So he went and lay down.'

He runs. A boy woken out of sleep hears his name and is on his feet and across the room, and the detail is affectionate: whatever else is true of him, when somebody calls him in the night he goes at once.

'And the LORD called again, "Samuel!" and Samuel arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call, my son; lie down again."'

The second time, and note that Eli is patient. I did not call, my son. No irritation at being woken twice before dawn by a child; he calls him son and sends him back to bed.

'Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.'

Stop here, because this is the verse the chapter turns on and it is easy to read past.

Samuel did not yet know the LORD.

Consider who is being described. This boy was given to God before he was conceived. He was brought to the sanctuary as a toddler and has lived there ever since. He wears a linen ephod. He ministers to the LORD daily; the narrator has said so three times. He sleeps in the room with the ark of the covenant. His mother makes him a robe every year and there is not a word of complaint about him anywhere in the book.

He does not know God.

Now set that beside the other verse in this book that uses those words. Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD (2:12).

The same phrase, and everything hangs on one word that appears in one of them. Samuel did not yet know the LORD. Eli's sons simply did not.

One is a boy who has never been introduced. The other is two men who have had every opportunity and have made up their minds. The distance between them is not their conduct on the night in question; it is the direction they are facing.

Take this personally if you were raised in it. It is entirely possible to grow up inside the building, to know the services and the songs and the shape of the thing, to serve in it faithfully and be thought well of, and to have had no personal dealings with God at all. Samuel is the proof, and his case is the hopeful one: the yet was about to expire.

Note also who is doing the work here. Samuel does not seek God; God calls Samuel, by name, three times, while the boy is asleep and has no idea who is speaking. Nobody in this chapter comes looking for the LORD. He comes looking for a child in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD called Samuel again the third time. And he arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." Then Eli perceived that the LORD was calling the boy. Therefore Eli said to Samuel, "Go, lie down, and if he calls you, you shall say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place. And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, "Samuel! Samuel!" And Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant hears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the LORD called Samuel again the third time. And he arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." Then Eli perceived that the LORD was calling the boy.'

Third time, and the old man works it out.

Give him this. He is blind, his family is under sentence, he has not heard from God himself in who knows how long, and it takes him three attempts — but he gets there. And what he perceives is not that somebody is calling, but who: the LORD was calling the boy.

'Therefore Eli said to Samuel, "Go, lie down, and if he calls you, you shall say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.'"'

Here is the one good thing Eli does in this book, and it should be said clearly.

He does not tell the boy to come and fetch him so that he can hear it too. He does not ask what the message is or arrange to be present. He teaches a child how to answer God and sends him back to bed alone.

The words he gives him are exactly right. Speak, LORD, for your servant hears. Not listen, LORD, for your servant is speaking, which is what a great deal of prayer amounts to. The posture is: you talk, and I am here to receive it.

There is something else in it that Eli cannot have missed. He is sending the boy to hear a word he has every reason to think will be against himself, and he sends him anyway, with the correct form of words. Whatever else the man was, he did not try to keep God quiet.

'So Samuel went and lay down in his place. And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, "Samuel! Samuel!" And Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant hears."'

Two details before the message.

The first: the LORD came and stood. The three earlier calls were a voice. This time God comes, and stands, and calls him by name twice over, the way a person is addressed when what follows matters — Abraham on the mountain, Moses at the bush, Saul on the Damascus road.

The second is a small thing and readers have noticed it for centuries. Eli told him to say speak, LORD, for your servant hears. Samuel says speak, for your servant hears. He leaves out the name.

The text does not tell us why, and it would be easy to make too much of it. It may be nerves. It may be that a boy who has just realised who is standing in the room does not find the name easy to say out loud. What he does say is the whole of the substance, and God answers it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message, when it comes, is about Eli. God is about to do a thing at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle (v. 11); he will fulfil against Eli everything already spoken about his house, from beginning to end (v. 12). And the charge is put more sharply than the man of God put it in chapter 2: the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them (v. 13). Then the oath: this iniquity shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Two words carry the indictment. He knew, and he did not restrain. Not that he approved, not that he joined in, not that he was deceived. He had the information and the authority and used neither.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is terrible and it is specific. This is a sentence on one priestly family, not a general rule that sin can put a person past forgiveness — and the cruelty of it, for priests, is that the one thing their house possessed was the machinery of atonement, and it is closed to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Samuel, "Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle. On that day I will fulfill against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end. And I declare to him that I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them. Therefore I swear to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the LORD said to Samuel, "Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle."'

The first word of God to Samuel is a word of judgment, and it is about the household he lives in.

Think what is being asked of him. A boy of perhaps twelve, raised by this old man, is given his first message from God, and it is the destruction of the man who taught him the words to say it with.

The image is physical: ears that ring. It is the sensation after a very loud noise, and God uses it of what Israel will feel when the news comes. The phrase is used twice more in Scripture, both times of national catastrophe (2 Kings 21:12; Jer. 19:3).

'"On that day I will fulfill against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end."'

Nothing new is being announced. This is confirmation of the oracle the unnamed man of God brought in chapter 2, and God says so: all that I have spoken concerning his house.

So Eli has already had this warning, in detail, from a prophet, and has had time to act on it. Between chapter 2 and chapter 3 the sons are still in office.

'"And I declare to him that I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them."'

Now the charge, and it is sharper than chapter 2's version.

Two words carry it. Knew, and restrain.

He knew. That is stated as a fact and it is not in dispute; chapter 2 told us he kept hearing about it from everybody in the country. There is no ignorance to plead.

He did not restrain them either. Not that he approved, not that he encouraged them, not that he was taken in. He had the authority to stop it — he was the high priest and their father, and the law he administered prescribed death for far less — and he used it to have one conversation.

God does not charge Eli with his sons' sin. He charges him with his own, and it is a sin of omission committed with full information over a period of years.

'"Therefore I swear to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever."'

This is the most frightening verse in the chapter and it must be handled exactly.

What it says is that for this house, this iniquity, there will be no sacrifice that removes it. God swears to it. And the cruelty of the sentence, for a priestly family, is precise: the one thing they possessed, the machinery of atonement itself, is the thing shut against them. They had made a living out of the offerings; the offerings will do nothing for them.

Now say what it does not mean, because a verse like this can do great damage to an anxious reader. It is not a general statement that a person's sin can put him beyond forgiveness. It is a judicial sentence on one household in one generation, in a specific matter, spoken through a named prophet. There is no comparable oracle standing over anybody reading this.

What it does establish is that sacrifice is not a machine. Eli's family had assumed that the system they administered would cover whatever they did, because it always had. God tells them the altar is not a laundry, and that a man who despises the offering cannot then shelter behind it.

The letter to the Hebrews says the same thing to Christians in almost the same shape: if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins (Heb. 10:26). The warning is not that Christ's blood is insufficient. It is that there is no other, and a man who treats it with contempt has nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel lies awake until morning, opens the doors of the house of the LORD as usual, and is afraid to tell Eli (v. 15). Eli calls him and puts him under oath to hide nothing (vv. 16-17), so Samuel tells him everything. And Eli says: it is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him (v. 18). Then Samuel grows, and the LORD is with him and let none of his words fall to the ground, and all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knows he is established as a prophet (vv. 19-20). And the LORD appears again at Shiloh (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Eli's answer sounds like the finest submission in the book, and it is also the problem. He accepts the verdict and changes nothing; the sons are still at the altar in chapter 4. Resignation is not repentance, and it is much easier.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter opened with the word of the LORD rare and closes with God revealing himself at Shiloh by the word. And a word that does not fall to the ground is one that comes true — the test Moses gave for telling a real prophet from a false one (Deut. 18:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. And Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli. But Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." And he said, "Here I am." And Eli said, "What was it that he told you? Do not hide it from me. May God do so to you and more also if you hide anything from me of all that he told you." So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he said, "It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. And Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli.'

He lies there until it is light, and then he gets up and does his job.

That is the detail worth noticing. He has been awake since before dawn holding the worst news in Israel, and what he does at first light is open the doors of the house of the LORD, which is what he does every morning. The routine goes on while he works out how to say it.

He is also afraid. The narrator says so without excusing it and without criticising it. A boy of twelve has been given a message that destroys the only family he has, and he does not want to deliver it.

'But Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." And he said, "Here I am."'

My son, again. And here I am, again, this time to the right person.

'And Eli said, "What was it that he told you? Do not hide it from me. May God do so to you and more also if you hide anything from me of all that he told you."'

The old man puts him under oath, in the strongest form the language has, to conceal nothing.

He knows what is coming. He has had one prophet already. And he insists on hearing the whole of it from a frightened child, with a curse attached to any softening.

There is a kind of courage in that which deserves to be named. Most of us, given the chance to avoid the specifics of a judgment we already suspect, would take it.

'So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he said, "It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him."'

Eli's answer is, on the face of it, magnificent.

It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him. There is no protest, no bargaining, no attempt to argue the sentence down. He does not blame the messenger, or question whether the boy heard correctly, or plead his years of service. He acknowledges whose word it is and submits to it.

Job said something similar on his ash heap and it is counted to him for righteousness.

Then nothing.

Look at what happens next in the story, which is nothing. The sons are not removed. There is no attempt to restrain them, no discipline, no repentance, no change of any kind. One chapter later Hophni and Phinehas walk out of Shiloh carrying the ark of the covenant into a battle, and their father lets them, and they die exactly as promised.

So weigh the sentence again. Let him do what seems good to him can be the voice of faith, and it can be the voice of a man who has decided that nothing can be done and is therefore relieved of doing anything. From the outside the two are indistinguishable. The difference shows up afterwards, in whether anything changes.

Eli accepted the verdict and never restrained his sons. That is the whole tragedy of him, and it is a common enough shape: submission to God's sovereignty employed as a reason to leave sin where it is. Resignation is not repentance. It is much easier, and it can be made to sound more spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground. And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD. And the LORD appeared again at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.'

Three statements, and the third is a beautiful piece of Hebrew.

He grew — the book keeps saying it, chapter by chapter, while the house of Eli shrinks. The LORD was with him, which is the highest thing this history ever says about anybody. And God let none of his words fall to the ground.

The picture is of a word dropped and lying in the dust: something said that came to nothing. Not one of Samuel's did. Every word he spoke as a prophet arrived.

That is precisely the test Moses laid down for distinguishing a true prophet from a man inventing things: when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken (Deut. 18:22). Samuel passes it from the first message, and the first message was against the man who raised him.

'And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD.'

The whole country, north to south, and the phrase is worth a glance in passing.

From Dan to Beersheba is the standard expression for the length of Israel, and the northern end of it is the town whose founding closed the book of Judges — taken by six hundred armed men from a quiet, unsuspecting people, renamed after their ancestor, and furnished with a stolen idol and a hired priest (Judg. 18:27-31). It has settled into the language as simply the top of the map.

What all Israel knows is that Samuel is established as a prophet. The country has not had this for a long time. There is a man again through whom God speaks.

'And the LORD appeared again at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.'

Now read the last verse of the chapter against the first.

Verse 1: the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision.

Verse 21: the LORD appeared again at Shiloh... by the word of the LORD.

The famine is over. That is what has happened in twenty verses, and it happened because God called a sleeping child by name three times in the dark and the child eventually said speak, for your servant hears.

Consider how God chose to break the silence. Not by restoring the priesthood, which was beyond saving; not by a sign in the sky, or an army, or a reformation of the sanctuary. He raised up one person who would listen, and spoke to him, and that was enough to end a famine in a whole nation.

Mark the means: by the word of the LORD. God revealed himself by speaking. That is how he has always chosen to be known — not first by displays of power but by speech.

That is why the New Testament opens its greatest argument exactly here. Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb. 1:1-2).

The rare word at Shiloh became a frequent one through Samuel, and prophet followed prophet for a thousand years, and then God said everything he had to say in a person. There has not been a famine of the word since, and there will not be another. The last hour before dawn ended.

3.theology:
A famine of the word (v. 1). The forms were all intact and God was not speaking. Amos names that condition as the worst of judgments — not a famine of bread but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11). A church can keep every outward thing running smoothly and be starving.

Did not yet know the LORD (v. 7). The pastoral heart of the chapter, and it is aimed at anyone raised inside the building. It is entirely possible to know the services, the songs and the shape of the thing, to serve faithfully and be well thought of, and to have had no personal dealings with God. Samuel is the proof — and his is the hopeful case, because the yet was about to expire. Note also who moves: nobody in this chapter goes looking for God. He comes looking for a child in the dark.

Knew, and did not restrain (v. 13). God does not charge Eli with his sons' sin. He charges him with his own — an omission committed with full information, over years, by a man with the authority to stop it and a law in his keeping that prescribed far more than he did.

Not atoned for by sacrifice or offering (v. 14). Handle exactly. It is a judicial sentence on one household in one matter, not a general rule that sin can put a person past forgiveness; no comparable oracle stands over any reader. What it does establish is that sacrifice is not a machine and the altar is not a laundry — a man who despises the offering cannot then shelter behind it. Hebrews says the same to Christians in the same shape (Heb. 10:26), and the warning is not that Christ's blood is insufficient but that there is no other.

Resignation is not repentance (v. 18). It is the LORD; let him do what seems good to him can be the voice of faith, and it can be the voice of a man who has concluded nothing can be done and is therefore relieved of doing anything. From outside they are indistinguishable; the difference shows afterwards, in whether anything changes. Nothing did.

The famine ends (vv. 19-21). God broke the silence not by reforming the priesthood, which was beyond saving, but by raising up one person who would listen. And the means is named: by the word of the LORD. That is how he has always chosen to be known — which is why Hebrews begins where it does. Long ago... God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb. 1:1-2). There has not been a famine of the word since, and there will not be another.
3.examples:
Then: A blind old priest, whose family was under sentence and who had not heard from God in years, worked out on the third attempt that the LORD was calling the child in the next room — and taught him the words to answer with, and sent him back alone to receive a message he must have known would be about himself.

Now: Two things, and they pull in opposite directions. Verse 7 is for anyone who grew up in church: you can serve in the building for years and not yet know the LORD, and the word to hold on to is yet — because God was the one doing the calling, three times, to a boy who had no idea who was speaking. And verse 18 is for anyone who has made peace with a sin in their family, their church or themselves and dressed the peace up as submission to God's will. Eli said exactly the right thing and removed nobody from office. Ask what actually changed after the last time you said let him do what seems good.

4.title: Ichabod: The Glory Has Departed
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines. They encamped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek.<sup>2</sup>The Philistines drew up in line against Israel, and when the battle spread, Israel was defeated before the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men on the field of battle.<sup>3</sup>And when the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said, "Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies."<sup>4</sup>So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.<sup>5</sup>As soon as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a mighty shout, so that the earth resounded.<sup>6</sup>And when the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said, "What does this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews mean?" And when they learned that the ark of the LORD had come to the camp,<sup>7</sup>the Philistines were afraid, for they said, "A god has come into the camp." And they said, "Woe to us! For nothing like this has happened before.<sup>8</sup>Woe to us! Who can deliver us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every sort of plague in the wilderness.<sup>9</sup>Take courage, and be men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you; be men and fight."<sup>10</sup>So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and they fled, every man to his home. And there was a very great slaughter, for thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.<sup>11</sup>And the ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.<sup>12</sup>A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and with dirt on his head.<sup>13</sup>When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God. And when the man came into the city and told the news, all the city cried out.<sup>14</sup>When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said, "What is this uproar?" Then the man hurried and came and told Eli.<sup>15</sup>Now Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were set so that he could not see.<sup>16</sup>And the man said to Eli, "I am he who has come from the battle; I fled from the battle today." And he said, "How did it go, my son?"<sup>17</sup>He who brought the news answered and said, "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great defeat among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured."<sup>18</sup>As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell over backward from his seat by the side of the gate, and his neck was broken and he died, for the man was old and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.<sup>19</sup>Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant, about to give birth. And when she heard the news that the ark of God was captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed and gave birth, for her pains came upon her.<sup>20</sup>And about the time of her death the women attending her said to her, "Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son." But she did not answer or pay attention.<sup>21</sup>And she named the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel!" because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband.<sup>22</sup>And she said, "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
4.overview:
Israel loses four thousand men, and the elders ask exactly the right question: why has the LORD defeated us today? They know whose hand it was, which is better theology than anything in Judges. Then they answer it themselves and send to Shiloh for the ark, that it may come among us and save us — making a box the subject of the verb save. And all the while there is a prophet in the land whose words do not fall to the ground, in the very building they sent the cart to, and nobody asks him anything.

The ark arrives to a shout that shakes the ground, and the Philistines are terrified: a god has come into the camp. Their facts are garbled and their instinct is sound — they think a person has arrived, which is more than the men cheering on the other side of the valley believe. Their answer to their own fear is to be men and fight. Israel loses thirty thousand, and the ark of God is captured, and Eli's two sons die on the same day exactly as promised.

A runner reaches Shiloh with four pieces of news in ascending order, and Eli absorbs the first three. It is as soon as he mentioned the ark of God that he goes over backwards and breaks his neck — the man charged with honouring his sons above God, dying at the other news.

And his daughter-in-law, dying in childbirth, is told she has borne a son and will not turn her head — the sentence Hannah wept for years to hear. She names the boy Ichabod, the glory has departed, and says it twice; and the second time she gives only one of her three reasons, and it is not her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel goes out against the Philistines, camps at Ebenezer, and loses four thousand men (vv. 1-2). The elders ask exactly the right question — why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? — and then answer it themselves: fetch the ark from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us (v. 3). So the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts is carried down to the camp, and Hophni and Phinehas come with it (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: They know whose hand defeated them; that is better theology than most of Judges. What they do not do is wait for an answer. Samuel has just been established in all Israel as a prophet of the LORD (3:20), and nobody sends for him. They had a word from God available and sent for furniture.
verseByVerse.examples: Read the grammar of v. 3: the ark is the subject of the verb save. That is the sin of the chapter, and it is Micah's exactly — now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest (Judg. 17:13). The right apparatus, operated as a mechanism.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines. They encamped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek. The Philistines drew up in line against Israel, and when the battle spread, Israel was defeated before the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men on the field of battle. And when the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said, "Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies." So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines. They encamped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek.'

The first clause and the second have nothing to do with each other, and that is the point.

Chapter 3 ended with God speaking again after a famine of the word, and a prophet established from Dan to Beersheba. Verse 1 reports it: the word of Samuel came to all Israel. And then the nation goes out to fight without any indication that it consulted him.

Note the place name, because it will come back. Ebenezer — stone of help. Israel loses two battles on this ground in this chapter, and three chapters later Samuel will set up a stone at the same spot and give it that name for a reason (7:12).

'The Philistines drew up in line against Israel, and when the battle spread, Israel was defeated before the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men on the field of battle.'

Four thousand dead, and the day is lost.

'And when the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said, "Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines?"'

Stop at the question, because it is a good one.

They do not say the Philistines were stronger, or that the ground was bad, or that they needed better equipment. They say why has the LORD defeated us — naming God as the agent of their own defeat. That is better theology than anything in the book of Judges.

Then they do not wait for the answer.

'"Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies."'

Read the grammar of that sentence and the sin of the chapter is visible in it.

That it may come among us and save us. The subject of the verb save is it. Not the LORD — the ark. A wooden box overlaid with gold has been made the saviour of Israel, in a sentence spoken by the elders of the nation.

Now consider what they had available instead. God had just broken a generation of silence. There was a prophet in the land whose words did not fall to the ground, known to every tribe from Dan to Beersheba. He was at Shiloh, where they sent the messengers. Nobody asked him anything.

They asked why has the LORD defeated us, and the man who could have told them was standing in the building they sent the cart to.

This is Micah's mistake with a national budget. Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest (Judg. 17:13). Get the right object, install it properly, and the outcome follows. It is religion as machinery, and the elders of Israel have just applied it to the ark of the covenant.

The ark was not a fraud. It was the real thing, made to God's own specification, the place where he had said he would meet with them. That is precisely what makes this so dangerous. Nobody in this chapter has abandoned the true religion; they have taken the genuine article and used it as a lever.

'So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.'

The narrator gives the ark its full title, and it is the longest form he has used yet: the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim.

He is not being ceremonious. He is telling us what they thought they were carrying and what they were actually carrying — the throne of the God of every army there is — and then he tells us who was carrying it.

Hophni and Phinehas were there with the ark. The two men whose deaths were promised in chapter 2 have their hands on it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark arrives and Israel gives a shout that makes the earth resound (v. 5). The Philistines hear it, learn what it means, and are terrified: a god has come into the camp... these are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every sort of plague (vv. 6-8). Their answer to their own fear is take courage, and be men... be men and fight (v. 9). And Israel is defeated, thirty thousand foot soldiers fall, the ark of God is captured, and Hophni and Phinehas die (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The Philistines have their facts wrong — plural gods, and the plagues put in the wilderness rather than in Egypt — and they are more nearly right than Israel. They think God himself has arrived. Israel thinks a box has.
verseByVerse.examples: Both halves of 2:34 land in one verse. The sign given to Eli was that his two sons would die on the same day, and here they do — and the writer mentions them second, after the ark.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a mighty shout, so that the earth resounded. And when the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said, "What does this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews mean?" And when they learned that the ark of the LORD had come to the camp, the Philistines were afraid, for they said, "A god has come into the camp." And they said, "Woe to us! For nothing like this has happened before. Woe to us! Who can deliver us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every sort of plague in the wilderness. Take courage, and be men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you; be men and fight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a mighty shout, so that the earth resounded.'

The cheer is enormous and it is entirely misplaced.

An army that had been beaten that afternoon is roaring, not because God has spoken or because anybody has repented, but because a box has arrived. There is no prayer recorded, no confession, no enquiry. Just noise.

'And when the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said, "What does this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews mean?" And when they learned that the ark of the LORD had come to the camp, the Philistines were afraid, for they said, "A god has come into the camp."'

Philistia is frightened, and its fear is more accurate than Israel's confidence.

Listen to what they say. A god has come into the camp. They do not think a religious object has been delivered; they think a person has arrived. And they are right, which is more than can be said for the men shouting on the other side of the valley.

'"Woe to us! For nothing like this has happened before. Woe to us! Who can deliver us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every sort of plague in the wilderness."'

Their theology is a mess and their instinct is sound.

They say gods, plural, because that is the only grammar they have. They put the plagues in the wilderness when the plagues were in Egypt. They have the story second-hand and garbled, four hundred years old, passed down among people who lost.

They have the essential thing exactly right: this is the God who did Egypt, and there is no standing in front of him. The Philistines of Aphek know more about the LORD than the elders of Israel do.

Note also what their memory preserves. Four centuries later, in a foreign army, on a hillside in Canaan, the exodus is still the thing everybody knows about the God of the Hebrews. It got out, and it stayed out.

'"Take courage, and be men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you; be men and fight."'

Then their response, which is honest.

No idol is sent for. They do not fetch Dagon from Ashdod to even the odds, though they easily could have and the next chapter shows they had him. They conclude that the situation is desperate and that the answer is to be men and fight.

Put the two camps side by side, because the writer has. Israel: a shout, and a box, and no prayer. Philistia: terror, an accurate assessment, and a decision to do the only thing they can. One of these armies is about to lose thirty thousand men.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and they fled, every man to his home. And there was a very great slaughter, for thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell. And the ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and they fled, every man to his home. And there was a very great slaughter, for thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.'

Thirty thousand. In the morning they had lost four thousand and thought the problem was that God was not with them; by evening they have lost seven times as many with the ark in the camp.

That is the answer to the elders' question, and it is delivered in the only language they were listening to. Why has the LORD defeated us today? He defeats them again, worse, with his own throne standing in their lines, so that nobody can say the ark was absent.

'And the ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.'

Two clauses, and the first is the one nobody in Israel thought possible.

The ark of God was captured. The chest that held the tablets of the covenant, with the mercy seat on top and the cherubim over it, the place where God had said he would meet with his people and speak from between the cherubim — loaded onto a Philistine cart and driven away.

Take the measure of what has happened. God allowed the sign of his own presence to be taken by pagans as a trophy, rather than let his people go on using it as a charm. He would sooner be carried into the temple of Dagon than be treated as a lucky object by Israel.

Sit with that, if you have ever assumed God is obliged to protect the institutions that bear his name. He is not. He has let a sanctuary fall, a priesthood end and the ark itself go into captivity, and the next chapter shows he was in no difficulty whatever while it happened.

Then the second clause, almost in passing: and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.

The sign given to their father has arrived. Both of them shall die on the same day (2:34). It is exact, and the narrator does not stop to point it out.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A Benjaminite runs the twenty miles to Shiloh with his clothes torn and dirt on his head (v. 12). Eli is sitting by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God (v. 13). He is ninety-eight and blind (v. 15). The messenger delivers four things in ascending order: Israel has fled; there has been a great defeat; your two sons are dead; and the ark of God has been captured (v. 17). As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli falls backwards off his seat, breaks his neck and dies (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Give the old man this at the end. He hears that both his sons are dead and stays upright. It is the fourth item that kills him, and his heart had been trembling for it before the runner arrived.
verseByVerse.examples: The book has kept finding Eli in a chair by a door — sitting by the doorpost when Hannah prayed (1:9), lying in his own place when God called the boy (3:2), and now sitting by the gate. He dies in it. He had judged Israel forty years.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and with dirt on his head. When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God. And when the man came into the city and told the news, all the city cried out. When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said, "What is this uproar?" Then the man hurried and came and told Eli.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and with dirt on his head.'

He runs about twenty miles, and everybody who sees him knows before he speaks.

Torn clothes and earth on the head are the recognised signs of mourning in that world. The messenger is wearing the news.

'When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God.'

The old man is at the roadside, and the narrator tells us what he was thinking about.

Not his sons. His heart trembled for the ark of God.

Give him that, at the end. He failed to restrain his boys for years, and God's charge against him was that he honoured them above the LORD. And on the last afternoon of his life, blind, at ninety-eight, sitting by the road because he cannot go and look, what he is afraid for is the ark. Whatever was wrong with the man, that was in him too.

He is also, once again, on a seat by a way in. This book keeps finding Eli in a chair beside a door — by the doorpost when Hannah came (1:9), lying down in his own place when God called the boy (3:2), and now by the gate. He will die in it.

'And when the man came into the city and told the news, all the city cried out. When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said, "What is this uproar?" Then the man hurried and came and told Eli.'

The town hears first and the high priest hears the town.

He is blind and cannot see the messenger arrive, and the news reaches him as a noise from a street he cannot look down. He has to ask what the shouting is.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were set so that he could not see. And the man said to Eli, "I am he who has come from the battle; I fled from the battle today." And he said, "How did it go, my son?" He who brought the news answered and said, "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great defeat among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured." As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell over backward from his seat by the side of the gate, and his neck was broken and he died, for the man was old and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were set so that he could not see.'

The narrator repeats it at the moment it matters most. In chapter 3 his eyes had begun to grow dim; now they are set, fixed, gone.

'And the man said to Eli, "I am he who has come from the battle; I fled from the battle today." And he said, "How did it go, my son?"'

My son. He has called Samuel that, and his own boys that, and now a stranger off the battlefield. It is the last thing he says.

'He who brought the news answered and said, "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great defeat among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured."'

Four items, and the runner delivers them in order of increasing weight.

Israel has fled. There has been a great defeat. Your two sons are dead. The ark of God has been captured.

Any one of the first three would flatten a man. And the messenger, who has run twenty miles and is not a trained diplomat, has instinctively put them in the order in which a priest of Israel would feel them.

'As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell over backward from his seat by the side of the gate, and his neck was broken and he died, for the man was old and heavy.'

Read that carefully, because it is the last kind thing the Bible says about Eli.

He heard that the army was routed and stayed upright. He heard that there had been a great slaughter and stayed upright. He heard that both his sons were dead — the two boys he had protected for a lifetime, whose deaths he had been told about twice by prophets — and he stayed upright.

As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, he went over backwards.

The man whose whole indictment was that he honoured his sons above God died of the other news. It does not undo the years of doing nothing, and God's sentence stood and was carried out. But the narrator wants us to know where the old priest's heart finally broke, and it was not at his own family.

Then a detail that is almost comic and entirely without malice: for the man was old and heavy. He had grown fat, and the chapter that told us why has not been forgotten — he had been eating the choicest parts of Israel's offerings (2:29). The last physical fact recorded about him is the shape the sin left on his body.

'He had judged Israel forty years.'

An obituary of six words for a man who held the highest office in Israel for four decades.

Forty years is a full generation, the same span given to the best judges in the previous book. He was not a wicked man; he was a weak one, and his epitaph records the length of his service and nothing he did with it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Phinehas's widow is at the point of giving birth, and the news kills her: the ark captured, her father-in-law dead, her husband dead (v. 19). The women tell her she has borne a son, but she did not answer or pay attention (v. 20). She names the child Ichabod — the glory has departed from Israel — and then says it again, and the reason she gives the second time is only one of the three: for the ark of God has been captured (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Set her beside Hannah. One woman wept for years for a son and sang when she had to give him away; the other is told she has a son and will not turn her head. Between them stands everything that has happened to Israel in four chapters.
verseByVerse.examples: Shiloh is never a sanctuary again. Psalm 78 says what happened — he forsook his dwelling at Shiloh... and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe (Ps. 78:60-61) — and Jeremiah makes it the standing threat to Jerusalem: go now to my place that was in Shiloh... and see what I did to it (Jer. 7:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant, about to give birth. And when she heard the news that the ark of God was captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed and gave birth, for her pains came upon her. And about the time of her death the women attending her said to her, "Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son." But she did not answer or pay attention. And she named the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel!" because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband. And she said, "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant, about to give birth. And when she heard the news that the ark of God was captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed and gave birth, for her pains came upon her.'

In one afternoon she loses her husband, her father-in-law and her nation's holiest possession, and goes into labour.

The book has not mentioned her before and will not mention her again, and she is not given a name. She is the wife of one of the two worst men in Israel, and she is about to speak the chapter's title.

'And about the time of her death the women attending her said to her, "Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son." But she did not answer or pay attention.'

The women say the best thing anybody could say to a dying mother in that world, and she does not turn her head.

You have borne a son. That is the sentence Hannah wept through a decade of festivals to hear. It is the whole of what the first chapter of this book was about, and the announcement is made here to a woman who cannot be reached by it.

Set the two women together, because the writer has built the book so that we would. Hannah: childless, mocked, praying in silence, given a son, and singing about God. This woman: given a son, and unable to hear it.

Between them stand four chapters, and everything that has happened in them.

'And she named the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel!" because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband.'

She names her son for a national catastrophe.

Ichabod — i-kabod, no glory, or where is the glory. And kabod, glory, is a word about weight: the heaviness, the substance, the sheer significance of God among his people. She is saying that the weight has gone out of Israel.

The boy will carry that name all his life. Every time anyone addresses him for the next sixty years they will say aloud what happened on the day he was born.

'And she said, "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."'

She says it twice, and the second time she gives only one reason.

Verse 21 listed three: the ark, her father-in-law, her husband. Verse 22 keeps one. For the ark of God has been captured.

A woman dying in childbirth, who has just lost her husband and her husband's father, states the disaster in its true order of magnitude on her way out. Her private grief is real and she does not put it first.

Now weigh the verdict itself, because she is right and she is not entirely right.

She is right that something has gone. Shiloh is finished; it is never a working sanctuary again in the Bible. The psalmist looks back at this day and says it plainly: he forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind, and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe (Ps. 78:60-61). Centuries later Jeremiah stands in the gate of the temple in Jerusalem and tells a congregation who thought their building made them safe: go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it (Jer. 7:12).

Where she is wrong is in the geography. She thinks the glory left Israel. In fact it went to Ashdod, and the next chapter is about what it did when it got there.

Nobody rescued it by an Israelite army, or ransomed, or recovered by a raid. It went into a pagan temple as a trophy, and demolished the god it was set beside, and came home seven months later on a cart pulled by two cows, with nobody in Israel having lifted a finger.

God did not need the ark defended. He had let it be taken precisely because his people had begun to think he did.

And the last word on Ichabod's name is not in this book. Centuries after a woman at Shiloh gasped out that the glory had departed, John writes the answer in one sentence: and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

The verb John uses for dwelt means pitched his tent. The glory that left the tabernacle at Shiloh came back, and not in a box.

4.theology:
The right question, unanswered (v. 3). They named God as the agent of their own defeat and did not wait to hear why. Samuel was established from Dan to Beersheba and was at Shiloh when the messengers arrived. They had a word from God available and sent for furniture.

Religion as machinery. That it may come among us and save us makes the ark the saviour. It is Micah's sentence with a national budget behind it (Judg. 17:13). And the danger is precisely that the ark was genuine — God's own specification, the place he said he would meet them. Nobody here abandoned the true religion; they took the real thing and used it as a lever.

The enemy is nearer the truth (vv. 7-9). Plural gods, and the plagues misplaced into the wilderness — a garbled memory four centuries old among people who lost. And they think a person has arrived, and they are right. Note too that they do not send for Dagon, though chapter 5 proves they had him. Israel shouts; Philistia fights.

God let it be taken (v. 11). He allowed the sign of his own presence to go to pagans as a trophy rather than let his people go on using it as a charm. He is not obliged to protect the institutions that bear his name — he has let a sanctuary fall, a priesthood end and the ark itself go into captivity — and chapter 5 shows he was in no difficulty whatever while it happened.

Where Eli's heart finally broke (vv. 13, 18). His heart trembled for the ark before the runner came, and he stayed upright through the news of both his sons and fell at the fourth item. It undoes nothing; the sentence stood and was executed. But the narrator tells us where the break came, and it was not at his own family. His last recorded word is my son, to a stranger.

Ichabod, and the geography of glory. Kabod is weight — the substance of God among his people — and she is right that it has gone. Shiloh is never a sanctuary again; Psalm 78:60-61 says God forsook it, and Jeremiah makes it the standing threat to anyone who thinks a building guarantees safety (Jer. 7:12). Where she is wrong is the map. The glory did not leave Israel; it went to Ashdod, and demolished the god it was set beside, and came home on a cart with nobody lifting a finger. And the last word on her son's name is John's: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14) — dwelt being the verb for pitching a tent. The glory came back, and not in a box.
4.examples:
Then: A defeated army sent twenty miles for a gold-covered chest, cheered when it arrived, and lost seven times as many men as it had that morning. The enemy, who had the story of the exodus garbled and second-hand, were the only people on the field who took the God of Israel seriously.

Now: Two things. The first is the elders' question, and it repays finishing as well as copying: they were right to ask why God had let it happen and wrong to stop asking before he answered. And the second is harder. The ark was not a superstition; it was the genuine article, God's own arrangement. Which means the warning here is not about false religion but about the true one — the sound church, the right doctrine, the disciplines that have worked before — quietly reclassified as the thing that produces the outcome. God would rather let such a thing be taken from you than let you go on operating it.

5.title: Dagon Falls Before the Ark
5.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.<sup>2</sup>Then the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon.<sup>3</sup>And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place.<sup>4</sup>But when they rose early on the next morning, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon was left to him.<sup>5</sup>This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.<sup>6</sup>The hand of the LORD was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrified and afflicted them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory.<sup>7</sup>And when the men of Ashdod saw how things were, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god."<sup>8</sup>So they sent and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to Gath." So they brought the ark of the God of Israel there.<sup>9</sup>But after they had brought it around, the hand of the LORD was against the city, causing a very great panic, and he afflicted the men of the city, both young and old, so that tumors broke out on them.<sup>10</sup>So they sent the ark of God to Ekron.
