But as soon as the ark of God came to Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people."<sup>11</sup>They sent therefore and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill us and our people." For there was a deathly panic throughout the whole city. The hand of God was very heavy there.<sup>12</sup>The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven.
5.overview:
The Philistines take their trophy to Ashdod and set it in the temple beside Dagon — which is what victors did with a beaten nation's god, and the position is the caption: your god stands in my god's house. In the morning Dagon is face down on the ground before the ark, in the posture of worship, and they pick him up and stand him back in his place, because he cannot do it himself.

The second morning he is face down again, and his head and both his hands are lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk is left. The head that knows and the hands that act, removed and left on the doorstep — and the psalm supplies the caption: idols have hands but do not feel, and those who make them become like them.

Then the most damning verse in the chapter, and it is about a doorstep. Dagon's own priests respond to the dismemberment of their god by making a rule never to tread on that threshold. The custom outlives them all. The evidence was total, and it was converted into a superstition.

After that, tumours — in Ashdod, then Gath, then Ekron, where the people are shouting before the cart is unloaded. Two emergency summits of the five lords, and the sum of Philistine theology is a decision about which town to move the box to. Not one person turns to the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Face Down Before the Ark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines bring the ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod and set it in the house of Dagon, beside the idol (vv. 1-2). In the morning Dagon has fallen face down on the ground before the ark, and they stand him up again (v. 3). The next morning he is face down again — and this time his head and both his hands are lying cut off on the threshold, and only the trunk is left (v. 4). Which is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon do not tread on that threshold (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Setting the ark beside Dagon is not storage; it is tribute. The captured god's furniture is placed in the victor's temple to show whose hand won. Overnight, the victor is found face down in the posture of worship.
verseByVerse.examples: The head and the hands are what a god is supposed to have — the organs of thought and of action — and they are removed and left on the doorstep. The psalm says it exactly: idols have hands but do not feel, and those who make them become like them (Ps. 115:4-8).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. Then the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon. And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place. But when they rose early on the next morning, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon was left to him. This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. Then the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon.'

They put it in the temple, next to the statue, and that is a statement rather than a storage arrangement.

When one nation beat another in that world, the victors took the loser's god home and set it in their own sanctuary, in front of their own deity. It said: our god defeated your god, and here is your god standing in his house as a servant. The ark is a trophy, and its position beside Dagon is the caption.

Dagon was the chief god of the Philistines, worshipped along that coast for centuries, with temples at Ashdod and Gaza. He is the god Samson will eventually bring down a roof on, and the god whose house Saul's head will hang in (Judg. 16:23; 1 Chron. 10:10).

'And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place.'

They open the temple in the morning and their god is lying on his face in front of the prisoner.

The posture is the point, and the Hebrew makes it unmistakable: face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. That is not how something falls over. That is how a man worships.

Their response is one of the funniest sentences in the Old Testament. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place.

Consider what is involved in that. Two or three men lift their god off the floor, brush him down, and stand him up again, because he cannot do it himself. Then they presumably go home. This is the deity they had just credited with defeating the God of Israel, and he requires assistance to remain upright in his own building.

Isaiah spent a whole chapter on precisely this — a man cuts down a tree, burns half of it to cook his dinner, carves a god out of the other half, and bows to it, and does not have the wit to say is there not a lie in my right hand? (Isa. 44:14-20).

'But when they rose early on the next morning, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon was left to him.'

Morning two is not a repeat. It is an escalation, and the details are chosen.

The head and the hands. Those are exactly the two things a god is supposed to have — the head that knows and the hands that act — and they are off, and they are lying on the doorstep where everybody coming in has to step over them. Only the torso is left: the part that does nothing.

The psalm that describes idols could be a caption for this room. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see... they have hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk — and then the line that turns it on the worshipper: those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps. 115:5-8).

Note also who is not present. There is no Israelite army, no priest, no prophet, no prayer. Israel does not know where the ark is. The whole thing is conducted overnight, in a locked pagan temple, by God, with nobody on his side within twenty miles.

An old man in Ophrah once said the only thing that needed saying about this kind of god: if he is a god, let him contend for himself (Judg. 6:31). Dagon has now had two nights to contend, and he cannot stand up.

'This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.'

Here is the most damning verse in the chapter, and it is about a doorstep.

Their god has been decapitated in his own temple by a box, twice, and what the priesthood of Ashdod produces in response is a rule about where to put your feet. They step over the threshold for generations. The custom outlives the incident and everybody knows why it exists.

Nobody concludes anything. Nobody says the obvious thing, which is that if the LORD can do this to Dagon in Dagon's own house then Dagon is not worth the stone he is cut from. The evidence was total, and it was converted into a superstition about a doorstep.

That is what the human heart does with evidence it does not want. It does not deny it — these men remembered the event so exactly that they were still avoiding the spot centuries later — it simply declines to draw the conclusion, and builds a small ritual around the place where the conclusion should have been.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Hand of the LORD Was Heavy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hand of the LORD is heavy on Ashdod, and the people are afflicted with tumours (v. 6). They convene the five lords and pass the ark to Gath, where the same thing happens to young and old (vv. 7-9). Gath sends it to Ekron, and Ekron cries out before it even arrives: they have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people (v. 10). So the lords are gathered again and the decision is to send it home, because there is a deathly panic through the whole city (v. 11). The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The hand of the LORD was heavy is the language of Egypt (Ex. 9:3), and so is the cry going up. The Philistines had told each other four chapters back that this was the God who did Egypt, and they were about to find out at first hand.
verseByVerse.examples: Not one person in Philistia turns to the LORD. Five cities, seven months, a demolished god and a plague, and the sum of the response is a committee deciding where to send the box next. Chapter 6 will show Israel doing the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the LORD was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrified and afflicted them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory. And when the men of Ashdod saw how things were, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god." So they sent and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to Gath." So they brought the ark of the God of Israel there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The hand of the LORD was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrified and afflicted them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory.'

The god of Ashdod is dealt with, and then the city is.

The hand of the LORD was heavy is a phrase with a history, and the Philistines themselves supplied it four chapters ago. When Moses warned Pharaoh what was coming, the words were: behold, the hand of the LORD will fall with a very severe plague upon your livestock (Ex. 9:3). The men at Aphek had said this was the God who struck the Egyptians. They were right, and the demonstration is now in their own towns.

What the tumours were is not certain and little in the sense depends on it. What the text is certain about is whose hand it was.

'And when the men of Ashdod saw how things were, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god."'

They have understood the situation exactly and drawn the wrong conclusion from it.

Read what they say. His hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god. They know who is doing this. They know their own god has lost. They state the whole case correctly in one sentence.

What they decide is that it must not remain with us.

'So they sent and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to Gath." So they brought the ark of the God of Israel there.'

A summit is convened, and its resolution is to move the problem to another city.

Gath is not consulted, so far as we are told. The men of Ashdod have a god they cannot fight and cannot get rid of, and the best that five rulers can manage between them is to pass him along.

verseByVerse.quote: But after they had brought it around, the hand of the LORD was against the city, causing a very great panic, and he afflicted the men of the city, both young and old, so that tumors broke out on them. So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But as soon as the ark of God came to Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people." They sent therefore and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill us and our people." For there was a deathly panic throughout the whole city. The hand of God was very heavy there. The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But after they had brought it around, the hand of the LORD was against the city, causing a very great panic, and he afflicted the men of the city, both young and old, so that tumors broke out on them.'

Gath gets what Ashdod got, and the writer adds two words: both young and old. Nobody is outside it.

'So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But as soon as the ark of God came to Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people."'

By the third city the news has travelled ahead of the cart.

Ekron does not wait to find out. The people are shouting before it is unloaded, and their complaint is not against the God of Israel but against their own leadership: they have brought around to us the ark... to kill us. The lords of the Philistines are now moving a weapon between their own towns and the citizens can see it.

'They sent therefore and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill us and our people." For there was a deathly panic throughout the whole city. The hand of God was very heavy there.'

The second summit reverses the first. The ark goes home.

Weigh how they put it: let it return to its own place. They are not releasing a prisoner or restoring stolen property; they are getting something out of the house.

'The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven.'

The last verse of the chapter is written in the language of Egypt again. The cry of the city went up to heaven — and in Egypt, on the night of the firstborn, there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead (Ex. 12:30).

Now stand back and take in what these two chapters have done.

Israel lost the ark because it treated the ark as a machine. The elders sent for it, cheered when it came, and were slaughtered. The conclusion any onlooker would draw is that the God of Israel had been beaten and his box had been taken as a prize.

Then, with no Israelite present, no army in the field, no prophet praying and nobody in the covenant nation even knowing where it was, God ran a campaign through five Philistine cities from inside a locked temple. He knocked down their god, dismembered him on his own doorstep, and made the rulers of Philistia hold two emergency summits about how to get rid of him.

He did not need defending. That is the point of chapter 5, and it is the answer to Ichabod. The glory had not departed; it had gone on tour.

Remember that whenever the church looks defeated and its enemies look established. God has been carried off as a trophy before, and the trophy demolished the temple it was displayed in.

Yet not one Philistine turns to him. Five cities, seven months, a broken idol, a plague, and a nation that says out loud his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god, and nobody worships. They want the God of Israel out of town.

Hold that, because the next chapter shows Israel saying exactly the same thing.

5.theology:
God needs no defending. With no Israelite present, no army in the field, nobody praying and nobody in the covenant nation even knowing where the ark was, God ran a campaign through five Philistine cities from inside a locked pagan temple. Israel could not protect the ark, and he did not require it to. That is the answer to Ichabod: the glory had not departed, it had gone on tour.

Let him contend for himself. Joash said the only thing worth saying about a god who needs defending (Judg. 6:31). Dagon had two nights to contend and could not stand up — and had to be lifted back into position by his own worshippers, which is Isaiah's whole argument about idols in one image (Isa. 44:14-20).

The doorstep (v. 5). This is what the human heart does with evidence it does not want. It does not deny it — they remembered the event so exactly that they were still stepping over the spot generations later — it simply declines to draw the conclusion, and builds a small ritual where the conclusion should have been.

Right diagnosis, wrong conclusion (v. 7). His hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god. They state the entire case correctly and decide that the answer is to move it to Gath. Knowing exactly who God is and wanting him somewhere else is a position a person can hold indefinitely, and Israel takes it up at 6:20.

The language of Egypt. The hand of the LORD was heavy (Ex. 9:3) and the cry of the city went up to heaven (cf. Ex. 12:30). The men at Aphek had said this was the God who struck the Egyptians (4:8). They were right, and the demonstration arrived in their own towns.
5.examples:
Then: A nation put the God of Israel in its temple as a prize, found its own god face down before him twice and in pieces the second time, lost its health in three cities over seven months, held two emergency summits — and produced, as its entire response, a rule about not stepping on a doorstep.

Now: Two things. When the church looks beaten and its opponents look established, remember that God has been carried off as a trophy before, and the trophy demolished the building it was displayed in. He is never in the difficulty his people assume he is in. And then the harder one: verse 5 is not really about Philistines. The question it puts is what you have done with the evidence you already have — whether there is some fact about God you have quietly refused to draw the conclusion from, and built a small habit around instead.

6.title: The Ark Returns
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The ark of the LORD was in the country of the Philistines seven months.<sup>2</sup>And the Philistines called for the priests and the diviners and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us with what we shall send it to its place."<sup>3</sup>They said, "If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty, but by all means return him a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand does not turn away from you."<sup>4</sup>And they said, "What is the guilt offering that we shall return to him?" They answered, "Five golden tumors and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines, for the same plague was on all of you and on your lords.<sup>5</sup>So you must make images of your tumors and images of your mice that ravage the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you and your gods and your land.<sup>6</sup>Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? After he had dealt severely with them, did they not send the people away, and they departed?<sup>7</sup>Now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke, and yoke the cows to the cart, but take their calves home, away from them.<sup>8</sup>And take the ark of the LORD and place it on the cart and put in a box at its side the figures of gold, which you are returning to him as a guilt offering. Then send it off and let it go its way<sup>9</sup>and watch. If it goes up on the way to its own land, to Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has done us this great harm, but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that struck us; it happened to us by coincidence."<sup>10</sup>The men did so, and took two milk cows and yoked them to the cart and shut up their calves at home.<sup>11</sup>And they put the ark of the LORD on the cart and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors.<sup>12</sup>And the cows went straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, and the lords of the Philistines went after them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.<sup>13</sup>Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. And when they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, they rejoiced to see it.<sup>14</sup>The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A great stone was there. And they split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box that was beside it, in which were the golden figures, and set them upon the great stone. And the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices on that day to the LORD.<sup>16</sup>And when the five lords of the Philistines saw it, they returned that day to Ekron.<sup>17</sup>These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron,<sup>18</sup>and the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both fortified cities and unwalled villages. The great stone beside which they set down the ark of the LORD is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.<sup>19</sup>And he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the LORD. He struck seventy men of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow.<sup>20</sup>Then the men of Beth-shemesh said, "Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up away from us?"<sup>21</sup>So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you."
6.overview:
After seven months the Philistines ask their priests how to send the ark back, and the advice is unexpectedly good. Do not send it empty; return a guilt offering — and the word is asham, the technical term from Leviticus. Five golden tumours and five golden mice, one for each city, models of the very things that hurt them, cast in gold. And then a history lesson from pagan diviners: why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? They have the exodus second-hand and four centuries old, and they reason from it correctly — which is more than the elders of Israel managed when they sent for the ark in the first place.

Then a test designed to fail. Two nursing cows that have never worn a yoke, their calves shut up behind them, a new cart, no driver. Untrained animals do not pull straight and nursing mothers go back to their young; the diviners say plainly that if the cart ends in a ditch the honest verdict is coincidence. And the cows walk straight down one road to Beth-shemesh, turning neither right nor left, lowing as they went — calling for their calves the whole way while their legs carry them the other direction.

Beth-shemesh looks up from the wheat harvest and rejoices. The cart becomes firewood and the cows become the offering; nothing is kept. And then seventy men die for looking into the ark, and the village asks two questions. The first is the best thing anyone says in three chapters: who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? The second is Ashdod's: to whom shall he go up away from us?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Guilt Offering, and a Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After seven months the Philistines call in their priests and diviners: what shall we do with the ark? (vv. 1-2). The advice is to send it back with a guilt offering — five golden tumours and five golden mice, one for each of the five lords — and to give glory to the God of Israel (vv. 3-5). Then a warning drawn from history: why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? (v. 6). And a test: a new cart, two milk cows that have never worn a yoke, their calves shut up at home, and nobody driving. If the cows walk to Beth-shemesh, it was the LORD; if not, it was coincidence (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The word they use in v. 3 is asham, which is the technical term for the guilt offering of Leviticus 5-6. Philistine diviners reach for the right category, and their instinct that you do not send God away empty-handed is sound.
verseByVerse.examples: The test is built to fail. Cows that have never been yoked do not pull straight, and cows separated from their calves go back to the calves; everything about the arrangement is designed to produce the wrong answer. It is honest experimental reasoning, and it is better than anything the elders of Israel managed in chapter 4.

verseByVerse.quote: The ark of the LORD was in the country of the Philistines seven months. And the Philistines called for the priests and the diviners and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us with what we shall send it to its place." They said, "If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty, but by all means return him a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand does not turn away from you." And they said, "What is the guilt offering that we shall return to him?" They answered, "Five golden tumors and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines, for the same plague was on all of you and on your lords. So you must make images of your tumors and images of your mice that ravage the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you and your gods and your land. Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? After he had dealt severely with them, did they not send the people away, and they departed?
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The ark of the LORD was in the country of the Philistines seven months. And the Philistines called for the priests and the diviners and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us with what we shall send it to its place."'

Seven months, and by the end of it the question is not whether to send it back but how.

'They said, "If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty, but by all means return him a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand does not turn away from you."'

The word the diviners reach for is a technical one, and they have it right.

Guilt offering is asham, the sacrifice of Leviticus 5 and 6, brought when a person has wronged God or a neighbour and must make restitution with something added. It is the category for damage done, and it is exactly the right one: they have taken something that was not theirs and there is a debt.

Their instinct is sound in another way too. Do not send it empty. You do not dismiss the God of Israel from your territory with an apology and nothing in your hands.

'And they said, "What is the guilt offering that we shall return to him?" They answered, "Five golden tumors and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines, for the same plague was on all of you and on your lords."'

Five and five, one set for each of the five cities, because the affliction was national.

The images are of the thing that hurt them. Models of their own tumours and of the mice that ravaged the land, cast in gold and sent back with the ark — an admission, in the most expensive material available, of exactly what God did to them and that he did it.

The mice have made many readers think of plague carried by rodents, and it is a reasonable guess. It is a guess, and nothing in the passage turns on it.

'"So you must make images of your tumors and images of your mice that ravage the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you and your gods and your land."'

Give glory to the God of Israel. A Philistine priest says it, and it is the correct instruction.

Note what it is not. It is not worship him, or turn to him, or abandon Dagon. Their own gods are still in the sentence: his hand from off you and your gods and your land. They intend to acknowledge his power, pay the debt, and keep their religion.

'"Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? After he had dealt severely with them, did they not send the people away, and they departed?"'

Here are pagan diviners preaching the exodus to their own nation.

Take the reasoning at full weight, because it is good. Egypt tried this. Egypt hardened its heart against this God, and the hardening did not work, and in the end they let the people go anyway after enormous loss. Learn from a nation that has already run the experiment.

They know the story. They have it four hundred years old and second-hand, and in chapter 4 they had the details muddled — and they can reason from it correctly to their own situation, which is more than the elders of Israel managed when they sent for the ark in the first place.

Israel had the exodus in writing and used it to justify a superstition. Philistia had it as a rumour and drew the right conclusion.

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke, and yoke the cows to the cart, but take their calves home, away from them. And take the ark of the LORD and place it on the cart and put in a box at its side the figures of gold, which you are returning to him as a guilt offering. Then send it off and let it go its way and watch. If it goes up on the way to its own land, to Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has done us this great harm, but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that struck us; it happened to us by coincidence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke, and yoke the cows to the cart, but take their calves home, away from them."'

Now the test, and every element of it is chosen to make the answer they want impossible.

Go through the arrangement. A new cart, never used for common work. Two milk cows — still nursing, and therefore with the strongest instinct an animal has running in them. Cows on which there has never come a yoke: untrained, unbroken, animals that have never pulled anything and do not know how to walk in a straight line under a beam.

Then the cruel refinement: take their calves home, away from them. The calves are shut up behind them, in the byre, calling.

'"And take the ark of the LORD and place it on the cart and put in a box at its side the figures of gold, which you are returning to him as a guilt offering. Then send it off and let it go its way and watch."'

Send it off and let it go its way and watch. No driver. Nobody leading them, nobody with a goad. The cart is pointed at nothing in particular and released.

'"If it goes up on the way to its own land, to Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has done us this great harm, but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that struck us; it happened to us by coincidence."'

Here is the hypothesis, stated in advance, with both outcomes specified.

That is what makes this remarkable. They have not designed a test they can pass. Untrained cows will not pull straight; nursing cows will turn back to their calves within a hundred yards. The natural result — the overwhelmingly likely result — is a cart in a ditch and two animals trotting home, and the diviners say plainly that if that happens the honest conclusion is coincidence.

They have built an experiment that will exonerate chance unless God overrules the strongest instinct in the animal.

Compare it with what Israel did four chapters ago. The elders asked the right question, refused to wait for an answer, and reached for the object. These men ask a question, design a fair test, name what each outcome would prove, and then watch.

There is a lesson in that which has nothing to do with divination. Honest enquiry that is genuinely prepared to be told coincidence is a better thing than religious certainty that never tested anything — and God, as it happens, is not reluctant to answer it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cows are yoked, the calves shut in, the ark and the box of gold loaded (vv. 10-11). And the cows go straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, with the five lords following behind as far as the border (v. 12). Beth-shemesh is reaping wheat in the valley and looks up and rejoices (v. 13). The cart stops at a great stone in Joshua's field; they break up the cart for firewood and offer the cows (v. 14). The Levites take the ark down, and sacrifices are made (v. 15). The lords watch and go home to Ekron (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Lowing as they went is the sentence that settles it. Every instinct in those animals was calling them back to their calves, and their legs carried them the other way down one road without deviating. The Philistines got their answer and it was not ambiguous.
verseByVerse.examples: The cart that carried the ark becomes the fire, and the cows that pulled it become the offering. Nothing is kept. And a great stone in a wheatfield is still there when the book is written, a witness to this day.

verseByVerse.quote: The men did so, and took two milk cows and yoked them to the cart and shut up their calves at home. And they put the ark of the LORD on the cart and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors. And the cows went straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, and the lords of the Philistines went after them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The men did so, and took two milk cows and yoked them to the cart and shut up their calves at home. And they put the ark of the LORD on the cart and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors.'

They do it exactly as prescribed, and the calves are shut in.

'And the cows went straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, and the lords of the Philistines went after them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.'

Three details in that verse, and each one closes off an escape route.

Straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh: the named town, the one the test specified, the nearest Israelite settlement over the border and a Levitical city. Along one highway: they did not wander and find it. They turned neither to the right nor to the left: the phrase used in the law for perfect obedience, applied here to two cows.

In the middle of it, the detail that makes the whole scene: lowing as they went.

They are calling for their calves the entire way. Every instinct in those animals is screaming to turn round, and their voices are doing it, and their legs are carrying them steadily in the opposite direction down a road they have never walked, pulling a load they have never pulled, without a driver.

The Philistines wanted to know whether this was the hand of God or coincidence. They were given an answer that could not be misread, and the writer lets the animals' distress stand in the middle of it, because that is what it cost to make the answer unambiguous.

The five lords walk behind the cart all the way to the border. They follow it to the edge of their own territory, watching, and then they stop and look.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. And when they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, they rejoiced to see it. The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A great stone was there. And they split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD. And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box that was beside it, in which were the golden figures, and set them upon the great stone. And the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices on that day to the LORD. And when the five lords of the Philistines saw it, they returned that day to Ekron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. And when they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, they rejoiced to see it.'

It is harvest, and the men are in the field with sickles, and they look up.

Picture what comes over the rise: two cows, lowing, pulling a new cart with no driver, and on the cart the ark of the covenant of the LORD, which nobody in Israel has seen for seven months and which everybody assumed was lost forever in a Philistine temple.

They rejoiced. Of course they did.

'The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A great stone was there. And they split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.'

The cart stops of its own accord at a stone in a named man's field, and Beth-shemesh does the right thing with everything in front of it.

The cart becomes the firewood. The cows become the offering. Nothing is kept — not the new cart, which was valuable, and not two healthy milk cows, which were a small fortune to a farming village. Everything that touched this journey goes up in smoke.

'And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box that was beside it, in which were the golden figures, and set them upon the great stone. And the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices on that day to the LORD.'

The Levites handle the ark, which is correct: Beth-shemesh was one of the towns given to the Levites, and lifting the ark was their work.

So far everything in the village is being done properly, and the day is a festival.

'And when the five lords of the Philistines saw it, they returned that day to Ekron.'

They watched the whole thing from the border — the arrival, the sacrifice, the joy — and then went home.

Nothing is recorded of what they thought. They had their answer: it was the hand of the God of Israel, not coincidence. They had said so in advance. And they turned round and went back to Ekron, and Dagon's temple was rebuilt in Ashdod, and Philistine history carried on.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron, and the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both fortified cities and unwalled villages. The great stone beside which they set down the ark of the LORD is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron, and the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both fortified cities and unwalled villages.'

The writer stops the story to list the contents of the box, city by city.

Five golden tumours for the five capitals, and golden mice not merely for the five but for every settlement they governed, fortified towns and open villages alike. The plague had reached the whole country and the restitution is itemised to match.

There is something almost legal about the care of it. This is a schedule of damages, drawn up by the debtor.

'The great stone beside which they set down the ark of the LORD is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.'

The stone is still there when the book is written.

Israel had a habit of leaving stones about — twelve out of the Jordan at Gilgal, one under the oak at Shechem, and in the next chapter Samuel will set up another and give it a name. They are not monuments to human achievement. They are answers to a question a child might ask years later, and this one answers: the ark came back by itself, and it stopped here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — Who Is Able to Stand?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then God strikes some of the men of Beth-shemesh because they looked upon the ark of the LORD, and there is great mourning (v. 19). And the men of Beth-shemesh ask two questions. The first is the right one: who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? The second is the same one Ashdod asked: and to whom shall he go up away from us? (v. 20). So they send to Kiriath-jearim: come down and take it up to you (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The first question is the best thing anyone says in these three chapters, and it is the question the ark exists to raise. Nobody may look into it; that was the point of the covering and the poles and the rules.
verseByVerse.examples: And then the sting. Philistia said the ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us (5:7). Israel says to whom shall he go up away from us? Two nations have now seen what God is, and both have asked for him to be moved somewhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: And he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the LORD. He struck seventy men of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow. Then the men of Beth-shemesh said, "Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up away from us?" So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the LORD. He struck seventy men of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow.'

The festival ends in a funeral, and the reason given is that they looked.

Two things first. The number is textually difficult — the Hebrew as it stands can be read as fifty thousand and seventy, which is impossible for a village, and the ESV prints the seventy that the sense requires. Nothing in the passage depends on the figure.

What the passage depends on is because they looked upon the ark of the LORD.

The law was not vague about this. The ark travelled covered; Aaron and his sons put the veil over it before the Kohathites came near, and the warning was explicit — they must not touch or look at the holy things, lest they die (Num. 4:5, 15, 20). It was carried on poles that were never removed, precisely so that nobody would handle it.

So this is not God being touchy about a glance. It is a village that has spent a joyful afternoon growing steadily more familiar with the most dangerous object in the world.

It is also deliberately placed. Chapter 5 has just shown God destroying Dagon and afflicting five pagan cities, and a reader could easily finish it thinking that holiness is dangerous to Philistines. Verse 19 says it is dangerous full stop. The ark did not become safe when it crossed the border.

Uzzah will discover the same thing on the same journey's last stage, generations later, when he puts out his hand to steady it and dies (2 Sam. 6:6-7).

'Then the men of Beth-shemesh said, "Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up away from us?"'

Two questions, and they could not be further apart.

The first is the best sentence anybody speaks in these three chapters. Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? That is the right question. It is the question the whole apparatus of the ark existed to raise, and it is the question the elders never asked when they sent for it as a battlefield charm. Isaiah asks it in the temple and thinks he is finished (Isa. 6:5). The answer, when it finally comes, is a person.

Then the second question undoes the first. To whom shall he go up away from us?

Now go back four verses in the previous chapter and hear Ashdod: the ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us (5:7).

They are the same sentence. A pagan city and a Levitical town in Israel, both having seen exactly who this is, and both asking for him to be taken somewhere else.

That is the sting of the chapter, and it should not be softened. Israel's instinct on meeting the holiness of God is identical to Philistia's. The Philistines wanted him out because he was breaking their god and their bodies. Beth-shemesh wants him out because seventy men are dead. In neither town does anybody say teach us how to come near.

'So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you."'

So the ark is passed on again, and this time by Israelites.

It has now been moved from Shiloh to a battlefield, from a battlefield to Ashdod, from Ashdod to Gath, from Gath to Ekron, from Ekron to Beth-shemesh — and now to Kiriath-jearim, where it will sit in a private house on a hill for twenty years, and then longer, until David finally goes to fetch it.

Nobody wants it near them. That is the honest summary of three chapters, and it is why the question in verse 20 matters so much.

Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? The men of Beth-shemesh meant it as a reason to send him away, and it is in fact the question the gospel exists to answer. Somebody was able to stand there, and did, on our behalf, and the whole point of him is that he came towards people rather than being sent up the road to somebody else.

6.theology:
Pagans reason better than Israel did. The diviners reach for the right sacrificial category (v. 3), tell their nation not to repeat Pharaoh's mistake (v. 6), and design a fair test with both outcomes named in advance (v. 9). Israel had the exodus in writing and used it to justify a superstition; Philistia had it as a rumour and drew the right conclusion. Honest enquiry genuinely prepared to be told coincidence is a better thing than religious certainty that never tested anything — and God is not reluctant to answer it.

Acknowledgement is not conversion (v. 5). Give glory to the God of Israel — and in the same breath, his hand from off you and your gods. They intend to admit his power, settle the debt, and keep their religion. The five lords watch the sacrifice at Beth-shemesh from the border and go home to Ekron.

Lowing as they went (v. 12). Every instinct in those animals was calling them back and their legs carried them the other way down one road without deviating. The writer leaves the distress in the middle of the miracle, because that is what it cost to make the answer unambiguous.

Holiness did not become safe at the border (v. 19). Chapter 5 could leave a reader thinking God is dangerous to Philistines. He is dangerous. The law had been explicit — the ark travelled covered, carried on poles, and the Kohathites were not to look at the holy things lest they die (Num. 4:20). A village spent a joyful afternoon growing familiar with the most dangerous object in the world. Uzzah finds the same thing on the last stage of the same journey (2 Sam. 6:6-7).

The two questions (v. 20). Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? is the question the ark existed to raise, and Isaiah asks it in the temple and thinks he is finished (Isa. 6:5). And then the same men ask Ashdod's question — to whom shall he go up away from us? (cf. 5:7). A pagan city and a Levitical town, both having seen who this is, both asking for him to be moved on. Nobody in either place says teach us how to come near.
6.examples:
Then: Five pagan rulers followed an unmanned cart to the border of their own country to see whether the God who had wrecked their temple and their health was real or whether they had been unlucky — and having been given an answer they themselves called decisive, they turned round and went home and rebuilt the temple.

Now: Two things, and the second is the uncomfortable one. First, the diviners' test is a better model of honest thinking than most religious certainty: they specified in advance what each outcome would prove and were genuinely willing to conclude coincidence. Second, verse 20. The right question and the wrong one come out of the same mouths in the same breath. It is entirely possible to grasp that God is holy, to be genuinely frightened of it, and to respond by wanting him at a manageable distance — and that instinct is not pagan. It was Israel's, in a Levitical town, on the day the ark came home.

7.title: Return to the LORD
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD and brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to have charge of the ark of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years, and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And Samuel said to all the house of Israel, "If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines."<sup>4</sup>So the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and they served the LORD only.<sup>5</sup>Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you."<sup>6</sup>So they gathered at Mizpah and drew water and poured it out before the LORD and fasted on that day and said there, "We have sinned against the LORD." And Samuel judged the people of Israel at Mizpah.<sup>7</sup>Now when the Philistines heard that the people of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. And when the people of Israel heard of it, they were afraid of the Philistines.<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel said to Samuel, "Do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines."<sup>9</sup>So Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. And Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.<sup>10</sup>As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines and struck them, as far as below Beth-car.<sup>12</sup>Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, "Till now the LORD has helped us."<sup>13</sup>So the Philistines were subdued and did not again enter the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.<sup>14</sup>The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel delivered their territory from the hand of the Philistines. There was peace also between Israel and the Amorites.<sup>15</sup>Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.<sup>16</sup>And he went on a circuit year by year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. And he judged Israel in all these places.<sup>17</sup>Then he would return to Ramah, for his home was there, and there also he judged Israel. And he built there an altar to the LORD.
7.overview:
The ark ends up in a private house on a hill, and twenty years pass in which all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD — a whole generation genuinely aching for him. And the next verse tells us what was on their shelves the entire time. Samuel puts a hinge in it: if you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods. He does not doubt the grief; he refuses to let it count as repentance by itself. Longing is not returning — and after twenty years, one man saying plainly what was required was enough. They put them away.

At Mizpah they draw water and pour it out, fast, and confess in four words: we have sinned against the LORD. And the moment they repent, the Philistines march — which is a pattern anyone who has done business with God will recognise, and is not evidence that the surrender was a mistake.

Then the sentence the whole book turns on. In chapter 4 they said let us bring the ark... that it may come among us and save us. Here they say do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us, that he may save us. The second half of each is nearly identical; everything before it has changed. Then they sent for equipment; now they ask for prayer.

The Philistines attack while the lamb is still burning, and God answers with thunder — the very thing Hannah sang about when there was no war and nobody listening (2:10), with her son now standing at the altar. And Samuel sets up a stone on the ground where the ark was lost and takes the name back: Ebenezer. Till now the LORD has helped us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Twenty Years of Longing, and One Instruction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Kiriath-jearim fetches the ark and lodges it in Abinadab's house on the hill, consecrating his son Eleazar to keep it (v. 1). Twenty years pass, and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD (v. 2). Then Samuel speaks for the first time since chapter 4: if you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only (v. 3). And they did — they put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth and served the LORD only (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty years of lamenting after the LORD with the Ashtaroth still in the house. Longing is not returning, and Samuel refuses to let the two be confused. His test is not a feeling but a removal.
verseByVerse.examples: Note the order in v. 3, because it is the order of every real repentance: if you are returning comes first, and the putting away is how you would know. The idols go out because the heart has turned, not in order to turn it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD and brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to have charge of the ark of the LORD. From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years, and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD. And Samuel said to all the house of Israel, "If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines." So the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and they served the LORD only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD and brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to have charge of the ark of the LORD.'

Its journey ends in a private house on a hill, in the care of one man.

There is no sanctuary to take it to. Shiloh is finished. So a family takes it in, and a son is set apart to look after it, and that is the arrangement for the next two decades — longer, in fact, because it is still there when David comes for it.

'From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years, and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD.'

Twenty years, and one clause to describe them: all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD.

The verb is a strong one — mourning, grieving, longing after him. This is not a nation that has forgotten God; it is a nation that misses him. Twenty years of ache.

Now read the next verse, which tells us what was in their houses the whole time.

'And Samuel said to all the house of Israel, "If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines."'

They had the idols the entire twenty years.

That is the thing to see here, and it explains why the lamenting achieved nothing. A whole generation grieved after the LORD, felt the loss of him keenly, knew that something enormous had gone out of the national life — and kept the Ashtaroth on the shelf.

Samuel's sentence separates the two with a hinge. If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods. He does not doubt the sincerity of their grief; he refuses to let it count as repentance on its own.

To long is not to return. A person can be genuinely and painfully aware of distance from God for years and never take one thing out of the house, and the ache itself can become a substitute for the removal — because it feels like devotion, and it costs nothing.

Note the order, though, because the order matters and it is easy to get backwards. If you are returning... then put away. The idols go out because the heart has turned; they do not go out in order to turn it. Samuel is not prescribing a method for producing repentance. He is naming the thing that would show it had happened.

Now the two positive clauses, which are as important as the negative one. Direct your heart to the LORD — the word is about fixing, aiming, setting something firmly in one direction. And serve him only. Not chiefly. Not first among several. Only.

'So the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and they served the LORD only.'

They did it.

One verse, and after twenty years of grief the thing that had been standing in the way is carried out of the house. There is no record of an argument, a delay or a negotiated compromise. Samuel says put them away and they put them away.

It is the first national repentance in this history, and it took one man saying plainly what was actually required.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel gathers all Israel at Mizpah to pray for them (v. 5). They draw water and pour it out before the LORD, fast, and say we have sinned against the LORD (v. 6). The Philistines hear that Israel has assembled and come up, and Israel is afraid (v. 7). And the request they make is the opposite of chapter 4's: do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us (v. 8). Samuel offers a nursing lamb as a whole burnt offering and cries out, and the LORD answers him (v. 9). As the offering burns, the LORD thundered with a mighty sound against the Philistines and threw them into confusion (v. 10). Israel pursues, and Samuel sets up a stone: till now the LORD has helped us (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Compare the two assemblies. At Aphek they sent for a box and gave a shout that shook the earth, and lost thirty thousand men. Here they ask a man to keep praying. Same enemy, same nation, and one of these is a request for God and the other for equipment.
verseByVerse.examples: The thunder answers Hannah exactly. She had sung that the adversaries of the LORD would be broken and that against them he will thunder in heaven (2:10), when there was no war and nobody listening. Her son is standing at the altar when it happens.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you." So they gathered at Mizpah and drew water and poured it out before the LORD and fasted on that day and said there, "We have sinned against the LORD." And Samuel judged the people of Israel at Mizpah. Now when the Philistines heard that the people of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. And when the people of Israel heard of it, they were afraid of the Philistines. And the people of Israel said to Samuel, "Do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines." So Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. And Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you."'

He calls a national assembly, and what he offers to do there is pray.

Mizpah means watchtower, and it will be the place where Saul is presented as king in chapter 10. For now it is a hilltop where a prophet has told a nation to meet him.

'So they gathered at Mizpah and drew water and poured it out before the LORD and fasted on that day and said there, "We have sinned against the LORD." And Samuel judged the people of Israel at Mizpah.'

Three actions, and the first is unusual enough to be worth a moment.

They drew water and poured it out before the LORD. Nothing in the law prescribes this, and it appears nowhere else in quite this form. The best sense of it is what David does with the water from Bethlehem's well — he refuses to drink it and pours it out to the LORD (2 Sam. 23:16). It is a gesture of total emptying: this is ours, and we are giving it away, and it cannot be got back.

Then fasting, and then the confession, and the confession is four words long. We have sinned against the LORD. No explanation, no mitigation, no account of what the Philistines had done to them.

'Now when the Philistines heard that the people of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. And when the people of Israel heard of it, they were afraid of the Philistines.'

The moment the nation repents, the enemy attacks.

From the Philistine side it is sensible: a large gathering of Israelites on a hill looks like a muster, and you break that up before it becomes an army. But name the timing for what it is. Israel has just put away its idols, fasted, confessed and assembled to pray, and the immediate consequence is that the lords of the Philistines march.

That is a pattern anyone who has done business with God will recognise. The trouble frequently arrives immediately after the surrender, not before it, and it is not evidence that the surrender was a mistake.

'And the people of Israel said to Samuel, "Do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines."'

Now put this sentence beside the one in chapter 4 and the whole book turns on the difference.

Then: let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies (4:3).

Now: do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines.

The last half of each sentence is nearly identical — save us from our enemies. Everything before it has changed. In chapter 4 the subject of save was a box; here it is he. Then they sent for equipment; now they ask for prayer. Then they organised a transport; now they beg a man not to stop interceding.

Same nation, same enemy, and shortly the same ground. One of these produced thirty thousand dead.

'So Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. And Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.'

A nursing lamb — still with its mother, the youngest and most valuable kind — offered whole. Nothing kept back, nothing eaten.

Then the two clauses that carry the chapter: Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.

verseByVerse.quote: As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel. And the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines and struck them, as far as below Beth-car. Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, "Till now the LORD has helped us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel.'

The attack comes while the lamb is still burning, and God answers with weather.

The LORD thundered with a mighty sound. No angel, no plague, no Israelite tactics: a noise out of the sky at the moment of the assault, and an army that had beaten Israel comprehensively twice in this book goes to pieces in front of it.

Now hear where that verb came from.

Twenty-five years earlier a woman stood in this same story and sang: the adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven (2:10). She had no army, no standing and no reason to expect anything of the kind; she had just handed over a toddler at a corrupt shrine.

Her son is standing at the altar when it happens, and the thing she sang about is going on over his head.

'And the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines and struck them, as far as below Beth-car.'

Israel does the pursuing, which is real work and is theirs to do. God broke them; the men of Israel chased them.

'Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, "Till now the LORD has helped us."'

He sets up a stone, and the name he gives it is the name of the place where the ark was lost.

Go back to the first verse of chapter 4: they encamped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek. That is where Israel fetched the ark, gave the great shout, lost thirty thousand men and watched the covenant chest driven away on a Philistine cart.

Ebenezer means stone of help. The place had carried that name through the worst defeat in Israel's history, and it had been a bitter joke for twenty years. Samuel takes the name back.

Now weigh what he actually said, because the stone is more careful than the hymn that came from it. Till now the LORD has helped us.

Till now — hitherto, up to this point. It is not a prediction. Samuel does not say the LORD will always help us, or that the Philistines are finished forever, or that Israel has turned a corner it cannot turn back round. He marks the ground as far as they have come and says: this far, he has helped.

That is what a memorial stone is for, and it is why they were set up all over that country — twelve out of the Jordan, one under the oak at Shechem, one in a wheatfield at Beth-shemesh. They do not tell you what is coming. They stop you forgetting what happened, so that when the next trouble arrives you have something in the landscape to argue from.

Anyone can raise this stone tonight. Not God will fix it, which you do not know, but till now the LORD has helped us, which you do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — All the Days of Samuel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines are subdued and do not enter Israel's territory again, and the hand of the LORD is against them all the days of Samuel (v. 13). The captured cities from Ekron to Gath are restored, and there is peace with the Amorites too (v. 14). Samuel judges Israel all his life, riding a yearly circuit to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah and returning to his home at Ramah, where he also judges — and where he builds an altar to the LORD (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The territory lost in chapter 4 comes back. Not by a campaign to recover it, and not because Israel grew strong: it is handed back after one afternoon in which God thundered and a nation had already thrown away its idols.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause is the quiet one. Samuel builds an altar at home. The man who grew up in a sanctuary that God abandoned does not try to rebuild Shiloh; he sets up an altar where he lives and goes on circuit to the people.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Philistines were subdued and did not again enter the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel delivered their territory from the hand of the Philistines. There was peace also between Israel and the Amorites. Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. And he went on a circuit year by year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. And he judged Israel in all these places. Then he would return to Ramah, for his home was there, and there also he judged Israel. And he built there an altar to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the Philistines were subdued and did not again enter the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.'

The phrase that has been used against Israel all through these chapters changes direction.

The hand of the LORD was heavy against Ashdod, and against Gath, and very heavy at Ekron. Now the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel — not for an afternoon but for a lifetime.

Note the qualification, though, because the writer includes it deliberately: all the days of Samuel. The peace is tied to a man, exactly as every rest in the book of Judges was tied to a judge, and the reader who has just come through that book knows what that means. Samuel will grow old in chapter 8, and the first thing Israel will do about it is ask for a king.

'The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel delivered their territory from the hand of the Philistines. There was peace also between Israel and the Amorites.'

The lost territory comes back, and the way it comes back is the point.

No campaign of reconquest is described. Israel does not spend a decade rebuilding an army and retaking towns one by one. The cities are restored after a single afternoon in which a nation that had already thrown away its idols stood on a hill and asked a man to keep praying.

There is peace with the Amorites as well — the Canaanite population that the book of Judges said Israel had never managed to drive out and had ended up living among. Even that settles.

'Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. And he went on a circuit year by year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. And he judged Israel in all these places.'

He works a circuit, and the three towns are chosen with care.

Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder. Gilgal, where the twelve stones came out of the Jordan and the reproach of Egypt was rolled away. Mizpah, where the nation had just repented. Samuel rides between the places where God had met Israel, year after year, doing the ordinary work of settling disputes.

Mark what he is not doing. He does not attempt to rebuild Shiloh. The sanctuary he grew up in is gone, God has abandoned it, and Samuel does not spend his life trying to restore the institution that formed him. He goes to the people instead.

'Then he would return to Ramah, for his home was there, and there also he judged Israel. And he built there an altar to the LORD.'

He goes home, and he judges at home, and he builds an altar in his own town.

Ramah is where his mother lived, where she made him a little robe every year and could not keep him. He was given away from that house as a toddler. He comes back to it as a grown man and puts an altar in it.

Take the whole chapter beside the whole of chapter 4, because the book has set them side by side and the comparison is the lesson.

Chapter 4: the same enemy, the same nation, the same place name. They asked the right question and did not wait for the answer. They sent for the ark. They shouted so that the earth resounded. And they lost four thousand, and then thirty thousand, and the ark, and the priesthood, and the sanctuary, and the glory.

Chapter 7: they put away the idols. They poured out water and fasted and said four words about their own sin. They asked one man not to stop praying. And God thundered.

Nothing changed in the intervening twenty years except the direction of a nation's heart. Nobody had a better weapon, a larger army or a cleverer plan; they did not even have the ark, which was sitting in a private house on a hill and stayed there.

They had God, because they had stopped trying to operate him.

7.theology:
Longing is not returning (vv. 2-3). Twenty years of lamenting after the LORD with the Ashtaroth still in the house. The ache can become a substitute for the removal, because it feels like devotion and costs nothing. Note the order, which is easy to get backwards: if you are returning... then put away. The idols go out because the heart has turned; they do not go out in order to turn it. Samuel is not prescribing a method for producing repentance but naming what would show it had happened. And the positive half is as strong as the negative: direct your heart — fix it, aim it — and serve him only. Not chiefly. Only.

Chapter 4 answered. Same enemy, same nation, same ground — Ebenezer is named at 4:1 and again at 7:12. Then: a box made the subject of the verb save, a shout that shook the earth, thirty thousand dead. Now: idols out, a confession, and a request that one man would not stop praying. Nothing else changed. They did not have a better army or a cleverer plan, and they did not even have the ark, which stayed in a house on a hill. They had God, because they had stopped trying to operate him.

Trouble arrives after the surrender (v. 7). The lords of the Philistines march the moment Israel assembles to repent. It is militarily sensible and it is also the pattern, and it is not evidence that the surrender was a mistake.

Hannah's thunder (v. 10). Against them he will thunder in heaven (2:10) was sung by a countrywoman with no army and no standing, who had just handed over a toddler at a corrupt shrine. Her son is at the altar when it happens.

Till now (v. 12). The stone is more careful than the hymn that came from it. Hitherto — up to this point. Samuel does not say God will always help, or that the Philistines are finished. A memorial stone does not tell you what is coming; it stops you forgetting what happened, so that the next time trouble arrives you have something in the landscape to argue from. Anyone can raise that stone tonight: not God will fix it, which you do not know, but till now the LORD has helped us, which you do.

All the days of Samuel (v. 13). The peace is tied to a man, exactly as every rest in Judges was tied to a judge — and a reader who has just come through that book knows what that means. Samuel grows old in chapter 8, and the first thing Israel does about it is ask for a king.
7.examples:
Then: A nation grieved after God for twenty years without moving a single idol, and then moved them all in an afternoon because one man told it plainly what returning would look like. It stood on a hill, poured out water, fasted, said four words about its own sin, and asked for prayer — and God broke an army with a noise in the sky.

Now: Two things. First, verse 2 is a description of a great many sincere Christians: genuinely aware of distance from God, genuinely grieved about it, and genuinely unwilling to carry one particular thing out of the house. The test Samuel applies is not how strongly you feel it but what has actually left the building. Second, verse 12 is the discipline of memory, and it is deliberately modest. You do not know what God will do next; you do know what he has already done. Put the stone there and name it, because when the Philistines come back you will want something you can point at.

8.title: Give Us a King
8.text: <sup>5</sup>'Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations.' <sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Samuel, 'Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.' (ESV)
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the hinge of the entire book and one of the most theologically loaded chapters in the OT. The elders of Israel approach Samuel with a request that is, on its surface, entirely reasonable: Samuel is old, his sons are corrupt, and Israel needs strong, stable leadership. But God's response to Samuel reveals the theological depth of what has happened: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them. The request for a king is not merely a political preference; it is an act of religious apostasy, a rejection of the divine kingship.

The chapter is a masterpiece of theological irony. God grants the request — with devastating clarity about what it will cost. Samuel's warning about the king's demands (vv. 11–18) is not political commentary; it is prophetic description. The king will take your sons for his army, your daughters for his household, your best fields and vineyards and oliveyards, a tenth of your grain and flocks. You will be his servants. And then: you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day (v. 18). The warning is rejected: No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations (vv. 19–20). Like all the nations — the phrase that reveals the spiritual diagnosis. Israel was never supposed to be like all the nations. Israel was supposed to be the LORD's peculiar treasure, his royal priesthood, his holy nation (Ex. 19:5–6). The desire to be 'like all the nations' is the desire to un-be Israel, to exchange the peculiar dignity of divine election for the ordinary mediocrity of human kingship.

Yet God's gracious sovereignty does not end here. He will give them a king — and through that king's failure, he will prepare the way for the true King, the Son of David, the one in whom divine and human kingship finally unite in the person of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Request and Its Meaning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel's sons Joel and Abijah are corrupt judges at Beersheba. The elders of Israel demand a king like the nations. God tells Samuel: they have not rejected you but me.
verseByVerse.theology: The request for a king is theologically equivalent to idolatry: exchanging the LORD as king for a human substitute. The parallel in v. 8 — as they have forsaken me and served other gods, so they are doing to you — makes the connection explicit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's request is not unprecedented; God had anticipated it in Deut. 17:14–20. But the manner and motivation — 'like all the nations' — makes it sin rather than faithful planning. Now: Every generation of God's people is tempted to exchange his sufficiency for the world's solutions; the form changes, the theology remains.

verseByVerse.quote: When Samuel became old, he made his sons judges over Israel... Yet his sons did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice. Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah and said to him, 'Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's sons are Joel and Abijah — their names mean 'Yahweh is God' and 'my father is Yahweh.' The irony is bitter. Sons with names that proclaim the covenant God turned aside after gain and perverted justice — the exact same sins as Eli's sons, the exact same pattern of priestly and judicial corruption that Samuel was raised up to replace.
