verseByVerse.commentary: The divine verdict comes before the confrontation. God tells Samuel first, privately, what Saul has done and what it means: the kingdom is forfeit. 'I regret that I have made Saul king' - the language of divine grief over a wasted appointment, the same word (nacham) used of God's grief before the flood (Gen. 6:6). Samuel does not receive this word with detachment: he is angry, and he spends the whole night crying to the LORD. This is a prophet's intercession - desperate, prolonged, not resigned. But the answer does not change. The morning brings the brutal detail that Saul has set up a monument to himself at Carmel before returning. The man who began his kingship hiding among the baggage (10:22) has arrived at self-commemoration. Pride has taken root where fear of the LORD once stood. Sproul notes that the monument is the external symbol of the internal condition Samuel is about to expose: Saul has made himself the center of his own story.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, 'Blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD.' And Samuel said, 'What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?' Saul said, 'They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God, and the rest we have devoted to destruction.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bleating of the sheep is one of the great comic-devastating details of Scripture. Saul greets Samuel with pious enthusiasm — I have performed the commandment of the LORD — and the sheep begin to testify against him. Samuel's question is gentle and precise: he does not accuse; he simply asks about the sound. And Saul's answer immediately shifts blame: they have brought them — the people, not Saul. The passive voice, the distancing pronoun, the pre-emptive theological justification — it was for sacrifice — all show the practiced reflexes of a man who has been blaming others for years.

Samuel stops the excuse-making with a question: Why then did you not obey the voice of the LORD? The simplicity of the question is devastating. All the circumstances, all the explanations, all the religious rationale — stripped away in seven words. Alistair Begg observes that this is precisely what genuine pastoral confrontation looks like: not a lecture on the theology of obedience but a simple, unavoidable question that gets to the issue. Saul has no answer that doesn't implicate him further.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul said to Samuel, 'I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. I have gone on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and I have devoted the Amalekites to destruction. But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the best of the things devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Karnak.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Saul's self-defense is a masterclass in partial truth deployed as complete denial. He claims obedience - he did destroy the Amalekites, he did bring back Agag. But 'the people' took the best animals. The blame is distributed; the responsibility is deflected. The claim that the animals were kept 'to sacrifice to the LORD your God' is the most revealing phrase: not 'the LORD our God' but 'your God' - a subtle distancing, whether conscious or not, that the reader should not miss. Saul's relationship with God is becoming transactional, mediated through Samuel, increasingly secondhand. The sacrifice rationale is the kind of religious justification that mistakes the form of devotion for its substance - offering God what costs nothing (animals already captured) while withholding what he actually asked for (total obedience). Samuel's reply in verse 22 is one of the most incisive statements on worship in all of Scripture, and it is provoked by exactly this kind of self-serving religiosity.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said, 'Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's pronouncement contains two of the most important theological statements in the OT. The first — to obey is better than sacrifice — establishes the permanent priority of heart-obedience over ritual performance. This is not an anti-sacrifice statement; it is a statement about what sacrifice is for. Sacrifice was designed to express and accompany a heart of covenant faithfulness; it cannot substitute for that faithfulness. The prophets will repeat this with increasing urgency (Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8; Hosea 6:6), and Jesus will quote Hosea's version when challenged about his table fellowship (Matt. 9:13). The principle is as old as Cain and Abel: God looks at the heart first.

The second pronouncement — rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry — is even more startling. Saul did not practice divination or worship idols; he offered sacrifices to the LORD. But Samuel equates his disobedience with the darkest forms of paganism. The reason: both divination and rebellion seek to access power while bypassing God's revealed will. Both substitute human wisdom or human desire for divine command. Saul is an idolater in practice even while he is a worshipper in form — and the sentence is the same as for explicit idolatry: he has rejected you from being king.

Saul's response — I have sinned (v. 24), immediately followed by please honor me before the elders of my people (v. 30) — reveals that even this confession is incomplete. The man who says 'I have sinned' in the same breath as 'but please preserve my reputation' has not yet arrived at genuine repentance. His concern is for his public standing, not for his relationship with God. David, by contrast, when confronted by Nathan in 2 Samuel 12, will say only: I have sinned against the LORD. No buts, no requests, no image management. That is the man after God's own heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel hacks Agag to pieces before the LORD, then goes to Ramah. He never meets Saul again. The chapter ends with Samuel grieving for Saul and with the LORD regretting that he made Saul king.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD's 'regret' (nacham) is not a reversal of divine omniscience but an anthropomorphic expression of genuine divine sorrow — the same word used of God regretting the creation of humanity before the flood (Gen. 6:6). God is not indifferent to human failure; he mourns it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Samuel's grief for Saul is the grief of a parent for a child who has destroyed himself — present throughout the rest of his life (v. 35). It does not compromise his faithfulness to God; it coexists with it. Now: Grief for the spiritually lost or for the fallen leader is not weakness but love; refusing to grieve is the greater failure.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said, 'Bring here to me Agag the king of the Amalek.' And Agag came to him cheerfully... And Samuel said, 'As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women.' And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal. Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul. And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The execution of Agag by Samuel — a prophet and judge now performing the role of executioner — is deliberately jarring. It emphasizes that the sentence God commanded has now been carried out, belatedly, by the right person. Agag's cheerfulness (Surely the bitterness of death is past) is pathetically misplaced; he thought Saul's mercy was permanent. Samuel's words as he kills him — as your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless — are the theological ground of the execution: this is not cruelty but justice proportionate to Agag's own history of violence against God's people.

The final image of the chapter — Samuel to Ramah, Saul to Gibeah, and the statement that they never met again — is one of the most desolate endings in all of Scripture. Two men whose lives had been bound together since the anointing, now permanently separated. Samuel grieves; the LORD regrets. The word for regret — nacham — is the same word used in Genesis 6:6, when God regrets making humanity before the flood. It is anthropomorphic language for genuine divine sorrow: not a change in God's plan but a revelation of his genuine emotional response to human failure. God is not unmoved by Saul's tragedy. He mourns it — and his mourning is the measure of what Saul could have been.

15.theology:
The Priority of Obedience. Chapter 15 gives us the OT's clearest statement of the principle that will reappear throughout Scripture: God desires obedience rather than sacrifice, hearing rather than religious performance. This is not an anti-ritual statement but an anti-hypocrisy one. Sacrifice offered without obedience is an insult to God — it claims relationship while refusing its demands. The NT picks up this theme directly in Jesus' citation of Hosea 6:6 (Matt. 9:13; 12:7) and in his denunciation of the Pharisees who tithe mint and dill while neglecting justice and mercy (Matt. 23:23).

Genuine vs. False Repentance. The contrast between Saul's non-repentance in chapter 15 and David's genuine repentance in 2 Samuel 12 is one of the central character studies of the entire historical books. Both men sin grievously; both are confronted by a prophet; both say 'I have sinned.' But Saul's confession is immediately qualified by a request for public honor, while David's is followed by brokenness, prayer, and the acceptance of God's discipline. The difference is the direction of the heart: Saul's guilt management; David's God-seeking. The same gospel that calls us to repentance calls us to the specific quality of repentance David shows — not sorrow that we got caught, but grief that we have sinned against the God who loves us.
15.examples:
Then: Saul's trajectory from chapter 9 to chapter 15 is one of the Bible's most extended portraits of spiritual decline. It begins with genuine humility and Spirit-empowerment, passes through impatience and unlawful sacrifice, and ends in self-deception so complete that he genuinely believes he has obeyed. The incremental nature of the decline is the most frightening element: no single dramatic fall, just a slow accumulation of small compromises, each one building on the last, until the capacity for genuine self-knowledge is almost entirely gone.

Now: The chapter confronts every Christian with the question: is my obedience genuine or performed? Am I obeying what God requires, or obeying what is convenient while modifying what is costly? And when confronted with failure, does my response look like Saul's — excuses, blame-shifting, reputation management — or like David's — broken acknowledgment that I have sinned against the LORD? The answer to that question is the best available indicator of the state of the heart.

16.title: The LORD Looks on the Heart
16.text: <sup>7</sup>But the LORD said to Samuel, 'Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.' <sup>13</sup>Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. (ESV)
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the great pivot of 1 Samuel. Saul has been rejected; the new king is to be anointed. God sends Samuel to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, and the parade of sons begins. One by one, seven impressive young men pass before Samuel, and one by one God says no. The climax is the calling-in of the youngest, the overlooked, the one nobody thought to summon: David, the shepherd boy, is out keeping the sheep. And the moment he appears — he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome (v. 12) — God says: Arise, anoint him, for this is he.

But the chapter's theological heart is the divine declaration that stops Samuel in his tracks when he sees Eliab and thinks: surely this must be the LORD's anointed. God's correction — man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (v. 7) — is one of the most important verses in the entire Bible. It overturns every human system of valuation that ranks people by appearance, height, status, eloquence, or power. The God who sees the heart is the God of Hannah's song: the one who raises the poor from the dust and brings down the mighty from their thrones.

The chapter ends with David in Saul's court, playing the lyre to soothe the king's tormented spirit — the future king already serving the present king, the anointed hiding his anointing, the one chosen to replace a man whose own Spirit has departed. The proximity of David to Saul is both historical and theological: the old era and the new are already coexisting, the rejected and the chosen side by side.

sections.title: The Command to Bethlehem
sections.commentary:
God's command to Samuel — fill your horn with oil, and go — comes in the context of Samuel's grief over Saul. He has been mourning, perhaps for an extended period, unable to move forward. God's word to him is not harsh but brisk: How long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? The question is not a rebuke of grief itself — God himself grieved over Saul (15:35) — but a call to action. There is a time to mourn and a time to rise and go. Samuel's mourning has run its course; the next act of redemption history requires his obedience.

Samuel's concern — If Saul hears it, he will kill me — is understandable and honest. He is not exhibiting a lack of faith; he is acknowledging real danger. And God's provision — take a heifer, go to Bethlehem to offer sacrifice, invite Jesse's family — is not deception but prudent concealment. The mission is not yet public; the full disclosure of David's anointing can wait for God's timing. Calvin notes that God sometimes provides cover for his servants in dangerous situations, not because truth is to be hidden but because not all truth is to be spoken at all times. Samuel goes, and Bethlehem's elders tremble at his arrival — the prophet's visit was not always good news.

sections.title: The LORD Looks on the Heart
sections.commentary:
The parade of Jesse's sons is one of the most instructive scenes in Scripture about the gap between human perception and divine knowledge. Eliab is the firstborn — tall, presumably impressive, the obvious choice by every human metric. Samuel sees him and thinks: Surely the LORD's anointed is before him. The prophet who anointed Saul is about to make the same mistake again: judging by appearance. God's correction is immediate and categorical: Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him.

The reason given is the most important statement in the chapter: the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart. The Hebrew word for 'outward appearance' is einayim — literally 'the eyes.' Man judges by what the eyes can see: height, bearing, beauty, confidence, eloquence. God judges by the heart — the center of will, affection, and commitment. This is not anti-intellectualism or anti-beauty; it is an ontological claim about the nature of human dignity and divine perception. The qualities that matter to God are internal and invisible: faith, love, humility, desire for God. Saul had the impressive exterior and the failed heart; David is about to be revealed as the reverse — the unimpressive exterior with the God-devoted heart. Tim Keller writes that this verse is the beginning of the gospel's inversion of all human systems of worth: in the kingdom of God, the last are first, the least are greatest, and the shepherd boy is the king.

Seven sons pass before Samuel, and seven times the answer is no. The number seven in Hebrew is the number of completeness — all of Jesse's sons, and none of them. God's choice is not among the presented options.

sections.title: David Anointed: The Spirit Rushes Upon Him
sections.commentary:
The moment is charged with divine irony. Jesse has not even thought to call his youngest son; he has left him with the sheep. There remains yet the youngest (v. 11) — the word suggests not only chronological order but social insignificance. In the ancient world, the youngest son was the lowest in the household hierarchy. He tends the sheep because that's what the least important family member does. He is nobody's candidate for anything. And he is God's choice.

The description of David when he arrives is carefully balanced: ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome. God said not to look at the outward appearance — and now he describes David's outward appearance. The point is not that appearance is irrelevant but that it does not determine. David is handsome, but his beauty is not the reason he is chosen. Arise, anoint him, for this is he — the divine word precedes and overrides the visual impression.

Samuel anoints David with the horn of oil — the horn, not the flask Samuel used for Saul; the vessel of honor, the kingly symbol. And then: the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. The same language used for Saul in chapter 10 — the Spirit rushing upon the anointed — but with a crucial addition: from that day forward. Saul's Spirit-empowerment was episodic and conditional; David's is continuous. This is the mark of the man after God's own heart: the Spirit is not merely upon him for moments but with him as a permanent possession. The anointing of David anticipates the baptism of Jesus, at which the Spirit descends and remains (John 1:32–33), and ultimately the Pentecost outpouring in which the Spirit is poured out upon all flesh. David's anointing is the seedbed of the promise that all God's people would be Spirit-possessed kings and priests.

Sinclair Ferguson observes that the private anointing at Bethlehem — witnessed only by Jesse and his sons, with no public fanfare, in a family home rather than a national assembly — is characteristic of how God works. The decisive moments in redemption history happen privately, invisibly, before anyone else knows what has occurred. The eternal decree, the incarnation in a stable, the resurrection before dawn — all are witnessed by few or none, yet they determine everything. David is the anointed king from this moment; it will take years for the world to catch up.

sections.title: The Spirit Departs from Saul; David Enters His Court
sections.commentary:
The contrast of verses 13 and 14 is the sharpest in the chapter. Verse 13: the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Verse 14: Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him. The juxtaposition is not accidental — it is the narrator's theological statement about the transfer of the kingdom. The Spirit that empowers kingship has moved from the rejected to the chosen. Saul is left with the torment that follows the withdrawal of divine grace.

The 'harmful spirit from the LORD' is one of the most theologically difficult phrases in the OT. It is not that God is evil; it is that God uses even harmful spiritual realities as instruments of his justice. In Saul's case, the withdrawal of the Spirit — the divine presence that had sustained him — created a vacuum that was filled with the anxiety, paranoia, and instability that would characterize his remaining years. R. C. Sproul notes that this is not unjust punishment but judicial consequence: a man who rejected the Spirit's guidance over years cannot expect to enjoy the Spirit's stabilizing presence indefinitely. The torment is not arbitrary; it is the experiential reality of what it means to be abandoned by God.

The solution Saul's servants propose — a skilled lyre player — brings David into the story in the most understated way possible. He comes not as a rival king but as a musician and servant. He is obedient to his father's word, he ministers to the tormented king, and Saul loves him greatly. The future king is learning the royal court from the inside, serving the man he will eventually replace, honoring the office that has been spiritually vacated. Alistair Begg observes that David's willingness to serve Saul — the man who will eventually try to kill him — is the first instance of the grace pattern that will characterize his entire life: he gives honor where he is not required to, he serves where he could claim superiority, he waits for God's timing while being useful in the present moment. It is the grammar of Phil. 2:6–8: though he had every right, he did not grasp at it, but took the form of a servant.

16.theology: Divine Election and Human Surprise. Chapter 16 is the clearest OT illustration of elective grace: God's choice of David is entirely his own, not determined by family position, physical appearance, or human expectation. The youngest son of an unremarkable family in Bethlehem becomes the chosen king of Israel — not because of what he is by nature but because of what God sees in his heart and determines in his purpose. Paul's meditation on election in 1 Corinthians 1:26–29 is the NT counterpart: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth... God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise. The Bethlehem shepherd boy is the human prototype of the Bethlehem carpenter's son.
16.examples:
Then: David spent years between his private anointing and his public coronation, serving Saul, tending sheep, and fighting Goliath. The gap between calling and confirmation is a recurring feature of God's dealings with those he chooses. Joseph waited years between his dreams and their fulfillment; Abraham waited decades for Isaac.

Now: The chapter speaks to everyone who feels overlooked, underestimated, or left out when others are chosen and honored. The God who sent Samuel to Bethlehem to find the one nobody nominated is the same God who sees you — not your appearance, your position, your family line, but your heart. And the same God who kept David faithful through years of hiddenness before he crowned him is working in every gap between calling and confirmation in the lives of his people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from among Jesse's sons. Samuel is drawn to the tall, handsome Eliab. God corrects him: I do not look on the outward appearance; I look on the heart. Seven sons pass before Samuel and none is chosen. David, the youngest, is out keeping sheep. He is brought in, and Samuel anoints him. From that day the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David.
verseByVerse.theology: The central theological statement of the chapter is one of the most important in all of Scripture: Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (v.7). This is not merely an interesting observation about divine perception; it is the charter of a kingdom built on covenant faithfulness rather than impressive appearance. Saul was tall, handsome, impressive - and he failed. David is young, ruddy, overlooked by his own father - and he is God's choice. Sproul notes that this principle runs through all of Scripture: God consistently chooses the weak, the young, the overlooked to confound the wisdom of the world and demonstrate that the power belongs to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observes that Samuel's instinct toward Eliab is not foolishness but the natural human response. Eliab looks like a king. The correction he receives is the correction every human leader needs: appearances deceive, and God's choices regularly confound human expectations.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Samuel, Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary: Samuel is sent to Bethlehem with a horn of oil and a mission that must be carried out quietly - if Saul knew, he might kill Samuel. Jesse's seven sons are presented in order, and Samuel is drawn to each of the first seven. God's repeated rejection is a gentle education in divine aesthetics. The seven rejections prepare the ground for the eighth: the youngest son, not even invited to the sacrifice, out with the sheep. David is described as ruddy, with beautiful eyes and handsome - but these are noted after God has already declared the principle of heart-sight. His appearance is incidental; his heart is the point. When the oil runs from Samuel's horn onto David's head, the Spirit rushes on him. The transfer of anointing and Spirit has begun. The king-in-waiting returns to his sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-23 - David Comes to Saul's Court
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after David's anointing, the Spirit of the LORD departs from Saul and a harmful spirit torments him. His servants suggest that music from a skilled lyre-player might relieve the torment. David is recommended; he comes to the court and plays for Saul; Saul loves him greatly and makes him his armor-bearer.
verseByVerse.theology: The juxtaposition is deliberate and devastating: as the Spirit rushes on David (v.13), the Spirit departs from Saul and a harmful spirit torments him (v.14). Calvin notes that the departure of the Spirit is the natural consequence of the rejection of Saul: God does not force his presence on those who have rejected his authority.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes the profound irony: Saul unknowingly brings his replacement into his own court. David serves the man he will succeed; he plays the lyre for the king who will pursue him. The servant relationship that begins here will be tested to its breaking point in the chapters that follow.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him. And Saul's servants said to him, Behold now, a harmful spirit from God is tormenting you. Let our lord now command your servants who are before you to seek out a man who is skillful in playing the lyre, and when the harmful spirit from God is upon you, he will play it, and you will be well.
verseByVerse.commentary: The transition in these verses is stark: the Spirit has transferred from the official king to the shepherd boy. Saul is tormented; David is gifted. The recommendation reaches David without anyone knowing his identity as the newly anointed king. He comes to court as a court musician and armor-bearer - the most subordinate of positions. Saul loves him and finds relief in his music. The man who will replace him soothes his tormented spirit with the songs that will become the Psalter. God is arranging events with the patience of eternity: David is in place, learning the court, building the reputation that will carry him through everything that follows. The story is moving.

17.title: The Battle Is the LORD's
17.text: <sup>45</sup>Then David said to the Philistine, 'You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. <sup>47</sup>...that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand.' (ESV)
17.overview:
The story of David and Goliath is one of the most famous narratives in all of human literature — and one of the most misread. It is almost universally applied as a story about personal courage overcoming long odds, about the underdog defeating the giant. But the text will not support that reading. David himself insists on the correct interpretation: the battle is the LORD's (v. 47). This is not a story about David's courage, though he is courageous. It is a story about the LORD's champion fighting on behalf of a paralyzed people — and about the corporate nature of the victory that follows.

The theological structure of the chapter is the theology of substitutionary representation. Goliath proposes single combat: choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me. If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants (vv. 8–9). One man fights; everyone wins or loses depending on the outcome. The entire army of Israel is paralyzed with fear — dismayed and greatly afraid (v. 11) — because they have no champion who can face Goliath. David volunteers not as a hero but as a substitute: his victory will be Israel's victory. His conquest of Goliath becomes the basis for Israel's pursuit of the fleeing Philistines. They win because he won. This is the Christological heart of the story: Christ fought on behalf of his people against an enemy they could not face, and his victory — won entirely without their participation — becomes the basis of their liberation. As David's victory was credited to Israel, so Christ's victory is credited to all who are in him.

sections.title: The Challenge: A Man Who Cannot Be Faced
sections.commentary:
The narrator's description of Goliath is designed to produce the same response in the reader as in the Israelite army: overwhelming dread. Six cubits and a span — approximately nine feet nine inches. Bronze helmet, coat of mail, bronze armor on his legs, a javelin of bronze on his back. His spear's head alone weighs six hundred shekels of iron — about fifteen pounds. The armor bearer walks before him. He has been a warrior from his youth. Every detail accumulates toward the same conclusion: no man in Israel can face this.

Goliath's challenge — choose a man, let him come and fight me — is the ancient custom of single combat, champion versus champion. It was designed to settle wars without the full cost of battle. And it exposes Israel's deepest problem: they have no champion. The army that marched out to face the Philistines stands on the hillside, shouting at each other across the valley, and then retreating in fear twice a day, morning and evening, for forty days (v. 16). Forty days — the number of testing in Scripture. This is Israel's great test, and they are failing it completely.

R. C. Sproul notes that Goliath's taunting of the armies of the living God (v. 26) is the key to the chapter: this is not primarily a military confrontation but a theological one. Who is the living God? Is he powerful enough to deal with a nine-foot Philistine? Israel's paralysis is a failure of theology before it is a failure of courage: they have forgotten what kind of God they serve.

sections.title: David Arrives: The Shepherd's Vision
sections.commentary:
David arrives at the battle line not as a soldier but as a supply runner, bringing food to his brothers. His arrival is unheroic and ordinary — a boy on an errand, obeying his father's instructions. He reaches the lines just as the armies are forming up, leaves his provisions with the keeper of baggage, and runs to find his brothers. And then he hears Goliath taunt, and two questions burst out of him that define his entire theology: Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God? (v. 26).

The question reveals the lens through which David sees the situation. Every soldier in Israel sees a nine-foot man with bronze armor and a fifteen-pound spearhead. David sees an uncircumcised Philistine — a man outside the covenant, without the living God on his side — defying the armies whose God is alive and active. The size disparity is real; the theological disparity is overwhelming in the other direction. David's question is not bravado; it is accurate theology: the living God will not allow his name to be defied indefinitely.

Eliab's contemptuous response — I know your presumption and the evil of your heart; you have come down to see the battle (v. 28) — is the voice of the man God had rejected. The brother who was impressive enough to make Samuel think he was the LORD's anointed is now the one sneering at the shepherd boy who will be king. David's gentle deflection — What have I done now? Was it not but a word? — and his persistence in asking the same question reveal a man who is not deterred by human opposition when the honor of God is at stake. Alistair Begg observes that David's irritation at the taunting is the irritation of a man who loves God's glory: he cannot understand why no one else finds Goliath's defiance intolerable.

sections.title: David's Confession Before Saul
sections.commentary:
When David volunteers to fight Goliath, Saul's response is understandable: you are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a warrior from his youth (v. 33). The human assessment is correct. By every military metric, David cannot win. Saul's reasoning is the reasoning of the experienced general who has spent his career calculating human odds.

David's rebuttal is entirely theological, grounded in personal experience: when a lion came and when a bear came, he killed them both — the LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine (v. 37). This is the logic of Ebenezer: past divine faithfulness is the basis of present trust. The God who acted before will act again; the evidence for trusting him in the new crisis is the record of his faithfulness in the old ones. This is not naivety — it is experiential theology, faith built on the actual track record of God's deliverances.

Saul's armor on David is a comic scene with serious theology. Everything about Saul's armor is wrong for David — too big, too heavy, untested, borrowed. David cannot walk in it. He takes it off. He goes to face the most fearsome warrior in the ancient world with a staff, a sling, five smooth stones, and the name of the LORD of hosts. The choice is not merely tactical (though slingers were formidable); it is theological: David's weapons are chosen from the stream, not from the armory. He is not fighting on Saul's terms or Goliath's terms but on the LORD's terms.

sections.title: The Battle and Its Theology
sections.commentary:
Goliath's contempt for David — Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks? — and his curse by his gods is the final stage-setting for the theological verdict David is about to pronounce. David's speech to Goliath before the battle is one of the great confessions of faith in the OT: You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. The contrast is drawn with perfect clarity: Goliath's weapons versus the LORD's name. The issue is not courage versus cowardice, or David's skill versus Goliath's size; it is the name of the LORD versus the names of Philistia's gods.

The purpose statement in verse 46 is equally clear: that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. David is not fighting for personal glory or national pride; he is fighting for the honor of the living God before the watching nations. And verse 47 provides the deepest rationale: the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand. This is the comprehensive theology of holy war: the outcome is not determined by weapons but by the will of the LORD of hosts.

The stone from the sling strikes Goliath in the forehead, and he falls on his face to the ground. David stands over him and takes his own sword to cut off his head — the precise reversal of what Goliath proposed. And then: when the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled (v. 51). The army of Israel pursues, the victory becomes national, the plunder is shared. One man's combat becomes the whole people's liberation. This is the Christological pattern at the heart of the story: Christ fights the battle no human being can win, defeats the enemy who has held all humanity paralyzed, and his victory becomes the victory of all who are united to him. The battle is the LORD's — and the LORD's victory, won by his anointed representative, belongs to the whole people of God.

17.theology: Substitutionary Representation and the Champion. The structure of 1 Samuel 17 — one man fighting on behalf of a people who cannot fight — is the clearest OT type of substitutionary atonement in the historical books. David stands in for Israel, fights the battle Israel cannot fight, and his victory is credited to them. The people of Israel did not defeat Goliath; David did. But they inherit the victory. Paul's language in Romans 5:12–21 — the two Adams, each acting representatively on behalf of those who are in them — is the direct theological descendant of this story. And Hebrews 2:14–15 makes the connection explicit: Jesus, by his death, destroys the one who has the power of death, and by destroying death's champion, frees those who had been subject to slavery all their lives.
17.examples:
Then: The men of Israel had been hiding in fear for forty days. They had swords. They outnumbered the Philistines. They had the covenant God on their side. But they could not face Goliath — and they knew it. Their paralysis was not cowardice but accurate self-assessment: no natural man could beat a champion like Goliath.

Now: The believer faces an enemy — sin, death, the spiritual powers of darkness (Eph. 6:12) — that no natural human being can defeat. The Christian life is not about generating enough personal courage to beat enemies that are too strong for us. It is about trusting the Champion who has already fought and won, whose victory is credited to us through union with him, and whose Spirit empowers us to pursue the enemy that he has already routed. The battle is the LORD's — and his victory is ours in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-30 - The Philistine Challenge and David's Arrival
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistine champion Goliath, nine feet tall in full armor, issues a daily challenge for forty days. The Israelite army is paralyzed with fear. David arrives at the battlefield on an errand from his father, hears the challenge, and asks who this uncircumcised Philistine is that he should defy the armies of the living God.
verseByVerse.theology: Goliath's challenge is a theological provocation: he is not merely challenging Israel's army; he is defying Israel's God. David's question reframes the entire situation. The army sees a giant; David sees a blasphemer defying the living God. The theological perception is the difference. Sproul notes that forty days of unchallenged blasphemy is the background against which David's faith shines most brightly: he is not naive about Goliath's size; he is clear about God's honor.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur notes that Goliath's daily defiance is a portrait of how the enemy operates: through intimidation, repetition, and the slow erosion of confidence in God. David's arrival is the arrival of faith that has not been eroded.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to the men who stood by him, What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
verseByVerse.commentary: The description of Goliath's armor is overwhelming: a bronze helmet, a coat of mail weighing 125 pounds, bronze greaves, a bronze javelin, a spear with a shaft like a weaver's beam and an iron point weighing fifteen pounds. This is not a man; this is a walking fortress. David arrives on an errand - delivering cheese and grain - and hears the morning challenge. His question is not rhetorical; it is theological. Who is this uncircumcised Philistine? He is outside the covenant, outside the protection of Israel's God. He is defying the armies of the living God - and the living God is not a dead idol. David does not feel the size of the giant; he feels the offense to God. His brother Eliab mocks his faith as pride and presumption. David ignores the mockery and asks the question again.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David offers to fight Goliath. Saul offers his armor; David refuses it and goes with five smooth stones and his sling. Goliath is contemptuous. David declares that the battle is the LORD's. He runs toward Goliath, slings a stone into his forehead, and Goliath falls dead.
verseByVerse.theology: The battle is settled before the first stone is thrown. David's declaration in vv.45-47 is the theological center: You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's. Sproul calls this the definitive Old Testament statement on the theology of spiritual warfare.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson notes that David's refusal of Saul's armor is not theatrical but strategic: it would suggest the battle would be won by conventional means. David goes as himself - shepherd, sling, stones, and the name of the LORD. The victory will be unmistakably divine.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to the Philistine, You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand... For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: David addresses Goliath with a declaration of war in God's name. The three weapons Goliath brings are answered with one: the name of the LORD of hosts. The purpose of the coming victory is explicitly stated: that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. This is missional warfare - the battle is not simply for territory but for the knowledge of God among all peoples. David then runs toward Goliath, slinging the stone while still in motion. The stone sinks into Goliath's forehead; he falls. David stands on him and cuts off his head with Goliath's own sword. The Philistines flee. What forty days of paralysis could not accomplish, faith accomplishes in one smooth stone.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, Abner, whose son is this youth?
verseByVerse.commentary: The closing scene returns to the question of identity: who is this young man? Saul, who had loved David as an armor-bearer in chapter 16, apparently does not recognize him. The young man holding Goliath's severed head is the son of Jesse of Bethlehem, the one on whom the Spirit of the LORD rushed, the one whose heart God saw. He is the coming king. The man asking the question does not yet know it.

18.title: Jonathan's Covenant and Saul's Jealousy
18.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. <sup>8</sup>And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, 'They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?' (ESV)
18.overview:
Chapter 18 introduces two relationships that will define the rest of 1 Samuel: Jonathan's love for David and Saul's hatred of him. Both relationships begin at the same moment — immediately after the victory over Goliath — and they could not be more different. Jonathan strips himself of his robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt and gives them to David. Saul strips David of his independence and begins a campaign of jealous elimination that will last until his death. Both men recognize in David something extraordinary; they respond to it with opposite spirits.

Jonathan's covenant with David is one of the most remarkable relationships in the Bible. Its theological significance is profound: Jonathan is the crown prince, the natural heir to Saul's throne. By covenanting with David, by giving him his princely garments, Jonathan is effectively abdicating — not in despair but in love, recognizing that God has chosen David and choosing to align himself with God's choice rather than his own dynastic interest. This is a picture of self-giving love that Paul will describe as the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). Jonathan surrenders the kingdom to benefit David; Jesus surrenders glory to benefit us.

sections.title: Jonathan's Covenant: Love That Surrenders
sections.commentary:
The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David — the Hebrew verb suggests binding, weaving together, as if two threads become one fabric. This is not a sentimental or merely emotional attachment; it is a covenant commitment, sealed by the giving of the most precious things Jonathan possessed: his robe (the mark of royalty), his armor, his sword, his bow, his belt. These were not merely expensive objects; they were the symbols of Jonathan's identity as prince and warrior. By giving them to David, Jonathan is doing something theologically extraordinary: he is acknowledging that David's calling supersedes his own.

Sinclair Ferguson writes that Jonathan's covenant with David is the OT's clearest human picture of grace. Jonathan had every natural reason to see David as a rival — the young man who stole the people's hearts, who would eventually take the throne that should by inheritance have been Jonathan's. Instead he sees in David what God sees: the man after God's own heart, the one God has chosen. And he responds not with competition but with love, not with grasping but with giving. The Christological resonance is unmistakable: Jesus, the one who had every right, did not hold to it but gave himself in covenant love for those whom the Father had given him. Jonathan is not Jesus — but he images something of Jesus that no other OT figure quite matches.

sections.title: Saul's Jealousy: The Song That Destroyed a King
sections.commentary:
The women's song — Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands — is one of the most innocent and most destructive songs in Scripture. It was meant as praise to both; it was received by Saul as a threat. What more can he have but the kingdom? — the question reveals the state of Saul's soul: he has already accepted the conclusion that David is his rival, and every evidence of David's success confirms it. Saul cannot hear praise for David without calculating what it means for himself.

R. C. Sproul observes that Saul's jealousy is the spiritual disease that the rejection of God's grace produces. A man who is secure in God's love can celebrate another's success; a man whose identity depends on comparison cannot afford to. Saul's kingdom was given to him by God's appointment, and he treated it as a possession to be defended rather than a stewardship to be discharged. When David's popularity threatened that possession, the defensive instinct kicked in and jealousy became the engine of his subsequent actions. The very success God gave Saul should have produced gratitude; instead it produced the terror of a man who has built his house on sand and watches the tide come in.

David's wise behavior in every situation (vv. 5, 14, 15, 30) — the repeated narrator's statement that he succeeded wherever he went, that the LORD was with him — is the contrast the chapter requires. David did not maneuver for position; he simply served faithfully, and God gave the success. The man after God's own heart does not need to secure his own future because he trusts the God who holds it.

sections.title: The Two Attempts to Kill David
sections.commentary:
Saul's two attempts to kill David through marriage — offering Merab to motivate David to fight the Philistines fatally, then offering Michal as a trap requiring a hundred Philistine foreskins — are the actions of a man whose paranoia has moved from thought to plan. He has ceased to be a king managing a threat and become a father manipulating his daughters as instruments of murder. The degradation of Saul's character is total: in chapter 9 he was a humble young man concerned about his father's donkeys; by chapter 18 he is engineering the death of his servants through marital politics.

The detail that Michal loves David (v. 20) is the only place in the OT where a woman is said to love a man first — typically the verb goes the other direction. It is a mark of David's genuine human attractiveness: people love him. Jonathan loved him. Michal loves him. The people love him. Even the servants of Saul speak well of him to his face (v. 22). The contrast with Saul — whom the people fear rather than love, whose servants are tools rather than friends — is complete. The man who is loved by God is loved by people; the man who has rejected God's love is isolated by his own jealousy. Saul becomes ever more afraid of David, not because David threatens him but because the LORD is with David — and David's relationship with God makes visible everything Saul has lost.

18.theology: Jealousy as Theological Disorder. Saul's jealousy is not merely a character flaw; it is a theological symptom. A person secure in God's love and God's appointment does not need to be threatened by another person's success. The root of envy is always a failure of trust: I do not believe God is enough, so I must protect what I have against those who would take it. Jonathan's freedom from envy — he gives away his inheritance without regret — is the fruit of a soul that has found its security in God rather than in position. The contrast between Jonathan's generosity and Saul's grasping is the chapter's deepest theological lesson.
18.examples:
Then: David did not respond to Saul's attempts with counter-plotting or with the complaint that he deserved better. He continued to serve faithfully, behave wisely, and trust God to manage the outcome. His consistent success in battle while Saul was trying to kill him is a running divine commentary on the situation.

Now: The chapter speaks directly to anyone who has experienced the jealousy of those in authority over them. David's response — serve faithfully, trust God's sovereignty, refuse to grasp the position God has not yet given — is the model of the believer who waits for God's timing rather than taking matters into their own hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 - Jonathan's Love and Saul's Fear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan immediately loves David with covenant-level friendship and gives him his royal robe, armor, and weapons - a symbolic transfer of the kingdom. David prospers in everything. But when the women sing Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands, Saul's affection turns to jealous rage.
verseByVerse.theology: Jonathan's giving of his robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt is profoundly significant: he is the crown prince, and he is giving David the symbols of royal succession. Whether consciously or not, Jonathan is recognizing what God has decreed. Calvin notes that Jonathan's selfless love for David is one of the most beautiful portraits of disinterested friendship in all of Scripture - a man who gives away the thing he has every right to keep.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller observes that the women's song is innocent and celebratory, not designed to wound. But Saul hears it as a political threat, and from that day he eyes David. Envy, once it takes root, sees enemies everywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. And Saul took him that day and would not let him return to his father's house. Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt.
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant between Jonathan and David is immediate, deep, self-sacrificial. Jonathan's gifts are royal symbols: the robe and armor of a crown prince, the sword, bow, and belt of a warrior. He is giving David his identity, his status, his weapons - everything except the throne itself. This is the act of a man who has glimpsed something that most men in his position would suppress. The women's song in verse 7 reveals what Saul's heart has been fearing: he is being eclipsed by the man his son has just covenanted with.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-30 - Saul's Attempts on David's Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul attempts to kill David three times: once with a spear while David plays the lyre; twice by placing him in increasingly dangerous military positions. David survives every trap. Saul offers his daughters as pawns in schemes that fail. The chapter ends: Saul was David's enemy continually.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between David and Saul intensifies: David behaves wisely in all his ways; Saul acts out of fear and jealousy. God is with David; the Spirit of God is absent from Saul. The three attempts on David's life reveal the escalating desperation of a man trying to undo God's purposes. Every scheme fails for the same reason - the LORD is with David. Ferguson notes that the repeated notation and the LORD was with him is the narrative's theological verdict.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur observes that the use of his own daughters as weapons against David represents the nadir of Saul's fatherhood - treating Merab and Michal as political instruments. This is what jealousy does: it corrupts every relationship.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house while David was playing the lyre, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand. And Saul hurled the spear, for he thought, I will pin David to the wall. But David evaded him twice.
verseByVerse.commentary: The escalation is rapid: from jealousy (v.8-9) to attempted murder (v.10-11) in a matter of verses. Saul hurls his spear twice; David dodges twice. Saul then tries subtler approaches: promote David, send him to dangerous battle positions, hope the Philistines kill him. David succeeds in every mission. The chapter ends with the devastating summary: Saul was David's enemy continually. What began as love (16:21) has become an obsession with murder. The king is lost.

19.title: The Hunter and the Hunted
19.text: <sup>9</sup>Then a harmful spirit from the LORD came upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. And David was playing the lyre. <sup>10</sup>And Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he eluded Saul, so that he struck the spear into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night. (ESV)
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is the chapter of escalation. Saul moves from covert plans to murder David to open declaration: he spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David (v. 1). The attempts multiply: the spear at home, the soldiers sent to his house at night, a second spear-throw during the Spirit's presence, the trap at Ramah. Three times David escapes, and three times the escape is providentially arranged — through Jonathan's intercession, through Michal's deception, through the Spirit of God overcoming Saul's messengers at Ramah.

The chapter reveals the utter collapse of Saul's self-control. The man who opened the book with impressive stature and apparent humility now sits in his house with his spear in his hand — a symbol of the paranoid, coiled tension that has become his permanent state. And in the darkest irony, it is while David plays the lyre to soothe Saul that Saul throws the spear at him. The ministry of grace is met with attempted murder. This is the dynamic between Saul and David for the rest of the book: the one who would save is pursued by the one he is trying to save.

sections.title: Jonathan's Intercession
sections.commentary:
Jonathan's response to his father's declaration is immediate and courageous: he speaks to Saul on David's behalf, reminding him of David's faithfulness and the military success David has brought to Israel. His argument is a masterpiece of pastoral persuasion: why then will you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause? (v. 5). He appeals to Saul's conscience, to the facts of David's track record, and to the theological principle of innocent blood. Saul listens — temporarily. He swears an oath that David shall not die.

Jonathan's willingness to intercede for David at personal cost — he is the crown prince defending the man who is his rival for the throne — models the kind of self-giving love that his covenant with David established. He is not neutral; he is actively working against his own dynastic interest for the sake of someone he loves and for the sake of justice. Alistair Begg observes that Jonathan's intercession here anticipates the role of the intercessor in the NT: someone who pleads on behalf of the accused before the one who has power over life and death, appealing to justice and mercy, at personal cost.

sections.title: The Spear, the Night Escape, Michal's Stratagem
sections.commentary:
Despite Saul's oath, the harmful spirit returns, and Saul throws the spear at David a second time. David escapes into the night, and Saul sends soldiers to his house to kill him at dawn. Michal — David's wife, Saul's daughter — saves him by letting him down through a window and placing a household idol under the covers to deceive the messengers. The scene is a tangle of deception and grace: Michal uses deception to preserve her husband's life, David escapes through a window by night, and the messengers are outwitted.

The household idol in the bed is a jarring detail. Its presence in David's house raises questions that the text does not fully resolve — whether it was Michal's or David's, whether it was tolerated or concealed. What is clear is that Michal's loyalty to David overrides her loyalty to her father, and she acts with quick thinking to preserve his life. The text does not approve of the deception or the idol; it simply records what happened. R. C. Sproul notes that God often works through the morally complicated decisions of imperfect people to accomplish his sovereign purposes — David's escape is genuine, whatever the means by which it was secured.

sections.title: The Spirit at Ramah: Saul's Messengers Prophesy
sections.commentary:
When David flees to Samuel at Ramah, Saul sends three successive groups of messengers to arrest him. Each group, when they arrive, encounters the company of prophets prophesying with Samuel over them, and the Spirit of God comes upon the messengers and they prophesy too. The final irony: Saul himself goes to Ramah, and the Spirit of God comes upon him, and he prophesies before Samuel and lies naked on the ground all day and all night. And the proverb rings out again: Is Saul also among the prophets?

The Spirit's work here is not the same as in chapter 10 — it is not empowerment for office but divine disruption of human plans. The Spirit overrides the murderous intent of the messengers and of Saul himself, using prophetic ecstasy as a means of preventing David's capture. The living God will not allow his anointed to be taken before his time. This is the same providential protection that will characterize David's entire fugitive period: not because David deserves it or earns it, but because God has made a promise about David's line and that promise cannot be broken by any human power. Tim Keller observes that the chapters of David's flight are a continuous demonstration of Romans 8:28: God works all things together for good for those he has called — including the schemes of a paranoid king and the deception of a soldier's wife.

19.theology: The Inviolability of God's Anointed. Chapter 19 demonstrates that Saul cannot kill David no matter how many resources he deploys — not because David is powerful but because God has chosen him. The Spirit disrupts the messengers, Michal deceives the soldiers, Jonathan intercedes before Saul. The protection is not uniform — David has to flee for his life repeatedly — but it is comprehensive: he will not die before his time, because God's purposes for him cannot be frustrated. This is the same promise that Paul summarizes in Romans 8:31–39: if God is for us, who can be against us?
19.examples:
Then: David's flight from his own house by night, with a teraphim in his bed, is one of the most undignified moments in the story of a man who will be the greatest king in Israel's history. The anointed king flees like a fugitive.

Now: The chapter speaks to all who are in situations where human power seems entirely arrayed against them. God's protection of his people does not mean they will not suffer; it means they will not ultimately be destroyed. The same Spirit who disrupted Saul's messengers is at work in every situation where the powers of this world seem to have the final word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-24 - The Hunter and the Hunted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul orders David's death. Jonathan intercedes and temporarily restores David to court. Another spear-throw drives David away permanently. Michal lowers him through a window. David flees to Samuel at Ramah. Saul's messengers and then Saul himself encounter the Spirit of God prophesying and cannot seize David.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is structured around multiple layers of protection for David: Jonathan's intercession, Michal's deception, Samuel's prophetic community, and the Spirit of God falling on Saul's messengers three times, then on Saul himself. Every attempt to seize David is supernaturally frustrated. Kidner notes that God uses the Spirit's falling on Saul not to bless him but to protect David - the same power that once filled Saul is now wielded against him.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that the household idol in David's bed is a troubling detail - why does Michal have an idol? The text does not comment; it simply records. The story's concern is David's escape, not Michal's spirituality. But the detail is a window into the compromised household David is leaving behind.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted greatly in David... And Saul also sent messengers to take David, and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers of Saul, and they also prophesied.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jonathan's intercession works temporarily; Saul swears not to kill David, and peace is restored. Then another battle victory triggers another prophetic episode in Saul, another spear thrown, another narrow escape. From here David does not return to court. Michal's deception of Saul's messengers buys David time but cannot hold indefinitely. At Ramah the scene of spiritual comedy unfolds: three sets of messengers fall into prophesying; finally Saul himself comes and prophesies all night, lying naked before Samuel. The question the people had asked long ago - Is Saul also among the prophets? - echoes here with dark irony. Yes, but not because God is with him; because God is protecting David from him.

20.title: Covenant Friendship
20.text: <sup>17</sup>And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul. <sup>42</sup>'Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.' (ESV)
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is the most intimate chapter in 1 Samuel — a long, painful, tender dialogue between two friends who are being torn apart by forces neither of them chose. Jonathan still struggles to believe his father would actually try to kill David; David knows with certainty that he is a dead man if he remains. Their conversation moves through confusion, grief, plan, and covenant, and ends with an embrace and tears and a farewell that they both somehow know is permanent.

The covenant Jonathan makes in this chapter — including the extraordinary provision for David's descendants after Jonathan's death (v. 15) — is one of the great acts of self-giving friendship in Scripture. Jonathan is signing away not only his own prospects but his children's. He asks David not to cut off his kindness from his house forever (v. 15), using the covenant word hesed — the same word used of God's covenant faithfulness to Israel. Jonathan is asking David to treat his family with the kind of love God shows to his people: loyal, undeserved, permanent. And David will do exactly this: in 2 Samuel 9, he will find Mephibosheth, Jonathan's crippled son, and bring him to the king's table for the rest of his life — the chapter that stands as 1 Samuel 20's fulfillment.

sections.title: The Question and the Plan
sections.commentary:
David's opening question — What have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life? — is the question of the innocent man who cannot understand why he is being hunted. He has done nothing but serve faithfully, fight victoriously, and honor the king. Jonathan's response — defending his father with the logic that Saul would not hide such a plan from him — reveals that Jonathan has not yet fully accepted what David already knows: Saul is determined to kill him.

The test Jonathan devises — David's absence from the new moon feast, explained by a plausible story, and Saul's response to be taken as the verdict — is a practical piece of intelligence-gathering that also serves as the final test of their friendship. If Saul is angry at David's absence, Jonathan will know the truth and tell David; if not, then David can return. The plan is simple and the stakes are absolute. Jonathan's promise — if my father intends to harm you, then also do so to me and more also — is a blood oath of solidarity: Jonathan is binding his fate to David's in the covenant God.

The section ends with Jonathan's covenant request: show me the steadfast love of the LORD (v. 14) — use the covenant word, hesed, to describe what Jonathan is asking for. He is asking David to treat him and his descendants with the same quality of love that defines God's relationship with his people. This is one of the most remarkable requests in Scripture: a prince asking a shepherd to promise him the quality of divine love. And David's agreement to it is a promise that will shape the entire subsequent history of the two houses.

sections.title: Saul's Rage Confirms the Verdict
sections.commentary:
The new moon feast is the test. David is absent; Saul notices on the first day but says nothing, assuming ritual impurity. On the second day, his patience breaks: Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today? Jonathan's explanation triggers the volcanic eruption that reveals Saul's true state: You son of a perverse, rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame... For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established.

The attack on Jonathan's mother is the act of a man who has lost all restraint — shaming his son by shaming his son's mother, equating Jonathan's love for David with political treachery. And when Jonathan defends David — Why should he be put to death? What has he done? — Saul hurls his spear at his own son. The man who has thrown spears at David now throws one at Jonathan. The paranoia has consumed the capacity for paternal love; Saul is at war with the living God and everyone associated with his purposes. Alistair Begg writes that Saul's attack on Jonathan is the clearest evidence of how completely his spirit has been taken over by the harmful spirit the LORD permitted: a father trying to kill his own son for defending an innocent man is not the action of a rational person but of someone whose soul has been surrendered to something dark.

sections.title: The Final Farewell
sections.commentary:
The communication of the verdict is done with the prearranged arrow signal — Jonathan sends the arrows beyond the lad, signaling danger. The practical purpose is to communicate without words; the emotional weight is immense. Then, when the servant has gone away, the two friends meet face to face and weep together, with David weeping more. The grief of this moment is the grief of a friendship severed by circumstances neither of them chose, by a father's madness and a kingdom's demand.

Jonathan's final words — Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever — are the most theologically weighty farewell in the OT. The covenant is permanent, even across death. The LORD is the guarantor. Jonathan knows, even if he does not say it explicitly, that David is going to be king. He is sending away the future king with a blessing and a covenant, surrendering his own future to the God whose purposes he cannot resist. Tim Keller writes that Jonathan's farewell is the noblest act of human love in the entire OT: he gives up everything — his inheritance, his proximity, his claims — so that God's anointed can fulfill God's purpose. In this he is an image, however incomplete, of the one who would say: Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends (John 15:13).

20.theology: Covenant Friendship as an Image of Grace. Jonathan's love for David — self-giving, covenantal, extending beyond his own death to his descendants, grounded in the character of God (the hesed of the LORD) — is the OT's clearest picture of how grace works. He does not love David because David can do anything for him; he loves David because God's election has knit their souls together and because Jonathan has aligned his will with God's purposes. This kind of friendship is not natural; it is grace. Paul's description of Christ's love in 2 Corinthians 8:9 and Philippians 2:6–8 captures what Jonathan images: voluntary surrender of rights and position out of love for another, to the other's benefit and one's own cost.
20.examples:
Then: Jonathan's covenant with David at a moment of crisis — when his father has just thrown a spear at him — is one of the most remarkable acts of faith in the entire OT. He chooses the covenant over self-preservation, God's anointed over his father's dynasty, the eternal over the immediate.

Now: The chapter challenges the contemporary church's understanding of friendship and community. Jonathan models the kind of friendship that modern culture can barely imagine: willing to suffer personal cost for the welfare of another, grounded in shared commitment to God's purposes rather than mutual benefit, extending across time and death. This is the kind of community the church is called to embody.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David and Jonathan devise a plan to test whether Saul still intends to kill David. At the New Moon feast, Saul's rage at Jonathan's defense of David reveals his murderous intent. Jonathan warns David with the arrow signal; the two friends weep together and part.
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant between David and Jonathan reaches its fullest expression here. Jonathan asks David to show steadfast love (hesed) to his household forever - the covenant word that binds them across time. David will honor this covenant in 2 Samuel 9, seeking out Jonathan's disabled son Mephibosheth. The parting of David and Jonathan is one of the most tender moments in Scripture: two men who love each other with covenant loyalty, weeping because they know they will not meet again as equals.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson notes that Jonathan's confrontation of his father is an act of covenant courage: he chooses David over his own dynastic interest, truth over self-preservation. When Saul hurls a spear at Jonathan himself (v.33), Jonathan sees clearly what he has always known: his father is lost. The kingdom belongs to David, and Jonathan is content with that.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, May the LORD take vengeance on David's enemies. And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul. Then Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.
verseByVerse.commentary: The plan is careful: David will be absent from the New Moon feast, Jonathan will present an excuse, and Saul's reaction will reveal whether the threat is real. Saul's explosion at Jonathan - Do you not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame? - confirms what David feared. The thrown spear at Jonathan (v.33) removes any remaining doubt. Jonathan gives the arrow signal in the field, and the friends meet one last time to weep and covenant. The weeping is genuine and the covenant is binding: the LORD will be between their families forever. This is not merely personal friendship; it is a covenant that will shape political history and provide for Jonathan's disabled son in chapter 9.

21.title: David at Nob
21.text: <sup>6</sup>So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it is taken away. (ESV)
21.overview:
Chapter 21 shows David in flight, making decisions under pressure that are not always admirable. At Nob, he deceives Ahimelech the priest — claiming to be on a secret mission for the king, hiding his fugitive status — in order to obtain bread and a weapon. He takes the consecrated showbread, which by law was reserved for the priests, and takes Goliath's sword. He then flees to the Philistine city of Gath, where he feigns madness before Achish to avoid being killed.

The chapter is one of the most theologically interesting in the book because Jesus himself will cite it. In Matthew 12:3–4, when challenged about his disciples eating grain on the Sabbath, Jesus says: Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? Jesus uses David's action not to justify lawlessness but to illustrate that genuine human need and the purposes of the kingdom can override ceremonial rules. David's example becomes a lens through which Jesus reads the relationship between the law's letter and the law's purpose.

sections.title: The Priest and the Consecrated Bread
sections.commentary:
Ahimelech's fear at David's arrival — Why are you alone, and no one with you? — suggests that a solitary David, without the military escort appropriate to his status, was an unusual and alarming sight. David's deception is both practical and theologically troubling: he claims to be on a secret mission for the king, knowing full well he is a fugitive. His need is genuine; his method is dishonest. The text records both without editorial comment, leaving the moral complexity for the reader to navigate.

The bread David receives — the Bread of the Presence (showbread) — was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath, replaced with fresh bread, and given to the priests to eat (Lev. 24:5–9). It was holy food, not intended for general consumption. Ahimelech's provision of it to David was an act of extraordinary generosity and perhaps recklessness; it will cost him everything (22:9–19). But the fact that Jesus cites this episode approvingly shows that the priest's instinct was right: when the genuine servant of God is in desperate need, the ceremonial law must yield to the moral law. The purpose of the showbread was to honor God and sustain his servants; it did exactly that when it fed David.

The sword of Goliath in Nob's tabernacle is a marvelous detail — preserved as a trophy, wrapped in cloth, kept behind the ephod. Its return to David's hand is both practical and symbolic: the champion who killed Goliath recovers his weapon in the hour of his greatest vulnerability. The God who gave David the victory at the Valley of Elah has not forgotten him in the fugitive's panic.

sections.title: The Madman of Gath
sections.commentary:
David's arrival in Gath — the home city of Goliath — is the act of a desperate man who has run out of better options. He is recognized immediately by the servants of Achish: Is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'? The same song that destroyed Saul's relationship with David now threatens David's life in Philistia. He is famous in all the wrong places.

His response — feigning madness, scrabbling on the doors, letting spittle run down his beard — is one of the most undignified episodes in the story of any biblical hero. The future king of Israel is playing the fool to save his skin. It works; Achish sends him away. Psalm 34 is David's meditation on this escape: I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears. He looked on the grotesque spectacle of a king feigning madness and saw God's deliverance. The point is not the method but the outcome: God preserved his anointed even through the most humiliating expedients. R. C. Sproul notes that 1 Samuel does not airbrush its heroes — David's fear and deception are recorded without flattery — because the Bible is interested in the God who saves imperfect, frightened people, not in the creation of moral exemplars.

21.theology: The Bread of the Presence and Its Fulfillment. Jesus' citation of the Nob episode in Matthew 12 establishes a theological principle with profound christological implications: the ceremonial law serves the purposes of the kingdom, not the reverse. When David needed bread, the showbread fed him. When the Son of David was present, the Sabbath law yielded to his presence and purposes. The bread that fed David in his desperation points forward to the One who is himself the Bread of Life, who gives his flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51), and who feeds his people not with twelve loaves of showbread but with the substance those loaves were always pointing toward.
21.examples:
Then: Ahimelech's generosity to David cost him his life (22:18). He acted rightly under pressure, with incomplete information, and was destroyed by Saul's paranoid retaliation. The innocent suffer in the wake of Saul's madness — and the blood of Nob's priests will be one of the ongoing griefs of David's fugitive period.

Now: The chapter teaches that genuine desperation sometimes drives God's servants to imperfect solutions, and God in his grace works through the imperfect solutions without endorsing them. David's deception at Nob is not held up as a model; David's God-centeredness in Psalm 34's reflection on it is.
