The believer in crisis is not required to be perfect in method; they are required to trust God with the outcome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David flees to the tabernacle at Nob and approaches the priest Ahimelech. He lies about his mission - claiming secret royal business - and receives the consecrated showbread and Goliath's sword. The narrator notes that Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, is present.
verseByVerse.theology: David's deception of Ahimelech is a moral failure with catastrophic consequences in chapter 22. Jesus cites this incident in Matthew 12:3-4 to establish that human need can take precedence over ritual regulation - but the story is not a simple hero narrative. It is a realistic portrait of a man under extreme pressure making imperfect choices, with consequences he cannot yet see.
verseByVerse.examples: Kidner notes that the presence of Doeg the Edomite in verse 7 is one of the most ominous details in the story. The narrator plants him here so that when the massacre of the priests occurs in chapter 22, the reader understands the chain of cause and effect. David's one lie will cost 85 priestly lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came to meet David, trembling, and said to him, Why are you alone, and no one with you?
verseByVerse.commentary: Ahimelech's trembling at David's arrival suggests he senses something is wrong. David's lie is smooth and specific: secret royal mission, his men meeting him elsewhere. Ahimelech accepts it and provides the showbread (the only bread available) and Goliath's sword - the weapon of David's greatest triumph, kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. The irony of David receiving Goliath's sword while fleeing for his life is not lost on the narrator. What he does not notice, or notices too late, is Doeg watching from the corner.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David flees to Achish king of Gath. The servants of Achish recognize him as the man of whom the Israelites sang. David feigns madness to avoid execution and is dismissed by Achish.
verseByVerse.theology: David's feigning of madness is a humiliating performance from a man who had been the hero of Israel. Psalm 34 and Psalm 56 are associated with this incident. The outer humiliation is accompanied by inner trust: This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles (Ps. 34:6). The suffering that looks like failure is the very place where the prayer-life of faith deepens most.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg notes that David's feigned madness in Gath becomes the occasion for some of his most beautiful psalms. This is how God works: the lowest points become the richest wells of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And David rose and fled that day from Saul and went to Achish the king of Gath. And the servants of Achish said to him, Is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in dances, Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands?
verseByVerse.commentary: The same song that triggered Saul's jealousy now endangers David in Gath. His fame is his liability: every Philistine knows his name. His response is extreme and effective: he behaves as if mad, scrabbling at the gate and drooling on his beard. Achish, disgusted, refuses to have a madman in his court. David escapes. The contrast with chapter 17 is almost unbearable: the young man who ran toward Goliath with five smooth stones and the name of the LORD now crouches and drools to survive. These are the psalms of the wilderness years - written not from positions of strength but from caves, from desperate hiding places, from the school of suffering through which God trains his king.

22.title: The Massacre at Nob
22.text: <sup>2</sup>And everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. There were about four hundred men with him. <sup>19</sup>And Nob, the city of the priests, he put to the sword; both men and women, children and nursing infants, oxen, donkeys and sheep, he put to the sword. (ESV)
22.overview:
Chapter 22 contains two scenes that could not be more different in their moral register. The first is the gathering of David's band at Adullam: the distressed, the indebted, the bitter — four hundred men who are, in every human sense, the dregs of Israelite society. David becomes their commander and shapes them into the most loyal fighting force in Israel. The second is Saul's massacre at Nob: eighty-five priests killed by Doeg the Edomite, and the entire city of Nob — men, women, children, infants, livestock — put to the sword. The chapter traces the diverging trajectories of the two anointed men: David gathering the broken and making something of them; Saul unleashing a bloodbath on the innocent.

The massacre at Nob is the chapter's theological center of gravity. It fulfills the prophecy of chapter 2:31–33 — the destruction of the Elide priestly line — but its immediate cause is Saul's madness and the treachery of Doeg the Edomite. The one Israelite who would not kill the priests (Saul's guards refused) was a foreigner, an Edomite, who had no covenant loyalty to prevent him. When Saul orders the killing and his own men refuse, he turns to Doeg — and the massacre that follows is the most atrocious act of the entire book up to this point.

sections.title: The Cave of Adullam: A King for the Broken
sections.commentary:
The gathering at Adullam is one of the most theologically significant details in the David narrative. Those who come to him are described in three categories: those in distress, those in debt, those who were bitter in soul. These are not David's natural constituency — they are the failures, the fugitives, the financially ruined, the emotionally desperate. They number four hundred, and David becomes their captain. From this unpromising material — the rejects and the wreckage of Israeli society — God will forge the mighty men who will secure David's kingdom and carry his name into legend.

Tim Keller observes that the cave of Adullam is the most perfect OT image of the church: the gathering of the unlikely, the broken, the socially marginal around the anointed king who makes something of them. The mighty men of 2 Samuel 23 — the warriors who perform extraordinary acts of valor — are the same people who arrived at Adullam with nothing. The transformation comes not from their own resources but from their relationship to David and the training he provides. This is precisely the pattern of the kingdom of God: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth (1 Cor. 1:26) — but God uses the things that are nothing to bring to nothing the things that are.

sections.title: Doeg's Betrayal and Saul's Paranoia
sections.commentary:
The scene in Saul's court at Gibeah reveals the depth of his paranoia. He accuses his Benjaminite officers of conspiracy — will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards? — and receives no response. They are afraid; they know the king is not rational. Into this silence steps Doeg the Edomite, who was present at Nob (21:7) and who now reports David's visit to Ahimelech with the calculated clarity of a man who knows exactly what he is doing.

Saul summons Ahimelech and all the priests of Nob. Ahimelech's defense is the defense of innocence: he did not know David was fleeing; he had always found David trustworthy; he had inquired of God for David before, as was his role. It is a genuine, dignified response that deserves acquittal. Saul sentences him to death anyway, along with all the priests of his house. His own soldiers refuse to execute the command — striking down the priests of the LORD was too clearly an act of sacrilege for even Saul's hardened guards. Doeg steps forward and kills eighty-five priests in one day.

The massacre extends to the entire city: men, women, children, nursing infants, livestock. This is Saul applying the herem — the utter destruction he refused to apply to the Amalekites — to the priests and servants of God in Israel. The theological irony is total: he preserved Agag when commanded to destroy him, and destroys the city of priests when commanded to honor them. His obedience is inverted — he destroys what God protects and protects what God commands him to destroy. Sinclair Ferguson writes that this is the final evidence of Saul's moral dissolution: the same king who began by being unwilling to touch even his enemies without divine authorization now massacres the household of God on the word of a foreign informer.

sections.title: Abiathar Escapes; David's Grief
sections.commentary:
One priest escapes: Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, who flees to David with the ephod. David's response to the news — I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house — is one of the most honest moments of self-knowledge in the entire David narrative. He does not make excuses; he accepts responsibility for his deception at Nob, which set the chain of events in motion. He cannot undo what has been done, but he can own it.

His invitation to Abiathar — Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life seeks my life. With me you shall be in safekeeping — is an act of covenantal responsibility. He created the danger; he will provide the shelter. Abiathar stays with David through the entire fugitive period and becomes his priest, carrying the ephod that enables David to inquire of the LORD. The tragedy of Nob thus produces one of the lasting resources of David's kingship: a faithful priest who is loyal precisely because David took responsibility for what his actions had caused. The God who writes straight with crooked lines is at work even here — bringing good from grief, provision from disaster, a priestly companion from a massacre.

22.theology: The Gathering of the Broken. The cave of Adullam is one of the defining images of the entire David story, and its Christological resonance is profound. The one who is himself rejected, fugitive, hunted, becomes the refuge for the rejected, the fugitive, the hunted. David does not require his men to have their lives together before he takes them in; he takes in the broken and makes them his. This is the grammar of grace: the King who is himself despised and rejected becomes the one around whom the despised and rejected gather, and makes them a kingdom. Isaiah 53's suffering servant and the gathering of the nations around him is anticipated in every person who scrambled to the cave of Adullam.
22.examples:
Then: The four hundred men at Adullam became, under David's leadership, the core of the most effective military force in Israel's history. God regularly does his best work with the raw material the world has discarded.

Now: The chapter addresses directly the person who feels too broken, too indebted, too distressed to be of any use to God. The cave of Adullam says otherwise. The King who gathered those four hundred gathers still — not the impressive, the qualified, and the whole, but the distressed, the indebted, and the bitter of soul. And what he makes of them is extraordinary.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David retreats to the cave of Adullam. His family comes to him; then those in distress, in debt, and discontented gather around him - 400 men. He places his parents in Moab for safekeeping. The prophet Gad directs him back to Judah.
verseByVerse.theology: The 400 men who gather at Adullam are described in unflattering terms: in distress, in debt, discontented. These are not the cream of Israel; they are the outcasts, the failures, the desperate. And David becomes their commander. Sproul notes that the community forming around David at Adullam is a type of the church - gathered from those whom the world has rejected, led by the one who has himself experienced suffering and humiliation.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller observes that David's care for his parents - taking them to Moab, outside Saul's reach - reveals the character of a man who remembers his family even in extremity. He is not just surviving; he is caring for those entrusted to him.

verseByVerse.quote: David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. And when his brothers and all his father's house heard it, they went down there to him. And everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. And there were with him about 400 men.
verseByVerse.commentary: The cave of Adullam becomes David's base of operations - his refuge, the location of several psalms. The community that gathers around him is the community of the marginalized: people with no place in Saul's organized society, people who are desperate enough to follow a fugitive. 400 men with nothing to lose, following a man anointed to be king but currently sleeping in caves. David organizes them, leads them, and turns them into the fighting force that will eventually become his royal army. God is building a king the slow way, through the school of the wilderness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul's rage overflows onto the priests of Nob. Doeg reports that Ahimelech assisted David. Saul orders his guards to kill the priests; they refuse. Doeg the Edomite executes 85 priests and then destroys the entire town of Nob. One priest, Abiathar, escapes to David.
verseByVerse.theology: The massacre at Nob is the darkest moment of Saul's reign. He murders the priests of God and extends the slaughter to an entire town. His own soldiers refuse the order. MacArthur notes that Saul has become what Israel was supposed to be protected from - a tyrant who murders those who serve God. David's guilt is his own: his lie to Ahimelech put the priest in jeopardy, and he acknowledges it directly to Abiathar: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur notes that the murder of the priests fulfills the prophecy against the house of Eli (2:31-36): not a single one of Eli's descendants would live to old age. God's judgment, even when executed through the wickedness of a man like Saul, is precise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to Doeg, You turn and strike the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests, and he killed on that day eighty-five persons who wore the linen ephod. And Nob, the city of the priests, he put to the sword; both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep, he put to the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary: The massacre is described with the same language used for the ban against the Amalekites that Saul refused to fully execute (15:3): men, women, children, infants, livestock. What Saul would not do against Israel's enemies, he does against Israel's priests. The irony is crushing. Saul's soldiers refuse the order - even hardened soldiers recognize sacrilege. Doeg the Edomite, a foreign mercenary, has no such compunctions. Eighty-five priests in linen ephods, then the entire town. One escapes: Abiathar, who flees to David. David receives him with grief and responsibility: Stay with me; do not be afraid. The fugitive king takes in the fugitive priest.

23.title: David Strengthens Himself in the LORD
23.text: <sup>14</sup>And David remained in the strongholds in the wilderness, in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand. <sup>16</sup>And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God. (ESV)
23.overview:
Chapter 23 traces David's fugitive life in increasing danger and isolation. He rescues Keilah from Philistine raiders, using the ephod to inquire of the LORD — only to discover that the city he has just saved will betray him to Saul. He moves to the wilderness of Ziph, where the Ziphites promptly offer to betray him to Saul. The Philistines attack Israel, buying David a temporary reprieve when Saul is forced to break off the pursuit. Through all of this, one verse stands out as the theological center of the chapter's second half: God did not give him into his hand (v. 14).

The chapter also contains the last meeting between David and Jonathan — at Horesh, in the wilderness, a secret rendezvous that is one of the most tender passages in the book. Jonathan comes to David and strengthened his hand in God (v. 16). He does not bring military support, political alliance, or material provision. He brings the word of God's promise, the assurance of God's calling, and his own covenant friendship. It is enough. The man who will become Israel's greatest king is sustained through his darkest season not by arms or armies but by a friend who strengthens his hand in God.

sections.title: The Rescue of Keilah and the Ingratitude of the Rescued
sections.commentary:
David's inquiry of the LORD about the Philistine attack on Keilah is the first use of the ephod Abiathar brought from Nob, and it establishes the pattern of David's leadership that distinguishes him from Saul: he inquires of God before acting, not after. When his men express fear — Behold, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines? — David inquires again, and God confirms the command. They go, they rescue Keilah, they save the city. And then: David inquires whether Saul will come, and whether the men of Keilah will surrender him. Yes to both. The city he has just rescued will hand him over to the man trying to kill him.

The ingratitude of Keilah is not the chapter's moral judgment on the city; it is the context in which David's trust in God is tested. He has done a good deed and been rewarded with the prospect of betrayal. This is the pattern of the anointed life: faithfulness does not guarantee human loyalty. The same God who told David to go to Keilah now tells him the truth about Keilah's intentions — and David receives both pieces of truth and acts accordingly. R. C. Sproul observes that David's practice of asking God twice — once to receive direction, once to confirm it when the situation changes — is a model of humble, persistent dependence on God's guidance rather than human wisdom.

sections.title: Jonathan's Last Visit: Strength in God
sections.commentary:
Jonathan's journey to Horesh — deep in the wilderness where David is hiding — is an act of extraordinary personal courage. He is the crown prince, the son of the man who has sent armies to kill David; his presence with David is a political declaration that could cost him his life. He comes anyway, because his covenant with David is stronger than his fear of his father. And what he brings is not food, or weapons, or military intelligence — he brings the word of God's promise: Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this.

The phrase strengthened his hand in God — wayechazzeq et-yado be-elohim — is one of the most important phrases in the entire David narrative. When human circumstances were completely against David — pursued, betrayed, isolated, hunted — Jonathan comes to him and reminds him of what God has said. This is the ministry of encouragement at its highest: not false positivity, not platitudes, but the specific word of God applied to the specific discouragement. Jonathan has nothing materially to offer; he offers the one thing that money cannot buy and armies cannot provide — the certainty of God's word and the presence of a faithful friend.

Alistair Begg writes that this scene is the pattern of all true pastoral friendship: coming to the one who is discouraged and strengthening their hand not in their own strength or yours but in God. The question Jonathan's visit raises for every Christian is: who is the person in your life who needs someone to come to their Horesh, to the wilderness where they are hiding, and remind them of what God has said? And are you willing to pay the cost of going?

sections.title: The Ziphites' Betrayal and the Last Escape
sections.commentary:
The Ziphites offer to betray David to Saul — twice (v. 19; 26:1). Saul's response — May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me — is one of the most chilling lines in the book. He uses the covenant blessing formula to praise those who are helping him murder the LORD's anointed. The language of piety in the service of murder is the mark of a soul that has completely lost its moral coherence.

The pursuit reaches its most intense moment in verse 26: Saul and his men on one side of the mountain, David and his men on the other, with Saul about to close in — and then a messenger arrives: Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid against the land. Saul breaks off the pursuit. God uses a Philistine attack to save his anointed from Saul. The place is named Sela-hammahlekoth — Rock of Escape, or Rock of Divisions — a permanent memorial to the moment when God divided Saul from David with a Philistine raid. The LORD who controls all the nations is never without a resource for the protection of his anointed. Psalm 54, written in response to the Ziphites' betrayal, captures David's theology of this season: Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life.

23.theology: Inquiring of the LORD. The repeated pattern in chapter 23 — David inquires of God, receives an answer, acts on it, and inquires again when circumstances change — is the model of Spirit-directed leadership that the entire David story offers as an alternative to Saul's self-directed leadership. Saul acts, then asks God to confirm his actions; David asks God, then acts. The difference is the direction of authority: David places God's word above his own judgment; Saul places his own judgment above God's word. This pattern of seeking God's direction is the practical expression of being a man after God's own heart.
23.examples:
Then: Jonathan's visit to Horesh was not only David's comfort — it was the last time the two friends would see each other alive. Jonathan died at Jezreel (ch. 31) before David became king. His final act of friendship — strengthening David's hand in God — was the most lasting gift he could have given.

Now: David's darkest season — hunted, betrayed, exhausted, isolated — is sustained by two resources: Jonathan's encouragement and God's protection. Both are gifts, neither is earned. The chapter calls the believer in their own wilderness season to the same resources: the word of God applied by faithful friends, and the sovereign protection of a God who does not give his anointed into the hand of his enemies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-29 - David Strengthens Himself in the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David rescues the town of Keilah from Philistine raiders, then flees when he learns the townspeople would betray him to Saul. In the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan finds David and strengthens his hand in God. The Ziphites betray David's location to Saul. David is nearly surrounded when a messenger diverts Saul with news of a Philistine raid.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is a series of narrow escapes, each time preceded by David inquiring of the LORD through the ephod. This consultation of God - asking direct questions and receiving accurate answers - is the practical expression of walking with God: before acting, ask. David does not move without divine guidance. Ferguson notes that David's consistent pattern of inquiring of the LORD is the discipline that distinguishes him from Saul, who acts on impulse and only belatedly, if ever, seeks God's guidance.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller observes that Jonathan's final appearance in the narrative (v.16-18) is a deliberate gift of the narrator: before the Ziphites betray David, Jonathan comes to strengthen his hand in God. The covenanting friend, the man who gave away his robe and weapons, comes one last time to say: God's purpose for you stands. Then he goes home and is never seen alive again.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God. And he said to him, Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jonathan's words are a covenant confession and a prophetic affirmation: You shall be king over Israel. He knows what God has decreed; he has accepted it; he has made his peace with it. He offers David what every person under sustained threat needs: not strategy or resources, but assurance that God's purposes have not changed. Strengthened his hand in God is the deepest form of pastoral care - not false reassurance but solid grounding in divine promise. The narrator's summary - Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand - is the theological commentary on all the narrow escapes. The pursuers are real; the protection is realer.

24.title: David Spares Saul at En-gedi
24.text: <sup>6</sup>He said to his men, 'The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed.' <sup>12</sup>'May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you.' (ESV)
24.overview:
Chapter 24 presents the supreme test of David's character. Saul is searching for him in the wilderness of En-gedi with three thousand chosen men. David and his men are hiding in the innermost part of a cave — and Saul enters the same cave, alone, to relieve himself. David's men see it as divine providence: Here is the day of which the LORD said to you, I will give your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you. David creeps forward and cuts off the corner of Saul's robe. And then his heart strikes him.

The restraint David exercises in this moment is not merely tactical or political; it is profoundly theological. He refuses to kill Saul not because it would be impractical but because Saul remains the LORD's anointed — and David will not raise his hand against the one God has placed in authority, even when that person is trying to murder him and even when the opportunity to end the pursuit forever is right in front of him. This is Paul's principle in Philippians 2:6 embodied centuries before Paul wrote it: though he had every right to seize the kingdom by force, he did not grasp at it. He waited for God's timing. He would not take what God had promised through the means God had not authorized.

sections.title: The Cave and the Cut Corner
sections.commentary:
The men's interpretation of the situation — that the LORD has delivered Saul into David's hand — is understandable and almost certainly sincere. They have been running for their lives, watching their leader hunted like an animal for years; surely this providential meeting in the cave is God's deliverance. But David refuses their interpretation. He cuts the corner of Saul's robe — a mark of superiority, a symbolic gesture, perhaps the nearest he allows himself to come to asserting his coming kingship — and immediately his heart condemns him even for that.

R. C. Sproul writes that David's heart striking him over the cut corner is one of the most remarkable evidences of his spiritual sensitivity in the entire narrative. He did not kill Saul; he did not wound him; he did not even confront him. He cut a piece of his robe in the dark. And that was too much. The man after God's own heart has a conscience calibrated so finely that even a symbolic act of assertion against the LORD's anointed registers as transgression. This is not scrupulosity; it is the deeply tender conscience of a man whose primary concern is the honor of God and the sacredness of divine appointment, even when that appointment has been used against him.

His rebuke to his men — The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him — is both a theological statement and a pastoral act of leadership. He is not only restraining himself; he is forming his men in the same theology. The way you treat those God has placed in authority tells you something about whether you actually believe in divine sovereignty or merely invoke it when convenient.

sections.title: David's Confrontation and Saul's Tears
sections.commentary:
After Saul leaves the cave, David follows him out and calls after him, bowing low. His speech is a masterpiece of covenantal argument: he holds up the corner of the robe as evidence that he had the opportunity and refused it. He appeals to God as judge: May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you. He quotes the proverb — out of the wicked comes wickedness — to distance himself from Saul's characterization of him as evil. He asks the rhetorical question: After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea! — presenting himself as utterly unthreatening, a mosquito in Saul's path, while making clear that God is his defender.

Saul's response is one of the most poignant and pathetic moments in the book. He weeps. He acknowledges that David is more righteous than he is. He acknowledges that God will give David the kingdom. He asks David to swear that he will not cut off Saul's descendants or blot out his name. And then — immediately — he goes home and David returns to his stronghold. Nothing changes. The acknowledgment does not produce repentance; it produces tears and words that evaporate as soon as Saul leaves the confrontation. In chapter 26, he will be pursuing David again. Sinclair Ferguson observes that the sorrow Saul shows here is what Paul calls 'worldly grief' (2 Cor. 7:10) — the grief that sees the truth, feels the weight of it emotionally, and then goes back to the sin. It is not the godly grief that produces repentance; it is sorrow for consequences rather than sorrow for sin against God.

24.theology: Not Grasping the Kingdom. David's refusal to seize the kingdom by killing Saul in the cave is one of the most powerful Christological types in all of the OT. Philippians 2:6 — though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped — describes Christ's voluntary restraint of his divine rights in the incarnation. David in the cave enacts the same pattern: he has what it takes to take what is rightfully his, and he refuses. The kingdom that God has promised through anointing and covenant he will not seize through murder. He will wait for God's timing, trust God's method, and suffer in the meantime. This is the theology of the cross before the cross: suffering willingly when power is available, in order to receive the kingdom in the way that God appoints.
24.examples:
Then: David's declaration — the LORD judge between us — is the covenant formula for resolving disputes without retaliation. He is not passive; he is handing the case to the supreme court whose verdict cannot be corrupted.

Now: The chapter speaks to everyone in a situation where they have the power to retaliate and the justification to do so. David's restraint was not weakness; it was theology made incarnate. The Christian who refuses to grasp what they are owed, who trusts God as judge, who refuses to take justice into their own hands — is living by David's principle and imaging Christ's own way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-22 - David Spares Saul at En-gedi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul enters a cave to relieve himself - the very cave where David and his men are hiding. David's men urge him to kill Saul. David secretly cuts off a corner of Saul's robe but refuses to strike him. He calls out to Saul after he leaves the cave and presents his case. Saul weeps and acknowledges that David will be king.
verseByVerse.theology: David's refusal to kill Saul is one of the defining moral moments of his life. He will not raise his hand against the LORD's anointed. The principle is not that Saul is innocent; David knows Saul is wrong. The principle is that the transfer of kingship belongs to God, not to David's initiative. He will not take by force what God has promised to give in his time. Sproul calls this one of the great demonstrations of covenantal submission in the Old Testament.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observes that David's conscience troubles him even for cutting the robe (v.5): even the lesser act feels like a violation of the anointed king's dignity. This sensitivity to the sanctity of God's appointments is what makes David great - not military skill or political cunning, but a deep reverence for God's sovereign ordering of human affairs.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to his men, The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed. So David persuaded his men with these words and did not permit them to attack Saul. And Saul rose up and left the cave and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary: The drama of the cave is almost comic in its setup: Saul, hunting David with 3,000 men, happens to enter the one cave where David and his men are hiding. David's men are certain this is the moment. David goes close enough to cut a corner of Saul's robe - proof that he could have killed him - but this small act troubles him. His subsequent speech to Saul from a distance is bold and eloquent: I have not sinned against you, though you hunt my life. May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you. He hands the judgment to God. Saul weeps and speaks the clearest acknowledgment he ever gives: You are more righteous than I.

25.title: Abigail: Wisdom That Stops a Fool
25.text: <sup>25</sup>'Let not my lord regard this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. But I your servant did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent. <sup>33</sup>And blessed be your discernment, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand.' (ESV)
25.overview:
Chapter 25 is a stand-alone moral drama with three characters who represent three types of response to the anointed king. Nabal (whose name literally means Fool) is the man of wealth, harsh and badly behaved, who repays David's protection with contempt. Abigail is his wife — intelligent, beautiful, quick-thinking — who intervenes to avert a massacre and wins David's heart and eventually his hand in marriage. David himself is tested and nearly fails: when Nabal insults him, he arms four hundred men and sets off for a bloodbath. Abigail's intervention is the grace that prevents David from doing the very thing he refused to do to Saul — taking justice by the sword instead of trusting the LORD.

The chapter ends with Samuel's death noted almost in passing (v. 1) — a quiet, dignified close to the greatest prophet since Moses — and with the theological verdict on Nabal's death: the LORD struck Nabal, and he died (v. 38). David does not need to take vengeance; the LORD handles it. The lesson David almost had to learn by bloodguilt he learns instead through Abigail's wisdom: Vengeance is mine, says the LORD (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19). He who waits for God's judgment can trust that it will come.

sections.title: Nabal's Folly
sections.commentary:
David's request to Nabal is reasonable and his men's conduct has been exemplary: they served as a wall of protection for Nabal's shepherds during the shearing season, a service that was worth something in the dangerous highlands of Carmel. The request — some food for the servants — is modest and the appeal well-framed. Nabal's response is savage: Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters. He dismisses David as a runaway slave, denies knowledge of who he is (which is obviously false — everyone in Judah knew who David was), and refuses everything.

The insult is calibrated to wound at its deepest point: it denies David's identity, his legitimacy, and his claims. And it works. David's response is immediate and visceral: Every man strap on his sword. Four hundred armed men begin the march to Nabal's estate. David has sworn to kill every male in Nabal's household by morning. The man who refused to harm the LORD's anointed when given the perfect opportunity in En-gedi is about to massacre a householder for an insult. The provocation is real; the response is catastrophically disproportionate. Alistair Begg observes that even the man after God's own heart can be ambushed by rage when his honor is challenged, and the danger is greatest not in the moral clarity of the cave but in the hot blood of a received insult.

sections.title: Abigail's Intervention: Wisdom as Grace
sections.commentary:
Abigail's response to the news of David's approach is both practical and prophetic. She loads donkeys with food, rides out to meet David, dismounts before him, falls on her face, and begins one of the longest and most remarkable speeches in 1 Samuel. She takes full responsibility for her husband's behavior, not because she is guilty but because she is wise enough to know that deflecting blame in this crisis will cost lives. She acknowledges David's calling, anticipates his future kingdom, and makes the crucial theological argument: if David kills Nabal, he will have worked salvation with his own hand — and God has been faithful all this time in keeping him from that.

Her key argument is theological: the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of the LORD, and evil shall not be found in you so long as you live... And the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God. She is not merely stopping a massacre; she is reminding David of who he is and what God has promised him. The man after God's own heart should not stain that heart with unnecessary blood. The bundle of the living — a beautiful image of covenant protection — is David's security, not his sword.

David's response — Blessed be your discernment, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt — is a model of the man who can receive correction from an unexpected source. He does not bristle at being corrected by a woman. He recognizes wisdom when he hears it and blesses the one who brought it. Tim Keller writes that David's receptivity to Abigail's rebuke is itself a mark of the man after God's own heart: he wants to do right more than he wants to be seen as right, and when someone shows him a better way, he takes it.

sections.title: Nabal's Death and David's Provision
sections.commentary:
Nabal's death ten days after his heart turns to stone within him is a divine judgment that vindicates David without requiring David's hand. The narrative pattern is perfect: David refrains, trusts God, and God acts. This is Romans 12:19 enacted: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. David learns in this chapter what he almost forgot: the God who protects his anointed is also the God who judges his anointed's enemies, and he does not need David's help to do it.

Abigail becomes David's wife after Nabal's death — a reward proportionate to her wisdom and loyalty. The same intelligence and theological clarity that saved lives becomes the companion of the future king. The chapter ends with a note about Ahinoam of Jezreel, David's other wife, and with the sad postscript that Saul has given Michal — David's first wife — to another man. The world of David's domestic life is as complicated as his political situation, and the narrator does not pretend otherwise. But in the center of the chapter stands Abigail, and her wisdom is the chapter's greatest gift.

25.theology: Trusting God's Vengeance. Chapter 25 teaches the theology of divine justice as the alternative to human retaliation. Abigail's argument — do not take vengeance; let the LORD handle Nabal — is the practical application of one of the OT's deepest principles (Deut. 32:35). The Christian is not called to passivity in the face of evil; David continued to lead and fight and protect. But he is called to restrain from personal retaliation, trusting that the God who sees all things will avenge what needs avenging in his own time and way.
25.examples:
Then: Abigail's intervention is sometimes described as manipulation or flattery. It is neither — it is prophetic wisdom: she tells David the truth about himself (what God has promised), the truth about his danger (bloodguilt), and the truth about his God (who fights for him). All three are accurate. Wisdom in a crisis is not saying what people want to hear but saying what is true in a way that can be received.

Now: The chapter holds three character studies: Nabal (the fool who denies reality and insults grace), Abigail (the wise who intercede for the foolish and restrain the righteous), and David (the righteous who nearly ruins everything in a moment of rage and is saved by unexpected grace). Most of us have been all three of these at different moments in our lives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-44 - Abigail: Wisdom That Stops a Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel dies. David's men protect Nabal's flocks and ask for provisions. Nabal insults them. David takes 400 armed men to exact revenge. Abigail, Nabal's wise wife, intercepts David with gifts and a speech that stops him from bloodshed. Nabal dies of a stroke. David marries Abigail.
verseByVerse.theology: Abigail's speech to David in vv.24-31 is a miniature sermon on providence and restraint. She names him as the future king before he is king and asks him to act like it: the kingdom coming will not be served by unnecessary bloodshed now. Keller notes that Abigail is a Christ-figure in miniature: she stands between the guilty party (Nabal) and the righteous wrath (David), bearing the gifts that secure peace.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that David's response to Abigail - Blessed be the LORD who sent you this day to meet me - is an acknowledgment that God sent her. He recognizes her as God's instrument of restraint.

verseByVerse.quote: But Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep already prepared and five seahs of parched grain and a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys. And she said to her servants, Go on before me; behold, I am coming after you. But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
verseByVerse.commentary: The story moves with the speed of a crisis: insult, rage, preparation for violence, and then Abigail in motion before David arrives. Her preparation is careful and comprehensive: bread, wine, sheep, grain, raisins, figs - the gifts of generosity that Nabal refused to offer. She does not tell her husband because there is no time and he would refuse. When she meets David on the road and falls at his feet, her words are not flattery but theology: she identifies herself as responsible for her husband's fault, praises David's righteousness, and argues from the future back to the present - the kingdom coming will not be served by unnecessary bloodshed now. David stops, receives her gifts, and thanks God for her. Nabal dies of a stroke when he sobers up enough to hear what almost happened. David sends for Abigail and she becomes his wife.

26.title: David Spares Saul Again
26.text: <sup>23</sup>'The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, for the LORD gave you into my hand today, and I would not put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. <sup>25</sup>Then Saul said to David, My son, may you be blessed. You will do many things and will succeed in them.' And David went his way, and Saul returned to his place. (ESV)
26.overview:
Chapter 26 is a second opportunity to kill Saul, structurally parallel to chapter 24 but with important differences. This time David does not stumble on Saul by accident — he actively seeks him out in his camp, enters the camp at night with Abishai, and stands over the sleeping king with a spear in the ground at his head. Abishai volunteers to do what David refused to do at En-gedi: God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice. David refuses again, with the same theological reason: the LORD's anointed is inviolable.

The chapter deepens the En-gedi theology by making the refusal active rather than passive. At En-gedi, David was hidden and discovered an opportunity. At Ziph, he walks into the camp intentionally and creates the opportunity. The refusal in chapter 26 is therefore more costly, more deliberate, and more theologically significant. He takes the spear and the water jug — symbolic of Saul's power and provision — as evidence of what could have been done, and then calls across the valley in the dark. The exchange between David and Saul ends as before: with Saul's tears and David's skepticism. But this time David's final words are more expansive and more theological.

sections.title: Into the Camp at Night
sections.commentary:
The Ziphites betray David again (v. 1), and David's response is not flight but reconnaissance: he sends scouts, confirms Saul's location, and then goes himself with Abishai. The deep sleep that falls on the entire camp — a deep sleep from the LORD (v. 12) — is the narrative's way of making clear that divine protection is operating at every level. Three thousand soldiers, Abner the commander of the army, Saul himself — all are in a supernatural sleep. David walks through the camp unchallenged, takes the spear and the water jug, and withdraws. God has put the entire royal army to sleep to demonstrate to David — and to us — that his anointed is inviolable when God wills it.

Abishai's logic — God has given your enemy into your hand this day — is the same logic David's men offered at En-gedi, and it is not irrational. Every circumstance of the situation suggests divine provision for David's self-defense. But David applies the same theological principle: who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless? And he adds a further element: As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish. David is not passive about the outcome; he is specific about the means. God will deal with Saul; David is not to be the instrument.

sections.title: The Confrontation Across the Valley
sections.commentary:
David's call across the valley — rebuking Abner for failing to protect the king, holding up the spear and water jug as evidence — is a masterpiece of strategic communication. He makes Abner look incompetent before the entire army while simultaneously demonstrating his own loyalty to Saul. The message is clear: if I had intended to harm him, you would all be dead. The fact that the king's spear and water are in my hands proves the king was in my hands. I chose not to use the opportunity.

Saul's response — I have sinned; return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have made a great mistake — sounds like genuine repentance. But David's response is telling: he does not return. He thanks Saul for the admission, states his own principle (the LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and faithfulness), and then says goodbye. He knows Saul well enough to know that the emotional admission will not last. And indeed it does not: in the very next chapter (27:1), David says to himself, I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul, and flees to Philistia.

Saul's final words to David — You will do many things and will succeed in them — are a prophetic blessing from a broken king. Even in his failure, Saul recognizes what God is doing, and his parting words are the last kindness he will ever show to the man whose throne was promised before his own was established. Then: David went his way, and Saul returned to his place. The finality of that separation anticipates the final chapter — they will never have this kind of conversation again. The next time we see them in relation to each other, Saul will be seeking a witch and David will be in Philistia, and there will be no more touching scenes at the edge of a dark valley.

26.theology: Patience as Theology. David's twice-refusal to kill Saul is not merely a display of personal virtue; it is a theological commitment to the principle that God's purposes are to be accomplished by God's methods. The kingdom that God has promised through anointing, through Samuel, through Jonathan's covenant, and through Abigail's prophecy is to come through God's timing and God's way — not through assassination in a cave or a midnight spear-throw. David's patience is not passivity; it is faith in the specific form of refusing to pre-empt divine action. This is the theology of the cross before the cross: the refusal to take power by violence, trusting instead in the God whose ways are higher than our ways.
26.examples:
Then: The two episodes together (chs. 24, 26) form a diptych of royal patience. Different circumstances, different methods of restraint, the same theological ground: the LORD's anointed is inviolable by human hands. David holds this principle even when Abishai (who is a better soldier than a theologian) argues strenuously against it.

Now: The principle that God's purposes are to be achieved by God's methods runs through the entire NT. Paul's instruction not to repay evil for evil (Rom. 12:17–21), Peter's call to entrust yourself to the faithful Creator (1 Pet. 4:19), and Jesus' own refusal to call down angels at Gethsemane are all downstream from David's theology in the cave and the camp.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ziphites betray David again. David and Abishai infiltrate Saul's sleeping camp, take his spear and water jar. From a safe distance David calls out to Abner and Saul. Saul again acknowledges David's righteousness.
verseByVerse.theology: The second sparing of Saul deepens David's theology: As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish. The LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD's anointed (v.10-11). David has articulated a theology of divine timing: God will deal with Saul; David's role is to wait. MacArthur observes that Abishai's framing - God has given your enemy into your hand this day - is sincere and plausible. But providence does not equal permission. The fact that God arranged access does not mean God authorized the killing.
verseByVerse.examples: Kidner notes that the supernatural element of the sleeping army - a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them - makes this scene explicitly providential. David and Abishai walk through 3,000 sleeping soldiers and stand over the king himself. God is staging the demonstration of David's restraint.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abishai said to David, God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice. But David said to Abishai, Do not destroy him, for who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?
verseByVerse.commentary: David takes Saul's spear and water jar as proof and withdraws. From the hill he calls out to Abner, shaming him for failing to guard the king, and then to Saul. Saul's response echoes En-gedi: I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm. The reconciliation is temporary; David does not trust it (v.25). But the pattern is sealed: twice David could have killed Saul and did not. The kingdom will come through God's timing, not David's opportunity.

27.title: David Among the Philistines
27.text: <sup>1</sup>But David said in his heart, 'Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand.' (ESV)
27.overview:
Chapter 27 shows David at his most pragmatic and his most morally ambiguous. He flees to Achish of Gath for a second time — not in panic this time, but as a calculated political move — and is given the border city of Ziklag as a base. For sixteen months he lives among the Philistines, conducting raids against Israel's enemies while deceiving Achish into thinking he is raiding Israelite territory. The chapter is honest about the moral complexity: David lies to Achish consistently, and the text does not directly condemn it. But neither does it praise it.

David's opening statement — I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul — is a moment of faith failure. He has had two miraculous deliverances in the previous two chapters; God has demonstrated repeatedly that he will not allow Saul to destroy him. And yet, in a moment of exhaustion and discouragement, David reasons from circumstances rather than from promise. The practical consequences of his decision — sixteen months in Philistia, deception of Achish, a battle against his own people averted only by Philistine suspicion (ch. 29), and the disaster at Ziklag (ch. 30) — are all traceable to this chapter's decision. Yet even here, God's sovereignty is not absent: the city of Ziklag becomes David's, and his raids destroy the enemies who will otherwise have been thorns in the side of his future kingdom.

sections.title: The Calculation of Despair
sections.commentary:
The phrase David said in his heart contrasts sharply with the preceding chapters' pattern of David inquiring of the LORD. When he faced the Keilah crisis, he asked God; when he faced Nabal's insult, God intervened through Abigail; when he faced Saul's pursuit, he trusted in divine protection. Now, exhausted and discouraged after years of flight, he calculates from circumstances rather than from covenant. His reasoning is not unreasonable on its own terms: Saul has three thousand soldiers; the wilderness of Judah offers limited long-term security; Philistine territory is outside Saul's jurisdiction. The logic is military and political — and it lacks God entirely.

Sinclair Ferguson writes that the most dangerous moments in the Christian life are not the dramatic temptations where the wrong path is obviously wrong, but the tired seasons where reasonable conclusions lead to faithless decisions. David is not abandoning God; he is not converting to Philistinism; he is simply making a pragmatic move that he believes will ensure his survival. But he is doing it without asking the God who has sustained him through every previous crisis, and the sixteen months in Philistia that follow are marked by the compromises that pragmatism without prayer inevitably produces.

sections.title: Ziklag and the Raids
sections.commentary:
Achish gives David Ziklag, a border city in the south of Judah, as his base. This detail becomes significant: after Saul's death, Ziklag becomes the base from which David begins his return to Judah, and the city remains in Davidic possession (v. 6). God is providing, even through David's faithless calculation, a staging ground for the kingdom to come. The sovereignty of God works not only through faithful decisions but, apparently, through faithless ones — though the faithless decisions carry their own costs.

David's raids against the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites — ancient enemies of Israel — are military necessity and covenantal judgment simultaneously. But his deception of Achish — claiming to have raided Judahite territory when he has actually raided the enemies of Judah — is a sustained lie that compromises his integrity and will nearly cost him everything in chapters 28–29. R. C. Sproul notes that the moral trajectory of living outside the will of God tends toward accumulating compromises: one deception requires another, one pragmatic move creates the conditions for the next. David is not a villain in these chapters, but he is a man who has stepped out from under the umbrella of divine guidance into the wet world of self-managed circumstances, and he is getting rained on.

27.theology: Faith in the Tired Season. Chapter 27 is the OT's most honest portrait of faith failure in the midst of genuine exhaustion. David is not an apostate; he is a tired man who stops looking up and starts looking around. The consequences are real but not permanent — God will restore him in chapters 29–30, and the disaster at Ziklag (ch. 30) will produce the most important statement in the entire David narrative: David strengthened himself in the LORD his God (30:6). The faithless chapter produces the desperate chapter that produces the great chapter of renewal. God does not abandon his anointed even when his anointed abandons the practice of seeking him.
27.examples:
Then: Sixteen months in Philistia left David with the compromises, the deceptions, and the near-catastrophe of being required to fight against Israel. Every one of those costs is traceable to the opening verse of the chapter: I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul.

Now: The chapter speaks to every believer in the exhausted season who makes decisions from circumstances rather than from covenant. The invitation at the end of such a chapter — as David found it — is always the same: strengthen yourself in the LORD your God. Not in the circumstances, not in the military calculation, not in the political alliance, but in the God whose promise does not expire when you stop claiming it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David concludes there is no long-term safety in Israel and flees to Achish king of Gath with his 600 men. Achish gives him Ziklag as a base. For sixteen months, David raids Israel's southern enemies while deceiving Achish into thinking he is raiding Judah.
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 27 is one of the morally complex passages in David's story. He deceives Achish systematically, conducting raids that serve Judah's interests while convincing the Philistine king he is attacking Judah. Kidner notes that the narrative neither commends nor condemns David's strategy. What is clear is that David is at a low point of faith: verse 1 records his inner reasoning - one day I shall perish by the hand of Saul - which is the voice of despair rather than trust.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that the sixteen months at Ziklag are not presented as a triumph but as a survival strategy in a broken situation. David is not at his best here. He is doing what he can with what he has, under conditions that his own earlier choices helped create.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said in his heart, Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: The reasoning is understandable: sixteen months in Israel, two narrow escapes, and Saul still hunting him with 3,000 men. David calculates that Philistia offers safety that Judah does not. The calculation is correct in its premises but reflects a faith that has momentarily lost its grip on the promises. Achish gives him Ziklag, and David uses it as a base for raids against Israel's enemies - Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites. He leaves no survivors who might report to Achish what he is actually doing. The moral descent from the heights of chapter 24 to the complexity of chapter 27 is real. God does not abandon David in this season - but the silence of divine communication during these months is itself instructive.

28.title: Saul and the Witch of Endor
28.text: <sup>15</sup>Then Samuel said to Saul, 'Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?' Saul answered, 'I am in great distress, for the Philistines are warring against me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, neither by prophets nor by dreams. Therefore I have summoned you to tell me what I shall do.' <sup>17</sup>'The LORD has done to you as he spoke by me, for the LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David.' (ESV)
28.overview:
Chapter 28 is the darkest chapter in 1 Samuel and one of the most theologically extraordinary in the entire Bible. Saul, facing a Philistine army and receiving no divine response — no dreams, no Urim, no prophets — resorts to the one thing he has personally outlawed: consulting a medium. He disguises himself, travels by night to Endor, and asks the woman to bring up Samuel. What happens next has puzzled commentators for millennia: Samuel actually appears, and the word he speaks is the final divine verdict on Saul's reign.

The chapter is structured around a devastating irony. Saul disguises himself to hide who he is from a medium — only to be recognized (through his request alone, v. 12) as the king. He has expelled the mediums and spiritists from the land as a matter of policy, and now he is one of their clients. The very thing he forbade, he now seeks. And the appearance of Samuel — whether the LORD permitted a genuine appearance or used the occasion for his own purposes — delivers the final word that the anointed prophet had first spoken in chapter 15: the kingdom is gone, and tomorrow Saul and his sons will be with Samuel in death.

sections.title: God's Silence and Saul's Desperation
sections.commentary:
The Philistine threat is real: a great army assembled at Shunem, with Israel encamped at Gilboa across the valley. Saul is afraid — the narrator twice notes his terror, using a word that suggests visceral dread. He inquires of the LORD by dreams, by Urim, by prophets — and receives nothing. The silence is not new; it has been building since chapter 15. The God who spoke daily to Samuel, who answered David's repeated inquiries through the ephod, has gone utterly silent for Saul. This is not merely the absence of guidance; it is judicial silence: the God whom Saul has repeatedly rejected has, with dreadful finality, withdrawn.

Saul's request to the medium — bring up Samuel for me — is the theological endpoint of his rejection of God's appointed channels. He expelled the mediums; he has no prophets he can trust (Samuel is dead); the Urim returns nothing. So he goes to the very source he destroyed. This is the grotesque logic of a life that has shut every legitimate door: when God's word through legitimate means is closed, the temptation is to seek it through illegitimate ones. But the illegitimate channels bring not guidance but judgment. The medium's terrified reaction when Samuel actually appears — she expected to perform a ritual, not encounter the actual dead — suggests that even she was unprepared for what happened.

sections.title: Samuel's Last Word
sections.commentary:
Samuel's appearance — whether literal or providentially arranged — is the most solemn moment in Saul's story. His opening question — Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up? — locates Samuel in the place of rest, the realm of the righteous dead, from which Saul has now disturbed him. And his message is not new: it is the repetition and confirmation of what he said in chapter 15, now brought to its final form. The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David. Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his fierce anger against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you this day.

The connection back to chapter 15 is explicit and deliberate: the sin that lost the kingdom — the failure to execute the Amalekites — is the reason for the military disaster about to happen. The chickens have come home to roost with terrible precision. And then the most chilling prediction in the OT: Moreover, the LORD will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. Tomorrow. He has less than twenty-four hours. Samuel in death delivers the verdict that Samuel in life delivered, with the same authority and the same theological precision. The word of God, even from the mouth of the dead, retains its power.

Saul's collapse — falling full length on the ground, refusing food — is the response of a man at the absolute end of himself. The woman and his servants finally persuade him to eat, and he rises and goes away in the night. There is no prayer, no repentance, no desperate cry to God. There is only the darkness of Endor and the long road to Gilboa. Alistair Begg writes that Saul's final night is the portrait of a man who has been given every opportunity to repent and has squandered them all — and who now faces, with full clarity, the consequence. The mercy he refused to receive is no longer on offer. Tomorrow he will be with Samuel.

28.theology: The Silence of God as Judgment. The three channels of divine communication that Saul tries — dreams, Urim, prophets — are the legitimate means God established for his people to hear his voice. Their complete silence is not divine absence but divine judgment: the God who answered Samuel every time he called now answers Saul not at all. This is the judicial hardening that began in chapter 13 and has been building ever since. The OT knows this terror and names it (Amos 8:11–12; Micah 3:7); the NT knows it too (Matt. 7:22–23). The most fearful possibility is not that God says no to our prayers but that he says nothing at all.
28.examples:
Then: The witch of Endor is never condemned in this chapter — she acts with compassion toward Saul, feeding him and urging him to eat. The moral complexity of the chapter extends even to her: she is practicing something forbidden, and yet she is more humane to Saul than anyone else in his life at this point.

Now: The chapter warns every generation about the temptation to seek supernatural guidance outside the channels God has established. When legitimate means seem silent — when prayer seems unanswered, when Scripture seems dark, when godly counsel is unavailable — the temptation is always to reach for the illegitimate. Saul's example says: do not. The silence of God may be a season, not a permanent withdrawal; the illegitimate channel brings only judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-25 - Saul and the Witch of Endor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines mobilize for war against Israel. Saul, terrified, inquires of the LORD and gets no answer - no dreams, no Urim, no prophets. In desperation he seeks a medium at Endor, disguised. The woman raises Samuel, who delivers a final devastating word: tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between Saul's silent God and David's responsive God is the theological climax of the Saul narrative. Saul cannot hear from God because he has cut himself off from God through persistent disobedience. The message Samuel brings is unambiguous: God has torn the kingdom from you; the LORD will give Israel into the hands of the Philistines; tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. MacArthur notes that Samuel's message from beyond death is not comfort but verdict: Saul's condemnation is sealed.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observes that the witch's evident terror at the appearance of Samuel suggests that what she expected and what actually appeared were very different things. She was accustomed to demonic counterfeits; what she got was the real prophet. God permits the real Samuel to appear to deliver the final verdict on Saul.

verseByVerse.quote: When Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets. Then Saul said to his servants, Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her.
verseByVerse.commentary: The silence of God is the most terrible experience in the chapter. Saul tries everything legitimate: dreams, Urim, prophets. Nothing. God has nothing to say to him. The man who once had the Spirit rushing on him now consults a medium - an act his own law forbids. Samuel's appearance to Saul is his last appearance in the book, and it is a verdict: Why do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy? Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. Saul collapses. The woman's compassion in feeding him before he goes is a small human grace at the edge of catastrophe.

29.title: David Sent Away from the Battle
29.text: <sup>6</sup>Then Achish called David and said to him, 'As the LORD lives, you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me in the campaign. For I have found nothing wrong in you from the day of your coming to me to this day. Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you. <sup>9</sup>...but the commanders have said, He shall not go up with us to the battle. Now then rise early in the morning with the servants of your lord who came with you.' (ESV)
29.overview:
Chapter 29 is a chapter of divine rescue through human suspicion. David is marching with the Philistine army to fight Israel — the worst possible position for the future king of Israel to be in — when the Philistine commanders notice his presence and demand his removal. Achish is satisfied with David's loyalty, but the Philistine lords are not: they remember Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands, and they are not willing to have a potential traitor at their backs in battle. David is sent back to Ziklag.

The chapter is an elegant piece of providential rescue. David has maneuvered himself into an impossible situation through the faithless chapter-27 decision to take refuge in Philistia. He cannot refuse to march with the Philistines without destroying his cover story; he cannot march with them against Israel without betraying his people. God resolves the dilemma without requiring David to make the impossible choice: the Philistine commanders make the choice for him. David is sent away — graciously, by his host — and returns to find a different disaster waiting at Ziklag.

sections.title: The Commanders' Suspicion
sections.commentary:
The Philistine commanders' objection to David is entirely reasonable from a military standpoint: What are these Hebrews doing here? They remember the song — Saul's thousands, David's ten thousands — and they are not confident that a man with that kind of following in Israel will remain loyal to Philistia when he sees Israelite soldiers dying in battle. Their concern is legitimate; David's true loyalties are exactly what they suspect.

Achish's defense of David is generous and based on sixteen months of observed behavior: you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me in the campaign. For I have found nothing wrong in you from the day of your coming to me to this day. He has been deceived perfectly. David has been exactly what Achish believed him to be — a loyal client — because David was careful to ensure that no evidence of his actual raids reached Achish's ears. The deception has been complete and is now about to be providentially interrupted.

sections.title: God's Rescue Through Human Suspicion
sections.commentary:
Achish's dismissal of David is gracious and almost apologetic: As the LORD lives — the Philistine king invoking the God of Israel in his oath, which is itself a remarkable detail — you have been honest, and to me it seems right. He sends David away not because of any failure on David's part but because the political realities of the alliance require it. And David's response — what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king? — is either a masterful piece of continued deception or a genuinely ambiguous speech that works on two levels: it protests loyalty to Achish while being entirely true from David's perspective, since his real lord is the LORD of Israel whose enemies include the Philistines.

R. C. Sproul writes that God often rescues his people from the consequences of their faithless decisions through the most unexpected means — in this case, through the suspicion of pagan military commanders. David did not deserve to be rescued from the position he had put himself in; he was there through lack of faith. But God's commitment to his anointed is not contingent on the anointed's faithfulness at every moment. The rescue is gracious; its instrument is human suspicion; its purpose is to bring David back to Ziklag in time for the disaster that will teach him to strengthen himself in God rather than in his own schemes.

29.theology: Providence Through the Unlikely Instrument. Chapter 29 belongs to the category of chapters where God's sovereignty works most visibly through human instruments that have no intention of serving divine purposes. The Philistine commanders are not trying to rescue David from a moral dilemma; they are protecting their military flank. Yet God uses their suspicion to extract his anointed from an impossible situation. This is the grammar of Romans 8:28 applied to a specific moment: God works all things together for good for those who love him — including the military politics of pagan commanders and the suspicious memories of a song about ten thousands.
29.examples:
Then: David returns to Ziklag to find it burned and his people taken captive (ch. 30). The rescue from one crisis delivers him directly into another. This is frequently how God works: the deliverance from one impossible situation is not the end of the story but the means by which we arrive at the more important impossible situation where the deeper lesson is to be learned.

Now: The chapter encourages the believer who has maneuvered themselves into an impossible situation to watch for God's unexpected rescue, which may come through the most unlikely instruments. It does not excuse the faithless decisions that created the situation — the cost of chapter 27 is still coming in chapter 30 — but it does testify that God's commitment to his people outlasts their failures.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 - David Sent Away from the Battle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistine commanders object to David's presence in the army, fearing he might defect to Saul in battle. Achish reluctantly sends him home to Ziklag.
verseByVerse.theology: God's providential care for David is visible in the Philistine commanders' suspicion. David has been maneuvered into a position where he might be forced to fight against Israel. The Philistine commanders' distrust solves the problem David's own deception created. Kidner notes that this is the pattern of providence throughout the David narrative: God protects his servant through the working of human motivations - suspicion, jealousy, admiration, fear - to accomplish his purposes.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that David's protest at being sent away may be genuine or tactical. Either way, he goes home to Ziklag - arriving at exactly the right moment to face the crisis of chapter 30.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the commanders of the Philistines said, What are these Hebrews doing here? And Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, Is not this David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel, who has been with me now for days and years, and since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him to this day?
verseByVerse.commentary: Achish's defense of David is ironic: since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him - he trusts David completely, and David has been systematically deceiving him for sixteen months. The Philistine commanders are more perceptive than their king: this man fought for Israel; in the heat of battle he might turn against us. Their suspicion is theologically correct even though motivated by self-interest. Achish delivers the news to David with genuine regret, and David departs back toward Ziklag and the crisis that awaits him there.

30.title: David Strengthened Himself in the LORD His God
30.text: <sup>6</sup>And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God. <sup>8</sup>And David inquired of the LORD, 'Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them?' He answered him, 'Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue.' (ESV)
30.overview:
Chapter 30 is the crucible chapter of the David narrative. He returns from the Philistine dismissal to find Ziklag burned to the ground and his people — wives, sons, daughters — taken captive by Amalekite raiders. His men weep until they have no more strength to weep, and then they blame David and speak of stoning him. He is at his lowest point since the whole fugitive adventure began: exhausted, bereaved, politically isolated, and now facing a mutiny. And in that moment, the narrator places the single most important statement about David in the entire book: David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.

The chapter is a masterclass in how the man after God's own heart navigates absolute crisis. He does not collapse; he does not retaliate against the men who threaten to stone him; he does not make a military decision without divine guidance. He strengthens himself in God, he inquires of the LORD through the ephod Abiathar brought from Nob, he receives the divine directive to pursue, and he acts decisively on it. The rescue is complete: every captive is recovered, all the spoil is taken, and David even establishes a principle of equitable distribution — the spoil belongs equally to those who fought and those who guarded the equipment (vv. 24–25) — that becomes statute in Israel.

sections.title: The Disaster at Ziklag
sections.commentary:
The Amalekite raid on Ziklag while David was away with the Philistines is, from a human perspective, a catastrophic oversight. The city was undefended; the enemy struck at the softest target. The women and children — including David's own two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail — are all taken. There is no massacre; the Amalekites took captives for ransom or slavery. But the community's grief is total: they weep until they have no strength, which in the ancient world's idiom means weeping until physical exhaustion silences the voice.

The threat of stoning David is not mere frustration — it is a formal accusation of failed leadership, the community holding its captain responsible for the disaster that happened on his watch. And David is responsible: his decision to live in Ziklag as Achish's vassal created the vulnerability; his absence with the Philistine army created the opportunity. The disaster is the downstream consequence of the faithless chapter-27 decision. David cannot deny responsibility; what he can do is refuse to let the disaster become final.

The description of his response — David was greatly distressed — acknowledges the genuine weight of the moment. This is not a man who is above grief or fear. He is in exactly the kind of extremity that breaks lesser people. And then the extraordinary pivot: But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God. Alistair Begg writes that this is the decisive spiritual competence of the man after God's own heart: the ability, in absolute extremity, to self-preach.
