To gather the scattered evidence of past divine faithfulness, apply it to the present crisis, and draw strength not from circumstances but from the character of God.

sections.title: Inquiring of God: The Pattern Restored
sections.commentary:
David's first act after strengthening himself in God is to call Abiathar: Bring me the ephod. He does not act on instinct, does not make a military decision from experience, does not trust his own judgment about whether pursuit will succeed. He inquires of the LORD: Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them? The answer is unambiguous and comprehensive: Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue. God does not say go and see what happens; he gives a guarantee. The word David receives is a promise, not a probability.

The return to the pattern of chapter 23 — asking God, receiving a clear answer, acting on it — marks the theological rehabilitation that the Ziklag disaster has accomplished. David was strengthened in God rather than in himself (chapter 27) by the severity of the loss. The disaster was not arbitrary; it was formative. The man who said to himself in chapter 27, I shall now perish by the hand of Saul — reasoning from circumstances without inquiring of God — now asks God before he takes a single step. The Ziklag catastrophe has returned David to his theological foundation: the LORD who answers through the ephod, the LORD whose word is more reliable than any military calculation.

sections.title: The Recovery and the Principle of Equity
sections.commentary:
The recovery of every captive is precisely what God promised. The Amalekites, celebrating and feasting and spreading across the land, are hit before dawn and routed through the following day. Only four hundred escape on camels. Every person taken from Ziklag is recovered; the spoil from their other raids is captured additionally. The completeness of the recovery is emphasized because it is the fulfillment of the specific divine promise: you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue. God's word, when acted upon, does exactly what it says.

David's establishment of the equity principle — the spoil is shared equally between those who fought and those who were too exhausted to cross the brook and stayed behind guarding the equipment — is an act of covenantal justice that becomes lasting statute (v. 25). It reflects the same theological principle that runs through his whole story: David does not exploit the desperate for personal advantage; he builds his kingdom on justice and covenant faithfulness. The same David who refused to take Saul's life when he had the power establishes a rule that refuses to take advantage of the weaker members of his own company. The man after God's own heart governs by the character of the God whose heart he mirrors.

30.theology: Self-Counsel in the Crisis. The phrase David strengthened himself in the LORD his God is the great practical principle of the David narrative. In Psalm 42–43, David models the same technique in poetic form: Why are you cast down, O my soul? And why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God. He is preaching to himself, arguing against his own despair with the evidence of God's character and faithfulness. This is not positive thinking; it is applied theology: taking what you know to be true about God and deliberately applying it to the situation in which you find yourself. Every believer needs this capacity, because every believer will face a Ziklag — a moment when all visible supports collapse and only the knowledge of God remains.
30.examples:
Then: The two hundred men who were too exhausted to cross the Besor brook are treated by David with generosity rather than contempt — they receive an equal share of the spoil. The weak are not abandoned; the stragglers are included. This is both good leadership and a glimpse of the kingdom to come, where the last shall be first and the weakest shall receive the same wage as the strongest (Matt. 20:9–16).

Now: The chapter's central gift to the church is the practice of self-counsel: when all external supports are stripped away — when the threat is real, the loss is total, and the people who should support you are talking about stoning you — strengthen yourself in the LORD your God. Not in your circumstances, not in your record, not in human approval, but in the character and promises of the God who called you and who does not abandon his anointed in their darkest hour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-31 - David Strengthened Himself in the LORD His God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David arrives at Ziklag to find it burned and all the women and children taken by Amalekite raiders. His men weep until they have no strength to weep; then they blame David and speak of stoning him. David strengthens himself in the LORD his God. He pursues and recovers everything.
verseByVerse.theology: The verse David strengthened himself in the LORD his God (v.6) is the theological hinge of the chapter. He is at absolute bottom: his city burned, his family taken, his men ready to stone him. There is no human resource left. He goes to God. He inquires of the LORD; he pursues; he recovers everything - nothing was missing, whether small or great, sons or daughters, spoil or anything that had been taken (v.19). This is the theology of the Psalms enacted: the poor man cried, and the LORD heard him.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul observes that the equitable distribution of the recovered spoil - David insisting that those who guarded the baggage share equally with those who fought - becomes a statute in Israel. A moment of crisis produces a policy of justice. Character shows most clearly under pressure.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God. And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, Bring me the ephod. So Abiathar brought the ephod to David. And David inquired of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The scene at the ruins of Ziklag is one of the most desperate in David's life. The city is ash; his two wives are among the captives; his men are talking about stoning their commander. Everything has gone wrong. And then: David strengthened himself in the LORD his God. He turns to the LORD before he acts. He inquires through the ephod: should I pursue? Will I overtake them? Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue. God speaks. David acts. The abandoned Egyptian slave who leads them to the Amalekite camp is a gift of providence wrapped in ordinary humanity. David recovers everything. His policy of equal distribution is grounded in covenant justice: all Israel shares in what God has given to his servant.

31.title: The Death of Saul
31.text: <sup>4</sup>Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, 'Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me.' But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. <sup>13</sup>And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fasted seven days. (ESV)
31.overview:
First Samuel ends where it was always heading: on Mount Gilboa, on a lost battlefield, with the death of three of Saul's sons and the mortal wounding of the king himself. The chapter is spare and swift — twelve verses for the end of a forty-year reign. Saul, mortally wounded by Philistine archers, falls on his own sword rather than face torture and mockery at Philistine hands. His body is hung on the wall of Beth-shan. The men of Jabesh-gilead — whose rescue was Saul's first great act as king (chapter 11) — walk all night to retrieve his body and his sons' bodies, burn them, and bury their bones under a tree. They fast seven days.

The chapter does not moralize. It does not deliver a final verdict on Saul; it simply shows what happens. The contrast with the opening chapters is total: Israel at the beginning of 1 Samuel was crying for a king; Israel at the end has its king dead on a mountain, his armor in a Philistine temple. The word of chapter 8 has been fulfilled: you cried for a king; the king's demands will cost you everything. And yet the book does not end in despair — it ends with the loyalty of Jabesh-gilead, with men who remembered Saul's one great act of faithfulness and honored him in death even as he had failed in life. The men of Jabesh-gilead are the grace note at the end of a tragedy.

sections.title: The Battle of Gilboa
sections.commentary:
The Philistines fight against Israel and prevail. Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua — Saul's sons — are killed. The word has come true. At the Endor encounter, Samuel said: tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. It is tomorrow. Jonathan, the man who was more fit to be king than his father, dies on the same mountain as his father. His death is one of the most heartbreaking single facts in the entire book: the man who was most faithful, most discerning, most loving of God's purposes, dies in his father's catastrophe. The injustice of it is the kind that the book of Job and the Psalms know: the righteous suffer with the wicked, not because they are equally guilty but because they live in a world where sin's consequences are not always perfectly individuated.

Saul's wound from Philistine archers is mortal but not immediately fatal. He asks his armor-bearer to kill him; the man refuses out of fear. Saul takes his own sword and falls on it. His death is suicide — the only suicide of a named character in the OT — and it is the final act of a man who has spent his life seeking to control outcomes through his own will rather than God's, and who in death makes the same choice: taking the manner of his end into his own hands rather than submitting it to God. The armor-bearer, seeing the king dead, falls on his own sword too. R. C. Sproul observes that Saul's suicide is the logical conclusion of a life of self-determination: the man who could not submit to God's command in life cannot submit to God's timing in death.

sections.title: The Philistines Celebrate; Jabesh-gilead Honors
sections.commentary:
The Philistine celebration is comprehensive and deliberately humiliating: Saul's armor goes to the temple of Ashtaroth; his body is fastened to the wall of Beth-shan. The armor that should have protected him becomes an offering to the gods that defeated him; his corpse is displayed as a trophy. The man who wanted to be king like all the nations dies as a trophy of the nations' gods. The irony is theological: Israel's demand for a king 'like all the nations' produced a king whose death was celebrated by those nations as evidence of their gods' superiority.

But the final word belongs not to the Philistines but to the men of Jabesh-gilead. They walk all night — the phrase suggests a forced march, speed and determination — retrieve the bodies from the wall of Beth-shan, bring them home, burn them (possibly to prevent further desecration), bury the bones under a tamarisk tree, and fast seven days. The tamarisk tree echoes Saul's first appearance as king, when he sat under a tamarisk at Gibeah (22:6); the ending rhymes with the beginning. And the fast of seven days honors a king who did not deserve to be honored on any terms except this one: he was the LORD's anointed, and the men of Jabesh-gilead remembered what that meant.

Alistair Begg writes that the burial at Jabesh-gilead is both an act of covenant loyalty and a whisper of hope: even in the worst failure of a human king, the covenant community does not abandon the covenant forms. They bury their dead; they mourn; they maintain the bonds of loyalty that Israel was supposed to embody. And their act will be remembered: David, when he becomes king, will specifically honor the men of Jabesh-gilead for this loyalty (2 Sam. 2:4–7), and their bones — and Saul's — will eventually be brought to the ancestral tomb of Kish (2 Sam. 21:12–14). The story of Saul ends not with the Philistines' triumph but with human faithfulness, and it ends pointing toward the king who will come after — the one who was being anointed at Bethlehem while Saul was still reigning at Gibeah, the one who is already waiting at Ziklag to receive the news that will open the throne.

sections.title: The End of an Era and the Promise of What Follows
sections.commentary:
First Samuel ends with no resolution, no coronation, no triumph. David is in Ziklag, mourning the dead of Ziklag (chapter 30), about to receive news of Saul's death that will open the second book of Samuel and the coronation at Hebron. The end of 1 Samuel is deliberately open: the death of the rejected king creates the vacancy; the anointed king awaits. The reader who knows the story knows what comes next — David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam. 1:17–27), the coronation, the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, the covenant of the everlasting throne (2 Sam. 7). All of it is being born from the grief of Gilboa.

The theological conclusion of 1 Samuel is not the triumph of David but the confirmation of God's word. Everything the man of God said in chapter 2, everything Samuel said in chapters 12–15, everything the Spirit moved Hannah to sing in chapter 2 — all of it has come to pass. The anointed-one language of Hannah's song, the faithful-priest prophecy, the man-after-God's-own-heart election, the warning about what human kingship would cost — all fulfilled. And the final Messianic word of the book, implicit in every scene of David's story from the cave of Adullam to the cave at En-gedi to the strengthening at Ziklag, is this: there is one coming who will be all that David was and none of what Saul was; who will fight on behalf of his paralyzed people and win; who will not grasp the kingdom by force but receive it through suffering; whose Spirit will never depart; and in whom the horn of the anointed will be exalted forever. Hannah sang it at the beginning: He will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed. First Samuel has been one long, agonizing, glorious demonstration of what that looks like in real human history — and an irresistible pointer toward the one in whom it is finally, perfectly, eternally true.

31.theology:
The Tragedy of Saul and the Grace of God. Saul's death is the conclusion of one of Scripture's most complex and humanly sympathetic character studies. He was genuinely gifted, genuinely anointed, and genuinely destroyed by the choices he made over decades of self-reliant, fear-driven, self-justifying leadership. His tragedy is not that he was a monster but that he was a man who had everything required for genuine faithfulness and consistently chose something else. Sinclair Ferguson writes that Saul is the cautionary tale for every person who has received genuine gifts of the Spirit, genuine anointing for a task, and genuine opportunity — and who has spent those gifts on self-promotion rather than God's glory. The gifts were real; the outcome was real; the distance between them is the measure of what disobedience costs.

The LORD Looks on the Heart — Final Statement. The contrast between Saul and David, which is the organizing principle of the entire second half of 1 Samuel, ultimately rests on the principle announced in 16:7: the LORD looks on the heart. Saul had the appearance, the height, the early humility — and the heart that was oriented toward the approval of men and the maintenance of his own position. David had the ruddy face, the shepherd's background, the overwhelming obstacles — and the heart that, however imperfectly, sought God, returned to God, strengthened itself in God, and sang to God from every valley and every mountain. The LORD looked on the heart, and the Lord's anointed — the horn of God's salvation — took the throne, not because David deserved it but because God had chosen him, and God's choices are always larger than we can see from the outside of a cave at En-gedi or a hillside at Bethlehem.
31.examples:
Then: The men of Jabesh-gilead walked all night to honor a failed king because he was the LORD's anointed. Their loyalty is the last grace note of a book full of faithless choices and faithful interventions — a reminder that covenant community endures even when covenant leadership fails.

Now: First Samuel ends as it began: with ordinary human beings, in ordinary human circumstances, caught up in the extraordinary purposes of the living God. Hannah prayed at Shiloh; Saul died at Gilboa; David waited at Ziklag; and through all of it, the horn of the anointed was being exalted — slowly, painfully, surely — toward the day when the Son of David would ride into Jerusalem on a donkey and be crowned on a cross and rise from a garden tomb to take the throne that no Saul could hold and no David could keep, but only the one whose kingdom shall have no end.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The battle at Jezreel goes catastrophically for Israel. Jonathan and his brothers are killed. Saul is critically wounded by archers. He falls on his own sword rather than be captured. The Philistines display his body. The men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve and bury the bodies.
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's death is the fulfillment of Samuel's verdict at Endor and the logical outcome of a life lived in diminishing obedience to God. The narrative does not gloat. Saul's final act - refusing to be abused by uncircumcised Philistines and taking his own life - has a kind of terrible dignity. Sproul notes that the arc of Saul's story is the Old Testament's most sustained meditation on the tragedy of a life that begins with divine gifting and ends in self-destruction through disobedience.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur observes that the men of Jabesh-gilead's act of devotion to Saul's body is one of the most moving details in the book. They fasted seven days for him. Whatever Saul became at the end, he had once been their deliverer, and they honored that memory. This is the complexity of human moral history.

verseByVerse.quote: The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers. Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me. But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.
verseByVerse.commentary: The battle of Jezreel brings the narrative of Saul to its close. Three of his sons die beside him - Jonathan, Abinadab, Malchishua - including Jonathan, the one man in this story who never failed in loyalty either to his father or to his covenant friend. Saul's wounded body is found by the Philistines who cut off his head and display his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth. The man who was anointed to deliver Israel from the Philistines dies with his head mounted on a Philistine wall. The men of Jabesh-gilead travel through the night to retrieve his body, bury the bones under the tamarisk tree, and fast seven days. It is the most dignified ending the story allows. David will hear the news in 2 Samuel 1, and he will weep.
